item.title: [Empire Sports Media] Two home runs in six days give the Yankees an Austin Wells lift
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: The Yankees were down four runs when Austin Wells came up in the sixth inning Thursday. His solo homer did not erase the deficit, but it got New York on the board. item.content:encoded:
The Yankees were down four runs when Austin Wells came up in the sixth inning Thursday. His solo homer did not erase the deficit, but it got New York on the board. Two innings later, the Yankees had a 6-4 win over the Rays.
Wells finished 1-for-2 with a walk, two runs and a stolen base. It was his 14th home run of the season and his second since September 19. The Yankees have bigger bats, obviously. They still need something from the bottom of the order when a playoff starter handles the middle of it.
Wells is giving the Yankees more than one kind of at-bat
I liked the walk almost as much as the homer. Wells reached base twice and scored both times. The stolen base was another bit of pressure on Tampa Bay in a game that looked lost after five innings. New York got its decisive swing from George Lombard Jr., but Wells started the rally before the scoreboard made it interesting.
That matters because his job behind the plate is secure; his offensive production is the swing variable. A catcher hitting a homer once every few days changes the bottom third of a lineup. A catcher who can also take a walk gives the hitters behind him a chance to keep an inning alive.
October will test the bottom of the order
Two homers in six days do not guarantee a hot postseason. Wells has had cold stretches, and Thursday’s hit was his only one of the night. But he has picked up the bat at a useful time. With Ben Rice supplying middle-order power, the Yankees do not need Wells to carry the offense. They need him to make the opposing pitcher work and punish the occasional mistake. He did both Thursday.
More about:New York Yankees

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] MLB insider strongly cautions Yankees' Aaron Judge to change his rehab strategy after latest injury
item.dc:creator: Matthew Swigonski
item.description: If you’re an athlete, the last thing you ever want to do is miss playing time because of an injury. Not only does it hurt physically, but it’s a bit of an emotional wound to feel like you could be letting your team down. Even for stars like Aaron Judge, the frustration is very real. item.content:encoded:
If you’re an athlete, the last thing you ever want to do is miss playing time because of an injury. Not only does it hurt physically, but it’s a bit of an emotional wound to feel like you could be letting your team down. Even for stars like Aaron Judge, the frustration is very real.
But according to one MLB insider, the star’s preferred rehab strategy likely cost the New York Yankees dearly. In fact, it cost them a chance to have their best player during their Wild Card Series matchup against the Boston Red Sox.
While speaking on the The Baseball Insiders podcast, FanSided’s Robert Murray offered up his take on what led to Judge suffering a calf strain just days after returning to the Yankees lineup. And it’s something so simple that it may frustrate fans.
According to Murray, Judge will have to “change up his strategy” when it comes to returning from injury. He noted that the Yankees star has been resistant to rehab assignments throughout his career. That preference could have led to some unintended consequences this season.
“And I would definitely imagine that not having a rehab assignment and working his way back up is what contributed to this injury ultimately end up happening,” Murray said of Judge’s most recent injury setback.
Now that the Yankees are without their best player once again this season, it is probably time to change things up.
How can the Yankees best manage Aaron Judge's injury rehab process moving forward?
You could argue that a player could get injured just as easily playing in a minor league rehab assignment as they could in the majors. That might be true to a certain extent. But rehab assignments in minor league parks simply lack the same energy as a big league game.
There’s less of an incentive to stretch a single into a double or dive for a bloop single in front of you. For a player like Judge who always gives it his all, learning how to dial it down in the minor leagues could go a long way in preserving himself in the majors. Rehab assignments are thought of as essential to the ramp-up process for a reason. They help get a recovering body ready for the spotlight.
In his 11-year big league career, Judge has been placed on the IL nearly a dozen times. However, he’s only been on one rehab assignment during that time. In June 2019, the Yankees outfielder played five games with Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre before rejoining the team. He remained healthy that season until missing a game in September due to a sore shoulder.
Was that rehab assignment solely responsible for his long-term health? Probably not. But it may have helped Judge get back in the swing of things more effectively. Despite going 0-10 in his first three games back from that rehab assignment, he then went 8-14 over his next four games, including two home runs.
After missing three entire months this season, Judge jumped straight into the Yankees lineup and struggled through seven games. Judge collected just four hits in his 23 at-bats after returning from his IL stint. There was certainly a decent amount of rust for Judge to shake off from his prolonged layoff.
Although he struck out in more than half of those at-bats, there were also some promising signs that showed that he was starting to find his rhythm at the plate again. He smacked a three-run home run off of reliever A.J. Minter during the Yankees 8-3 win over the Minnesota Twins on September 14. It looked like he could potentially be gearing up for a major hot streak exactly when the Yankees could really use the help.
That hot streak obviously never happened, and Judge may not be able to return to the Yankees in the postseason.
As we’ve seen with the Los Angeles Dodgers and their lackluster approach to Shohei Ohtani’s injury, players can sometimes be unreliable when it comes to reporting discomfort or adhering to the best rehab practices. Ball players want to play ball. Everyone can understand that. But taking a conservative approach to injuries for players that have long histories with the IL could actually allow them to play when it matters the most. Judge wanted to rejoin the Yankees as quickly as possible, but it likely led to him missing even more games. Now the team’s offense may suffer for it.
They may not always like it, but players like Judge should be required to go on a rehab assignment moving forward. If they can't slowly ramp up their level of play, they may jump straight back into another injury.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Nor’easter forces Yankees game, CC Sabathia’s number retirement to be rescheduled in Friday doubleheader
item.dc:creator: Peter Sblendorio
item.description: The mighty nor’easter that’s expected to rock the East Coast all the weekend threw a curveball to the Yankees, whose game on Saturday night was preemptively rescheduled for Friday as part of a single-admission doubleheader. Although the Yankees’ final series of the regular season is inconsequential to the standings — they are locked into the American League’s No. 4 seed — the development affected fans who had planned to attend Saturday’s game against the Baltimore Orioles for CC Sabathia’s numbe
item.content:encoded:
The mighty nor’easter that’s expected to rock the East Coast all the weekend threw a curveball to the Yankees, whose game on Saturday night was preemptively rescheduled for Friday as part of a single-admission doubleheader.
Although the Yankees’ final series of the regular season is inconsequential to the standings — they are locked into the American League’s No. 4 seed — the development affected fans who had planned to attend Saturday’s game against the Baltimore Orioles for CC Sabathia’s number retirement ceremony.
The ceremony was rescheduled for Friday before the Yankees and Orioles began their first game of the day at 4:05 p.m. EDT.
Derek Jeter, Andy Pettitte, Dellin Betances and Chris Young were among the alumni attending the No. 52 retirement and Monument Park plaque unveiling at Yankee Stadium, where Sabathia called home for 11 of his 19 MLB seasons.
Sabathia — a culture-setting leader and ace who helped the Yankees win the 2009 World Series — entered the National Baseball Hall of Fame as a first-ballot inductee last year with a Yankees hat on his plaque.
Only tickets dated for Sept. 25 were eligible for Friday’s doubleheader. Tickets dated for Sept. 26 can be exchanged for a “similar regular season game at Yankee Stadium,” the Yankees announced.
As originally planned, the first 18,000 ticketed guests to arrive at the stadium Friday would receive a bobblehead depicting Knicks star Josh Hart in a Yankees jersey. Hart is the great-nephew of former Yankees catcher Elston Howard, whose No. 32 is retired by the team.
Officials warned of heavy rainfall, sustained winds of 25-35 mph and the potential of coastal flooding in New York, with the worst of it expected to occur from Saturday evening into Sunday afternoon.
The Yankees’ regular season finale remains scheduled for Sunday afternoon.
“I don’t worry about things out of my hands,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said after Thursday night’s 6-4 win against the Tampa Bay Rays. “Saturday’s out of the question. We’ll see what Sunday brings.”
Neither the Yankees nor Orioles have anything left to play for in terms of game results, though canceling Sunday’s game — and thus giving the Yankees a weekend of rest — could provide an inequitable advantage going into the playoffs.
The Yankees are set to begin their Wild Card series in the Bronx on Tuesday night, when the weather looks much clearer.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will begin a series against the Baltimore Orioles on Friday afternoon with a doubleheader.
Before the first game, the Yankees will retire legendary pitcher CC Sabathia’s number after he spent 11 seasons with the organization from 2009 to 2019. Sabathia made three All-Star teams and posted a 134-88 record with a 3.81 ERA during his Yankees tenure.
Derek Jeter Featured in Yankees’ Announcement
On Friday morning, the Yankees shared some important details about the pregame ceremony surrounding Sabathia’s jersey retirement, which will also feature MLB and Yankees legend Derek Jeter.
They revealed that Jeter will be in attendance alongside Andy Pettitte, Dellin Betances, and Chris Young.
“Today’s CC Sabathia Ceremony will begin at 3:15 p.m. Derek Jeter, Andy Pettitte, Dellin Betances, and Chris Young are set to join @CC_Sabathia as we honor his career and legacy,” the Yankees posted on X.
“All @yankeestadium gates will open to fans at 2:30 p.m., at which time distribution will begin for the September 25 scheduled promotional item (Josh Hart Yankees Bobblehead presented by Delta Air Lines for the first 18,000 guests in attendance).”
Today’s CC Sabathia Ceremony will begin at 3:15 pm. Derek Jeter, Andy Pettitte, Dellin Betances, and Chris Young are set to join @CC_Sabathia as we honor his career and legacy.
All @yankeestadium gates will open to fans at 2:30 pm, at which time distribution will begin for the… pic.twitter.com/Q8m2qGcWx8
— New York Yankees (@Yankees) September 25, 2026
How Long Were Jeter and Sabathia Teammates?
Jeter has long been a staple of the Yankees franchise after everything he accomplished during his illustrious 20-year career with the organization.
He made his MLB debut in 1995, and 14 years later, he became teammates with Sabathia, who joined the Yankees after already spending nine years in the league.
The two spent six seasons together as teammates from 2009 until Jeter retired after the 2014 season. They won a World Series together in 2009, which was Sabathia’s first and Jeter’s fifth.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees’ Anthony Volpe decision got tougher after one huge swing
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson

item.content:encoded:
For six innings Thursday, the Yankees trailed Tampa Bay 4-0. By the end of the eighth, George Lombard Jr. had turned the game around with a two-run homer. New York won 6-4, and the rookie finished 2-for-4 with a double, a homer and three RBI.
The comeback was fun. The shortstop question it leaves behind is less comfortable. Lombard also drove in a run with a seventh-inning double, then hit the decisive ball an inning later. He is giving the Yankees useful at-bats at the exact point they have to think about their October roster.
Anthony Volpe played Thursday and scored during the seventh-inning rally, but went 0-for-3 with a walk. One game does not settle his place on the roster. Lombard's growing body of work does make it harder to treat shortstop as a job Volpe gets back automatically.
Yankees can't ignore the at-bats Lombard is giving them
Lombard's homer was his seventh of the season. The number alone is not the argument for him. It is the way he has handled meaningful plate appearances while playing shortstop every day. In Thursday's win, he produced the first extra-base hit of the comeback and the last one that mattered.
The postseason roster discussion has included both Lombard and Volpe, but the club has not announced its choice. I would keep Lombard at shortstop if the Yankees opened a playoff series tomorrow. I am judging their current play, not closing the door on Volpe's future here.
0What do you think?Post a comment.
A good problem with a real consequence
The Yankees have enough infield options to find Volpe playing time if they want it. The harder decision is who starts at shortstop in a close playoff game. Lombard gave them another answer Thursday, and Rice's recent power surge has made this lineup look deeper than it did a month ago. There is no need to decide the entire October card today. Lombard has earned the chance to keep making that decision difficult.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] Yankees-Pirates David Bednar trade is evening out amid Rafael Flores Jr. breakout
item.dc:creator: Matthew Swigonski

item.content:encoded:
When the New York Yankees looked to shore up their bullpen last season, GM Brian Cashman knew that it wouldn’t come cheaply. The Yankees were ready to part ways with talented prospects if it meant a better chance at improving the ball club, and it has mostly paid off. After they made a deal with the Pittsburgh Pirates for pitcher David Bednar, some critics actually thought that the Yankees got away with highway robbery. But as it turns out, that trade was a win-win for both sides. And that's mainly because of Rafael Flores Jr.
Despite missing out on the playoffs in 2026, the Pittsburgh Pirates have had one of their best seasons in years. They even have an opportunity to finish over the .500 mark for the first time since the 2018 season. That success has largely been fueled by offensive breakout seasons from players like Flores Jr.
The young catcher has put the league on notice with an impressive stretch to close out the season. After hitting just four home runs in 65 games for Triple-A Indianapolis, Flores Jr. has gone on an absolute tear for the Pirates. In 43 games in the big leagues, he's launched 10 bombs and driven in 22 runs. His .910 OPS for the Buccos is also more than 200 points higher than his season mark in the minors.
For a Yankees club that has been severely lacking offensive production from the catcher position, it certainly stings to see yet another former player catch fire for another team. Similar to the season that Carlos Narváez had for the Boston Red Sox in 2024, Flores Jr. may be giving the Yankees a bit of seller's remorse. We will have to wait and see if Flores Jr. will be able to keep up his hot bat next season, but as of now, it appears that the Bednar trade has become about as even as it gets.
The Yankees needed David Bednar at any cost
Seeing Flores Jr. flourish in Pittsburgh is like seeing an ex become a millionaire overnight. You can't help but feel a little jealous at the type of season he's had while Austin Wells and Ali Sánchez struggle to supply any production at the plate. In a third of the games played, Flores Jr. has all but matched the fWAR of both Wells and Sánchez combined in 2026. The former highly-rated Yankees prospect is swiftly matching the hype.
Regardless of the price that they paid, Bednar has been an amazing pickup for the Yankees. In a season and a half, he’s collected 44 saves and his presence has really helped to stabilize the back end of the bullpen. His ability to routinely collect more than three outs in any game adds a level of versatility that eludes even some of the most elite closers.
In his 83 appearances for the Yankees over the last two seasons, Bednar boasts an ERA+ of 170 and a very respectable 1.011 WHIP. While he can sometimes flirt with danger and make ball games interesting, he has been as close to a sure thing to pick up a save as the Yankees have had in years.
Although his 1.9 fWAR doesn’t quite rank him among some of the 10 best relievers in baseball, the value he has brought to the Yankees is unmistakable. That means that he was worth the price that the Yankees paid to acquire him, even if the trade appears en route to becoming more balanced over time.
Good pitching will always be key for any team to win a championship. Preventing the other team from putting up crooked numbers is one of the most effective ways to come out on top at the end of a game. But it can be difficult to find and develop the level of pitching needed to achieve that. This can be especially true when it comes to late-inning relievers. That means a premium is usually paid.
We’ve seen the Yankees win and lose trades over the years. It's all part of the risk you take when you build a win-now team. Some of those trades hit, some don't. The Yankees needed a pitcher like Bednar to help them in the postseason so they pulled the trigger. And while trading Flores Jr. for that reason could benefit the Pirates more in the long run, a World Series title in 2026 would erase any feeling of regret for the Yankees.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees did not just win on Wednesday night; they sent a loud message to the rest of the league. In a 9-2 blowout against the Tampa Bay Rays, the Bronx Bombers showed they are ready for the postseason grind. This was not a lucky break. It was a complete team performance that left the Rays staring at the scoreboard in disbelief.
Rice and McMahon Lead the Charge
Ben Rice stepped up in a massive way, hitting his 40th and 41st home runs of the season. He started the scoring by crushing the first pitch from Mason Englert into the right-field second deck. ESPN reports that Rice hit a solo home run in the fourth inning to finish his fifth career game with multiple homers. He finished with three hits and is now tied for the American League home run lead with stars like Pete Alonso and Yordan Alvarez. That is the kind of power the Yankees need right now.
Ryan McMahon also left his mark by hitting a grand slam while tying his career best with five runs batted in. In the third, he increased the lead to 7-0 with his third career slam. The Rays had no answer for this lineup. They allowed eight runs and nine hits in just 4 2/3 innings from Englert, who was brought up to give starters rest. The Yankees offense is firing on all cylinders as the playoffs approach.
Cole Keeps the Pitching Strong
Gerrit Cole was solid on the mound, allowing two runs and three hits over 5 2/3 innings. He threw a season-high 105 pitches and struck out eight batters despite the high pitch count. The 2023 AL Cy Young Award winner now holds a 3.61 ERA and 131 strikeouts across 22 starts since returning from Tommy John surgery. Per USA Today, he has been a steady force since coming back in May. The Yankees need him healthy and sharp for the division series, and this start proves he is ready.
While the Yankees offense soared, the Rays struggled to find their rhythm. George Lombard Jr. homered for New York, and Cedric Mullins went deep for Tampa Bay, but it was not enough. The Rays manager Kevin Cash admitted that left-hander Shane McClanahan will not recover in time for the Division Series. This injury news hurts Tampa Bay, but the Yankees have no time to celebrate their own health issues.
Playoff Stakes Get Real
New York is guaranteed to host a best-of-three AL Wild Card Series beginning Tuesday. The victor will meet the Rays in a best-of-five Division Series. The Yankees have the edge, but the playoffs are a different beast. They must stay focused.
This win was a statement of intent. The team is clicking at the right time. They have the power, the pitching, and the depth to go deep. The Rays clinched the AL East title a day before, but the Yankees proved they can beat them when it counts. The season is not over. The real work begins now.

item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies dodged a major bullet on Thursday night. In the sixth inning against the Milwaukee Brewers, hit-machine Luis Arraez suffered a left ankle sprain while diving to beat out an infield hit. Following negative X-rays, interim manager Don Mattingly provided a cautious update on his star second baseman.
“Luis had an X-ray, and the results were negative [for a fracture],” Mattingly told reporters postgame. “I’m hopeful that he can play, but we’ll see… even if he can’t, someone else is going to have to step up.”
Arraez has served as an offensive engine for Mattingly since arriving via midseason trade. Mattingly relies heavily on the multi-time batting champion’s elite contact tool and high-on-base profile to set the table for Philadelphia’s power-heavy core as the club fights to lock up a National League Wild Card spot.
While the Phillies are also monitoring left-hander Jesus Luzardo’s impending return from the 15-day injured list, any potential absence for Arraez creates an immediate headline issue for Philadelphia’s offense with October right around the corner.
What do the Phillies lose without Arraez down the stretch?
Under Mattingly, Philadelphia pulled off a remarkable midseason turnaround to put themselves in prime position for a postseason berth. However, losing Arraez at this late stage would be a brutal blow for a lineup looking to finalize its playoff seeding.
Arraez boasts one of the lowest strikeout rates in Major League Baseball and consistently sets the table at the top of the order. Without his contact ability putting pressure on opposing rotations, the Phillies lose their primary catalyst to generate high-percentage scoring opportunities for sluggers like Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber.
Final stretch for the Phillies
Between Arraez’s health and Luzardo’s impending return to the pitching staff, the Phillies are aiming to close out the regular season on a high note as they put the finishing touches on their postseason push.
Heading into their final regular-season series against the Tampa Bay Rays, the Phillies have a chance to officially secure their ticket to October. A strong showing against Tampa Bay will allow Philadelphia to shift its focus entirely to playoff baseball.
Key takeaways
- Luis Arráez sprained his left ankle in the sixth inning against the Milwaukee Brewers.
- The 15-day injured list status of Jesus Luzardo is also being monitored.
- Philadelphia faces the Tampa Bay Rays in their final regular-season series to clinch postseason play.

item.title: [heavy.com] New York Yankees Urged to Acquire $126M Slugger to Replace Ryan McMahon
item.dc:creator: Cole Shelton

New York is heading back to the playoffs and will host the AL Wild Card series as the Yankees look to get over the hump finally. The Yankees will begin a three-game road series against the Baltimore Orioles on Friday. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees could be a team to watch this offseason to add another impact bat to the lineup.
New York is heading back to the playoffs and will host the AL Wild Card series as the Yankees look to get over the hump finally.
The Yankees will begin a three-game road series against the Baltimore Orioles on Friday.
New York Yankees Urged to Acquire Bo Bichette
The Yankees haven’t gotten much production from Ryan McMahon at third base, so New York should look to add an impact bat to replace him.
McMahon’s defense has been solid. But his bat is an issue, and he’s been considered a trade chip or DFA candidate this offseason. With that, Yankees analyst Stephen Parello of FanSided urges the team to acquire Bo Bichette this offseason.
“It might sound strange, but Bo Bichette could be a sneaky-good solution for the Yankees. While he got off to a frigid start in Queens that has depressed his overall line, he’s hit .291/.335/.440 since June 1. There’s also some reason to believe that getting away from the Mets’ dysfunction could help him rebound even more,” Parello wrote.
“What’s more, he could actually provide some things the Yankees need. Having another contact-forward bat would be nice, and he’d add some much-needed right-handed balance to the lineup. It seemed for a while that he was a shoo-in to opt in to his contract, but now, after a return to form, it’s thought to be a 50-50 chance that he tests the free-agent market again this winter. If he does, he deserves a long look.”
Bichette is in the first year of a three-year, $126 million deal but could opt out. If he does opt out, Bichette will have some suitors, and he could fit in nicely with the Yankees.
The slugger showed he can hit in the AL East with the Toronto Blue Jays, and his defense at third base is good enough. He’s hitting .259 with 17 home runs and 76 RBIs this season.
New York Right Now
The Yankees are set to play their final series of the season before the focus shifts to the playoffs.
New York will likely play the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card round. However, the team has dealt with a plethora of injuries, including to slugger Aaron Judge.
“I’m proud of the guys,” Judge said. “I’ve been proud of what they’ve done, proud of the young guys coming up and filling some holes for us. You know, seeing Spencer, how he’s really evolved every single time he got called up, gotten a little bit better, a little bit better. Our starting pitching doing what it’s done. You call up a guy like George Lombard [Jr.], 21 years old, to be the shortstop for the Yankees, and he’s just fit right in with this group. I’m just proud of the guys.”
The Yankees will play a doubleheader on Friday before ending the season on Sunday.

item.title: [heavy.com] Yankees' George Lombard Jr. Joins Mickey Mantle in Baseball History
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen

item.content:encoded:
It’s careful to not get ahead of ourselves.
It’s still the very early days of George Lombard Jr. with the New York Yankees. There are still so many possible permutations of the career of the young shortstop.
But the Yankees have been waiting for a shortstop that plays baseball like this.
The Yankees have been waiting for a young ballplayer who has talent like this.
Lombard looks, in many ways, like the next big thing.
And again — there’s no need to rush it. There’s no need for massive conclusions.
Instead, it’s worth just sitting in the moment of what Lombard is doing right now. And what he’s doing right now is already mighty impressive and, in some ways, historic.
George Lombard Jr. Home Run History
Lombard joined Mickey Mantle in Yankees history on Thursday night.
He did it be hitting a go-ahead home run for the Yanks in the bottom of the eighth inning against the Tampa Bay Rays. The game was tied 4-4, there was one guy on base, and then Lombard lifted off to deep left field.
George Lombard Jr. CRUSHES a second-deck, go-ahead homer 😤 pic.twitter.com/ULT8kJ2EKk
— MLB (@MLB) September 25, 2026
According to MLB Network’s Sarah Langs, Lombard became the second-youngest player in Yankees history to hit a go-ahead home run in the eighth inning or later.
The youngest was Mickey Mantle, who did it on July 29, 1952 — he launched a go-ahead grand slam in the ninth inning that day.
Lombard didn’t quite catch Mantle’s record, as he hit his homer at 21 years and 114 days, while Mantle was just 20 years and 283 days.
Still, incredible company. The Yankees rarely have had players break into the majors at this young an age. Lombard is breaking a lot of franchise trends, and he’s doing it in style.
George Lombard Jr. Stats
Lombard was expected to be a good player. The Yankees drafted him in the first round of the 2023 MLB Draft at No. 26 overall out of a high school in Florida, and his dad of the same name played in the big leagues himself.
Still, as Lombard climbed the ladder and moved up prospect rankings, people were generally more sure about him as a shortstop than him as a hitter.
So far, Lombard has proven he can hit. In an era of incredibly low batting averages, Lombard’s .243 is actually a tick above league average. In 41 games, he has four doubles, a triple, seven home runs and 22 RBI. Lombard’s OPS of .718 is solid for his first trip through MLB.
The hope will be that this is just the beginning and that he can lift up even higher as time goes along.
Even if he can’t, Lombard can still be a solid major league contributor in the Bronx.
But given all the considerations here, of age and stage and talent, Lombard is sure off to quite the start in pinstripes.

The game will be played as the first half of a single-admission doubleheader at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx, beginning at 4:05 p.m. Friday. The second game is scheduled to begin no later than 7:05 p.m., the team said. If the first game ends after 6:35 p.m., the second game will begin approximately 30 minutes after the f
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have moved Saturday’s game against the Baltimore Orioles, and CC Sabathia’s number retirement to Friday due to inclement weather, the team said in a release.
The game will be played as the first half of a single-admission doubleheader at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx, beginning at 4:05 p.m. Friday. The second game is scheduled to begin no later than 7:05 p.m., the team said.
If the first game ends after 6:35 p.m., the second game will begin approximately 30 minutes after the final out, according to the release.
CC Sabathia’s number retirement ceremony and Monument Park plaque unveiling will take place prior to the start of Game 1 on Friday.
Yankee Stadium gates will open at 2:30 p.m., and fans are encouraged to arrive by 3 p.m. for the ceremony. The Josh Hart Yankees bobblehead giveaway will begin at 2:30 p.m. for the first 18,000 fans in attendance, the team said.
Only tickets dated Friday, Sept. 25, will be valid for the doubleheader. Tickets for the originally scheduled Saturday game will not be accepted Friday.
Fans with tickets for Saturday’s game can exchange them for tickets to a similar regular-season game at Yankee Stadium, subject to availability, under the Yankees’ rain check policy.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] 4 Ryan McMahon replacements Yankees should already be dreaming about for 2027

item.content:encoded:
It's far too late to do anything about it this season, but the New York Yankees officially have a Ryan McMahon problem. It's been a year and a half now that he's been in pinstripes, and his performance with the bat has been worse than notorious frustrations like Joey Gallo, late-career DJ LeMahieu, and Isiah Kiner-Falefa, among others.
With a .208/.274/.344 line over 119 games this season, he has struggled against righties, is even more useless against lefties, and has arrived at a point where his good-but-not-great defense can no longer save his subpar bat.
Now that the case for an offseason DFA is clear, it's time to start thinking about potential 2027 replacements. There might not be a ton of high-end options, but there are a few that we can dream on.
Four dream Ryan McMahon replacements for 2027 if the Yankees shoot for the stars
Rafael Devers
Rafael Devers has been gaining buzz as a trade target for New York since the lead-up to the trade deadline. This would be a 180 in philosophy, as the whole reason things deteriorated between Devers and the Red Sox was growing concerns over his defense, and since arriving in San Francisco, he's primarily been a first baseman and DH. There's a school of thought, though, that George Lombard Jr.'s athleticism and defensive potential could help mitigate the defensive issues.
Devers hit 38 homers this year, and even a slow first half from him was light-years better than what McMahon has put up at any point in his career. Admittedly, this has become a bit more complicated due to questions about his status for Opening Day after undergoing core muscle surgery, and the Yankees would have to assume the vast majority of the nearly $200 million that the 29-year-old is owed, but his bat would be a perfect fit, and this would have the added benefit of tormenting Boston with a Raffy Revenge Tour.
Isaac Paredes
Another trade candidate, Isaac Paredes, could be an interesting option. The 27-year-old has long been on the Yankees' radar, and this winter could be their opportunity to get a deal done. The Houston Astros are never ones to help the Yankees out, but this could be a case where need aligns well enough for both squads that they have no other choice but to come to an agreement.
Houston is in a tough spot. Their horrid start put them behind the eight ball, and they're in a dogfight with the Texas Rangers for the AL West crown. The loser of the division chase might find themselves out of the Wild Card picture, and if that were to happen, it would mark the Astros' second consecutive playoff-less season. They've also fired general manager Dana Brown this summer, so changes are coming.
Paredes was subject to a slew of trade rumors last offseason because Houston has an infield logjam. Carlos Correa's injury cleared that up in 2026, but he'll be back next year and is under contract through at least 2028 (and possibly through 2032, depending on a series of vesting options). Meanwhile, they're also stuck with Christian Walker for another season, and Jose Altuve isn't going anywhere. Houston desperately needs pitching, and doesn't have a lot of room in their budget. Perhaps an Elmer Rodriguez-centric package could sway them.
Bo Bichette
It might sound strange, but Bo Bichette could be a sneaky-good solution for the Yankees. While he got off to a frigid start in Queens that has depressed his overall line, he's hit .291/.335/.440 since June 1. There's also some reason to believe that getting away from the Mets' dysfunction could help him rebound even more.
What's more, he could actually provide some things the Yankees need. Having another contact-forward bat would be nice, and he'd add some much-needed right-handed balance to the lineup. It seemed for a while that he was a shoo-in to opt in to his contract, but now, after a return to form, it's thought to be a 50-50 chance that he tests the free-agent market again this winter. If he does, he deserves a long look.
Zach Neto
This one requires some creativity, but there's a chance that New York could make this work. Zach Neto was the subject of a wave of trade rumors at the deadline, and according to Angels insider Jeff Fletcher of the OC Register, Los Angeles is expected to shop him again this offseason. The Red Sox and Rays were both rumored to be sniffing around the 25-year-old at the deadline, so making a deal for him could also be a defensive move.
Neto is a shortstop by trade, but if there's one knock on his game, it's that his range at the position is lacking. He does have a cannon for an arm, with his throwing power checking in at an 85th-percentile mark per Baseball Savant, so a move to the hot corner could maximize his defensive skill set.
The hiccup here will be the price. Neto is a perennial 30-30 candidate and doesn't hit free agency until 2030, so he won't be cheap to acquire. For this to work for the Yankees, they'd need to be able to hold onto Lombard Jr.; otherwise, they're simply trading one shortstop for another. That might not be possible on either team's end. Los Angeles acquired top prospect Arjun Nimmala from the Blue Jays for Jose Soriano, and the soon-to-be 21-year-old is tearing up Double-A. He could soon be ready to step in and take Neto's job.
This is the longest shot of them all, but it could help the Yankees extend their window well into Aaron Judge's decline. A core of Neto, Lombard Jr., Spencer Jones, Ben Rice, and Cam Schlittler could eventually usher in a new era without the club having to go through any sort of reset.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Analyzing Whether Yankees' Anthony Volpe Third Base Experiment Could Actually Work?
item.dc:creator: Michael Zeno; Unknown
item.description: As the New York Yankees try to sort out the final pieces of their playoff plan throughout this relatively meaningless final week of the regular season, there's one position that's quickly gaining interest and intrigue: third base. Ryan McMahon has gotten the lion's share of reps there over the course of the season, especially after the team began reducing the usage of a struggling Amed Rosario, whose bat and glove seemed to regress heavily in the offseason. José Caballero took over the position
item.content:encoded:
As the New York Yankees try to sort out the final pieces of their playoff plan throughout this relatively meaningless final week of the regular season, there's one position that's quickly gaining interest and intrigue: third base.
Ryan McMahon has gotten the lion's share of reps there over the course of the season, especially after the team began reducing the usage of a struggling Amed Rosario, whose bat and glove seemed to regress heavily in the offseason. José Caballero took over the position during McMahon's brief stint on the injured list, but has mostly ceded it back since.
However, Wednesday night's game notwithstanding, McMahon has struggled mightily offensively, so much so that he might be forcing the Yankees' hand. It doesn't help his case that he's regressed from a Gold Glove-caliber defender to a merely average one.
With McMahon's struggles, the Yankees have opened the door for someone else to take the position in October. While the most likely candidate is Caballero, Aaron Boone revealed Wednesday that an unlikely candidate is emerging: Anthony Volpe.
This could just be to have him ready as a depth option, but it could also be a sign that the team is weighing whether he could give the team the best chance to win at third base. There's reason to believe he can, but also reason to believe it might not be a good idea.
Why Anthony Volpe at third base may work
The simplest reason that it may work is that Volpe is a naturally gifted defender.
In three of his four years in the major leagues, he has graded out positively defensively while playing almost exclusively at the most demanding position, both in terms of range and arm strength.
In 2023, 2024, and 2026 combined, he had 25 Defensive Runs Saved, 21 Outs Above Average, and a 14 Fielding Run Value at the position while playing every day, three marks that were towards the top of the league.
The lone season he was not a good defender was 2025, when he played through a torn labrum for much of the season after an ill-fated dive on his non-throwing arm in May of that year. The immediate bounce-back after he returned from labrum surgery this season is proof that it wasn't spontaneous regression, but rather a fluke.
Still, with George Lombard Jr. grading out even better at shortstop in the minor leagues, Volpe was demoted in early August and asked to try other positions, which he's done since. In 93 innings at second base since being promoted back to the majors, he has 2 DRS and 1 OAA, looking clean and crisp throughout.
But what about third base? Most players who can handle shortstop tend to be even better at second and third base, something that the front office definitely hoped with Volpe after moving him off the position this summer. If he's good at shortstop, how great can he be elsewhere?
His range is undoubtedly his best attribute. Since coming into the league in 2023, Volpe has registered 10 runs of value off his range, which is higher than his actual total FRV of 8. If you remove his compromised 2025 data, he has 15 FRV worth of range value, while his arm and ability to turn double plays are both in the negatives.
So at third base, there's no doubt that Volpe would be very good at knocking down balls and snagging them to his left and right, potentially giving the Yankees a weapon to prevent doubles down the left field line.
But the fact that his arm has been a big negative at shortstop in his career will give some people pause about how good he can be at third base, a position that typically yields a bunch of long throws. That begs the question: does it matter?
Does arm strength matter at third base?
10 years ago, we'd have nothing but our eyes to determine how hard a guy can throw the ball. Fortunately, we have Statcast to help us now.
Volpe's arm strength has consistently been mediocre throughout his career, averaging between 81 and 82 miles per hour on his throws entering this year, when it has undoubtedly dipped due to the sample size at an easier position, per Baseball Savant. That mark consistently sat in the 30th percentile, well below average.
The average speed of a shortstop's throw in the majors is 86.2 mph. The average speed for a third baseman is 84.9 mph. It immediately dispels the belief that a third baseman has to have an equally strong arm, but where would Volpe stack up among those third basemen?
At 81-82 mph, Volpe would comfortably be below average at third base too, sliding in just above Kazuma Okamoto. Of the 53 third basemen with at least 50 throws, Volpe would be 38th.
How are the third basemen in his range defensively? Here are the 2026 defensive stats for the seven players in Volpe's immediate range:
Hao-Yu Lee: -3 DRS, -6 OAA, -4 FRV
Max Muncy (LAD): 3 DRS, 0 OAA, 1 FRV
Kazuma Okamoto: 2 DRS, -3 OAA, -3 FRV
Alex Bregman: 15 DRS, 9 OAA, 7 FRV
Max Muncy (ATH): -11 DRS, -6 OAA, -5 FRV
Brett Baty: 2 DRS, 1 OAA, 1 FRV
Caleb Durbin: 13 DRS, 5 OAA, 5 FRV
As you can see, it's an extreme mixed bag. Bregman and Durbin are two of the best defenders in baseball at their position despite not having a lot of zip on their throws, while Hao-Yu Lee and the Athletics' Max Muncy have been quite bad.
The fact that we have players from all different walks of life here suggests that arm strength doesn't matter nearly as much as some may believe. If a player has good range (the big calling cards of Durbin and Bregman), they can make up for maybe having to bounce a few. If they don't, it becomes a double negative.
It might also help to have a good first baseman at scooping. Paul Goldschmidt is one of the best of his generation at it (and this is now a Statcast stat!), but Luis García Jr. is quite mediocre. That said, the A's Nick Kurtz is significantly better at it than Boston's Willson Contreras and Chicago's Michael Busch.
So maybe arm strength just doesn't matter? If the Yankees deem that it isn't an issue, there should be no reservations about potentially deploying Volpe there come playoff time.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees erased a four-run deficit Thursday night, scoring six unanswered runs to rally past the Tampa Bay Rays, 6-4, in the series finale at Yankee Stadium.
Tampa Bay opened the scoring in the third inning after Taylor Walls walked and scored on a Yandy Díaz single that turned into an RBI double when Heliot Ramos’ throw toward third base got away. Junior Caminero followed with another run-scoring single.
Cam Schlittler made his final start of the regular season but was removed after three innings as the Yankees continued managing their starters’ workloads ahead of the postseason. Michael Fulmer and Tim Hill kept Tampa Bay in check before Caminero’s RBI double in the fifth extended the Rays’ lead to 3-0.
Tampa Bay added another run in the sixth after an error prevented the Yankees from completing a double play.
Austin Wells got New York on the board with a solo home run in the bottom half of the inning. The Yankees then erupted for three runs in the seventh.
George Lombard Jr. doubled home Ben Rice before scoring on a wild pitch. Paul Goldschmidt followed with a two-run single that tied the game at 4-4.
Lombard delivered again in the eighth, launching a two-run home run down the left-field line to put New York ahead. The homer was his seventh in 41 career games and gave him three runs batted in on the night.
Bradley Hanner protected the lead with a scoreless eighth and ninth innings to earn the first victory of his career.
Schlittler finished with a 1.95 earned-run average, a 0.92 walks-and-hits-per-inning ratio, 239 strikeouts and 47 walks across 193.2 innings in 33 starts.
The Yankees open their final regular-season series Friday against the Baltimore Orioles with a doubleheader beginning at 4:05 p.m. Game 2 will start no earlier than 7:05 p.m.

item.description:

25 Sep 2026, 08:10 GMT+10

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

25 Sep 2026, 08:10 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Brad Penner)
Rookie George Lombard Jr. hit an impressive tiebreaking two-run homer with two outs in the eighth inning as the New York Yankees overcame a four-run deficit and earned a 6-4 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays on Thursday night.
The Yankees (92-67) won for the 11th time in 16 games thanks to their late comeback that was sparked by Lombard.
Following a single by Amed Rosario off Steven Matz (5-6), Lombard snapped a 4-4 tie by lifting a 2-2 sinker into the second deck of the left field seats. It was Lombard's seventh homer in 41 games since joining the Yankees last month and his fourth in the past seven games.
Lombard also hit an RBI double during New York's three-run seventh and scored on a wild pitch to the backstop by Tampa Bay rookie Brody Hopkins.
Paul Goldschmidt had a tying RBI single in the seventh for the Yankees, who are 11-8 when tied through seven innings.
Austin Wells also homered for the Yankees, who had one hit through the first five innings and lost seven of 13 meetings with the top-seeded Rays (96-63).
New York ace Cam Schlittler allowed two runs (one earned) on three hits in three innings as he was limited to 70 pitches in his final start before the postseason. The right-hander struck out five and finished with 239 strikeouts to go along with a 1.95 ERA in his first full season.
Bradley Hanner (1-0) retired Junior Caminero to end the eighth and stranded a runner in the ninth for his first career victory.
Caminero had an RBI single and a run-scoring double as the Rays held a 4-0 lead into the sixth. Caminero needs one RBI to become the fifth player in team history with multiple 100-RBI seasons.
Yandy Diaz added a pair of hits, including a hit that scored a run on a throwing error by New York right fielder Heliot Ramos in the third.
Caminero gave the Rays a 2-0 lead with a single to center field and followed with a double off the left field fence before Tampa Bay took a 4-0 lead on an error by reliever Luis Gil.
Tampa Bay's Ian Seymour allowed one hit in five innings. He struck out three and walked none in a 58-pitch outing.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Cubs star Pete Crow-Armstrong joins MLB’s elite 40-40 club
Pete Crow-Armstrong joined the 40-40 club Thursday when the Chicago Cubs star stole his 40th base of the season Thursday against the Miami Marlins.
A favorite to win the NL MVP award, Crow-Armstrong became the seventh player with at least 40 homers and 40 steals in a season, joining a group that includes Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani and Atlanta Braves outfielder Ronald Acuña Jr. Jose Canseco was the first with the 1988 Oakland Athletics.
Related video above | 5 memorable Opening Day moments in baseball history
Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th homer during Sunday’s 9-1 win at Cincinnati, extending his career high. The 24-year-old drew a leadoff walk from Tyler Phillips in the first inning and swiped second base on the next pitch to Seiya Suzuki for his 40th steal in 47 attempts. Fans chanted “MVP” as the Wrigley Field videoboard proclaimed the feat.
Ohtani was the previous player with a 40-40 season, hitting 54 homers and stealing 59 bases for the 2024 Dodgers. Acuña hit 41 homers and swiped 73 bases for Atlanta in 2023.
Alfonso Soriano (2006 with Washington), Alex Rodriguez (1998 with Seattle) and Barry Bonds (1996 with San Francisco) are the other 40-40 players.
This story will be updated.

item.title: [Yardbarker] New York Yankees Make Depressing Announcement on Luis Gil
item.dc:creator: Simeon Kotto
item.description: The New York Yankees optioned Luis Gil to the Florida Complex League on Thursday night, pairing the move with the demotion of fellow right-hander Bradley Hanner ahead of a weather-compressed series against the Baltimore Orioles. The announcement itself was terse. The story behind it is not. Two seasons after Gil won American League Rookie of the Year, the 28-year-old has become a cautionary tale of how quickly a breakout can fade. In 2024, he looked like a rotation piece the Yankees could build
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees optioned Luis Gil to the Florida Complex League on Thursday night, pairing the move with the demotion of fellow right-hander Bradley Hanner ahead of a weather-compressed series against the Baltimore Orioles.
The announcement itself was terse. The story behind it is not.
Two seasons after Gil won American League Rookie of the Year, the 28-year-old has become a cautionary tale of how quickly a breakout can fade.
In 2024, he looked like a rotation piece the Yankees could build around: 15-7 with a 3.50 ERA, 171 strikeouts in 151⅔ innings, and a fastball that still touched the upper 90s. He was not a fluke filler. He pitched like someone who belonged in the middle of a contending staff.
What followed has been a slow unraveling. A high-grade lat strain wiped out most of 2025. When he returned in August of that year, he posted a respectable 3.32 ERA in 11 starts, but the underlying numbers told a different story.
Strikeout rate cratered. Walks climbed. Velocity dipped. The same four-seamer that once generated swings and misses suddenly looked hittable. The 2025 cameo was a mirage dressed up as a win-loss record.
2026 has been worse. Gil opened the year in Triple-A, earned a brief rotation look in April, and promptly allowed six runs in four innings against Houston. The Yankees sent him back down.
A later shoulder issue further interrupted his season. Recalled in late August, he was used almost exclusively in low-leverage relief.
The results were mixed at best: occasional clean innings mixed with walks and a homer problem that never fully disappeared. His 2026 line through Thursday sat at 1-2 with a 4.61 ERA in 27⅓ innings, a far cry from the pitcher who once looked like a mid-rotation lock.
Sending a former Rookie of the Year to the complex league is not a routine roster shuffle. It is a statement that the organization no longer sees him as a major-league contributor in the immediate term.
Whether this is a last-ditch reset, a roster crunch created by returning arms, or simply an admission that the command and stuff have not returned, the optics are grim. Gil still has years of team control remaining.
That fact only makes the disappointment sharper. The Yankees once believed they had found something special.
Two years later they are shipping him to the lowest level of the system before a series that should have been about playoff positioning, not roster housekeeping.
The 2024 version of Luis Gil feels like a different pitcher. The current one is still searching for him.

item.title: [On New Jersey] No. 52 forever: Yankees to cement CC Sabathia's legacy in Mo
item.dc:creator: Jonna Perlinger
item.description: There will never be another No. 52 in pinstripes. On Friday, the Yankees will make official what has felt inevitable for years, retiring CC Sabathia’s number and unveiling a plaque in his honor in Monument Park before New York’s 4:05 p.m. game against the Baltimore Orioles at Yankee Stadium. It is one of the highest honors the franchise can bestow, and for Sabathia, it comes barely a year after baseball gave him its highest honor. The big left-hander was inducted into the National Baseball Hall
item.content:encoded:
There will never be another No. 52 in pinstripes.
On Friday, the Yankees will make official what has felt inevitable for years, retiring CC Sabathia’s number and unveiling a plaque in his honor in Monument Park before New York’s 4:05 p.m. game against the Baltimore Orioles at Yankee Stadium.
It is one of the highest honors the franchise can bestow, and for Sabathia, it comes barely a year after baseball gave him its highest honor.
The big left-hander was inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 2025, making it to Cooperstown on his first ballot. Now No. 52 will hang permanently at Yankee Stadium, ensuring that the number Sabathia wore for all 11 of his seasons in the Bronx belongs to him forever.
Sabathia will become the 24th Yankees player or manager to have his number retired. Because No. 8 is shared by Bill Dickey and Yogi Berra, 52 will become the 23rd different number removed from circulation by the franchise. He is the first Yankee to receive the honor since Paul O’Neill’s No. 21 was retired in 2022.
A Hall of Fame Career That Found a Home in the Bronx
Sabathia’s road to Monument Park began before he ever put on pinstripes.
He debuted with Cleveland as a 20-year-old in 2001, developed into one of baseball’s premier starting pitchers and won the 2007 American League Cy Young Award. After a remarkable second half with Milwaukee in 2008, when he helped carry the Brewers into the postseason, Sabathia became the centerpiece of the Yankees’ aggressive offseason plans.
New York signed him to a seven-year, $161 million contract in December 2008, at the time the largest free-agent contract ever given to a pitcher.
He immediately delivered.
Sabathia went 19-8 with a 3.37 ERA across 34 starts in 2009, anchoring the rotation as the Yankees returned to the World Series. He was even better when October arrived, earning ALCS MVP honors after going 2-0 with a 1.13 ERA against the Angels. Weeks later, the Yankees were World Series champions for the 27th time.
It would be the beginning of an 11-season relationship between Sabathia and New York.
From 2009 through his retirement in 2019, Sabathia went 134-88 with a 3.81 ERA and 1,700 strikeouts as a Yankee. His name remains scattered throughout the franchise’s pitching record book, ranking fourth in Yankees history in strikeouts, seventh in starts, 10th in wins and 11th in innings pitched.
Sabathia was also a fixture when the games mattered most. In 21 postseason appearances for New York, including 18 starts, he went 8-4 with a 3.42 ERA. At Yankee Stadium, his postseason ERA was just 2.17.
Those numbers tell a large part of the story. They do not tell all of it.
Sabathia became one of the defining personalities of his Yankees era, a clubhouse leader whose importance stretched well beyond what happened every fifth day. By the time he threw the final pitch of his career in 2019, he had long since become synonymous with the pinstripes.
First-Ballot Hall of Famer
Baseball made Sabathia’s place among the game’s greats official in January 2025.
In his first year of eligibility, Sabathia received 86.8 percent of the Baseball Writers’ Association of America vote, easily clearing the 75 percent needed for election into the National Baseball Hall of Fame. He was officially inducted in Cooperstown on July 27, 2025.
His complete career resume left little question about his Cooperstown credentials.
Across 19 Major League seasons with Cleveland, Milwaukee and New York, Sabathia finished 251-161 with a 3.74 ERA. He pitched 3,577 1/3 innings, made six All-Star teams, won a Cy Young Award and struck out 3,093 batters.
He also joined one of baseball’s most exclusive pitching clubs.
Sabathia is one of just 15 pitchers in Major League history to record at least 250 victories and 3,000 strikeouts. When he reached those milestones, only fellow Hall of Famers Randy Johnson and Steve Carlton had done both as left-handers.
And when it came time to decide which team would be represented on his Hall of Fame plaque, Sabathia chose the interlocking NY.
Cooperstown may celebrate his entire career, but Sabathia has made clear where he considers home.
Sabathia’s place in baseball history is already secure, but the family name is still very much part of the game. I had the chance to catch up with him during MLB All-Star Week this summer, just days after the Brewers selected his son, Carsten Sabathia III, in the 2026 MLB Draft. Given CC’s own memorable run in Milwaukee, the connection felt especially fitting, and I asked him if watching his son turn pro had him tempted to pull a LeBron-and-Bronny and come out of retirement for one last chance to share the field.
Another Left-Hander Among Yankees Pitching Royalty
Now Sabathia’s legacy will have a permanent home in center field alongside some of the greatest pitchers to ever wear pinstripes.
When Mariano Rivera received his Monument Park plaque in 2016, he became the ninth Yankees pitcher honored there, joining Lefty Gomez, Whitey Ford, Red Ruffing, Allie Reynolds, Ron Guidry, Goose Gossage, Andy Pettitte and Mel Stottlemyre. Sabathia will add another name to that pitching fraternity.
Several members of that group have an additional distinction that Sabathia will now share.
Ford’s No. 16, Rivera’s No. 42, Pettitte’s No. 46 and Guidry’s No. 49 have all been retired by the Yankees. On Friday, Sabathia’s No. 52 joins them.
There is something especially fitting about Sabathia taking his place alongside Pettitte and Rivera.
They were there with him in 2009, when Sabathia arrived in New York carrying enormous expectations and immediately helped deliver a championship. Derek Jeter’s No. 2, Jorge Posada’s No. 20, Rivera’s No. 42 and Pettitte’s No. 46 have all since been retired. Sabathia now becomes the fifth member of that 2009 championship team to receive the same honor.
Seventeen years after that group brought a World Series trophy back to the Bronx, another piece of the 2009 Yankees will become a permanent part of the ballpark.
52 Forever
Sabathia arrived in New York as an ace with a massive contract and expectations to match.
He leaves his mark on the franchise as something much bigger.
World Series champion. ALCS MVP. Clubhouse leader. More than 1,700 strikeouts in pinstripes. First-ballot Hall of Famer.
And now, forever, No. 52.
Future generations of Yankees fans walking through Monument Park will see Sabathia’s plaque among the franchise’s legends. They’ll look beyond the center-field wall and see his number alongside Ford, Rivera, Pettitte, Guidry and the countless icons who came before him.
Players will come and go. Rotations will change. New aces will take the mound in the Bronx.
But no Yankee will wear 52 again.
That one belongs to CC.

item.description:
Cam Schlittler made his final start of the regular season Thursday night. Will his next be in Game 1 of the wild-card series on Tuesday?
Access the Yankees beat like never before

item.content:encoded:
Cam Schlittler made his final start of the regular season Thursday night.
Will his next be in Game 1 of the wild-card series on Tuesday?




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
The Yankees aren’t saying and insist they haven’t decided on their postseason rotation with less than a week to go before the playoffs start.
Before a 6-4 comeback victory over the Rays at the Stadium, pitching coach Matt Blake said that Max Fried is in “heavy consideration” to pitch Game 1 on Tuesday, while Schlittler — who threw 70 pitches in an intentionally abbreviated outing against Tampa Bay — was also in the mix.
And Gerrit Cole, according to Blake, isn’t guaranteed a start in the wild-card series.
With Schlittler and Fried seemingly locked in to a start, Blake said Game 3 would go to Cole or Carlos Rodón.
“Both guys have pitched well down the stretch,’’ Blake said of Cole and Rodón. “All four guys are good options. It’s just a matter of making sure we check in, see where they’re at and finding the best fit for whoever we play.”
Their opponent is still undetermined, as Boston was unable to clinch the fifth spot in the American League after losing to Cleveland on Thursday.
Regardless of who the Yankees end up playing, part of the equation with the rotation will be rest, since Schlittler would be pitching on his fifth day if he went in Game 1 on Tuesday in The Bronx.
Cole, another option, would be on his sixth day, while Fried — as well as Rodón — would be on his seventh day.
Asked if they could be overthinking the situation by not just naming Schlittler the Game 1 starter after his Cy Young-worthy season, Blake said, “Certainly.”
Schlittler finished his first full year in the majors with an AL-best 1.95 ERA, as well as 239 strikeouts.
The ERA is third best in franchise history, trailing only Spud Chandler (1.64 in 1943) and Ron Guidry (1.74 in 1978).
“He’s earned the right to pitch Game 1,’’ Blake said prior to Schlittler’s final outing, in which he allowed two runs, one earned, in a meaningless game. “We’re taking inventory of all our starters and giving us the best chance to advance in the three-game series.”
And that could leave Cole out and ready for a potential ALDS matchup against the Rays.
“If we don’t have him as one of our three starters or out of the pen, he’d be available for [ALDS],’’ Blake said. “I don’t know where we’d go.”
Shop Yankees Merch
Blake said they could go with all four starters on the wild-card roster, understanding the challenges of putting those pitchers in an unfamiliar role.
“Any of those guys that haven’t pitched out of the pen in a while, you’ve got to make sure you’ve got a clear plan for them and they understand what role they’ll be in because you probably get one shot if we use one of these starters out of the pen,’’ Blake said. “They’re not gonna pitch two games [in the series].”

item.content:encoded:
Major League Baseball’s playoffs are coming soon and Alex Bregman will be a part of it.
Of course he is.
Bregman made baseball history Thursday, Sept. 24 when the Chicago Cubs clinched a National League wild-card berth with a victory over the Miami Marlins. And for the 10th consecutive year, injured eye willing, Bregman will take part in the postseason, this time with a twist.
Bregman, the Cubs’ 32-year-old third baseman, will become the first position player to play postseason baseball 10 consecutive seasons with multiple teams. In fact, he’s done it with three ballclubs – eight straight years with the Houston Astros and then the past two with the Boston Red Sox and Cubs, as he settled for good in Chicago by signing a five-year, $175 million contract in January.
And it seems like wherever Bregman goes, October baseball follows.
Texas loves him anyway
Bregman was a two-time All-Star and two-time champion in Houston, the brash young slugger in his first full season when they won the 2017 World Series, the MVP runner-up when they lost the 2019 Series in seven games.
After bearing much of the scorn for the club’s 2017 sign-stealing scandal, he was the chastened veteran on the 2022 squad that won a second World Series, this time without a cloud of controversy to follow.
Yet Bregman’s chops as a club cornerstone gained greater veracity a year ago, when he left the Astros and, combining his production with his baseball smarts and clubhouse gravitas, lifted the Red Sox to the postseason for the first time in three years as the Astros missed the playoffs for the first time since 2016.
Those vibes were as attractive to the Cubs as Bregman’s career .846 OPS when they pursued him after he opted out of his contract with Boston. And it’s all come together in Wrigleyville: Thanks to a second-half surge, Bregman has hit 26 home runs, posted an .804 OPS and produced 5.4 WAR, second only to presumed MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong on the Cubs.
“Anytime Alex Bregman is playing an Alex Bregman brand of baseball, it’s just good for the program,” Crow-Armstrong told USA TODAY Sports last month.
And if he manages to play just days after suffering a gruesome eye injury, the legend will only grow.
Heroes of the fall
Bregman’s postseason constancy has put himself among some legendary and curious October stalwarts.
Advertisement
Unsurprisingly, the consecutive postseasons list is littered with alumni from the three dominant playoff groups of the wild-card era: The 1990s Atlanta Braves, the late-century New York Yankees and the current batch of Los Angeles Dodgers.
Yankees closer Mariano Rivera tops the list, appearing in 13 consecutive postseasons from 1995-2007, followed by Derek Jeter, whose 12-year streak began a year after Rivera’s playoff debut.
Catcher Jorge Posada and Braves Hall of Famers Chipper Jones and Tom Glavine all played in 11 consecutive postseasons. As did lefty reliever Mike Stanton, who did it with four teams – the Braves, Red Sox, Yankees and Texas Rangers – between 1991-2002.
Who let him in?
Bregman, longtime Dodgers closer Kenley Jansen and Hall of Famer Greg Maddux all reached 10 consecutive postseasons. Current Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman and longtime third baseman Justin Turner are at the nine-year mark, Freddie winning a World Series championship with Atlanta in 2021 and two more in L.A. the past two seasons.
Retired Dodgers lefty Clayton Kershaw leads the “but for” category: He pitched in eight consecutive postseasons from 2013-2020, and would have made it 13 in a row if not for injuries in 2021 and 2024. Same with Braves Hall of Famer John Smoltz – he was present for all of Atlanta’s 14 consecutive division titles yet underwent Tommy John surgery in 2000.
And several likely 2026 participants had streaks broken thanks to one unlucky season – such as slugger Kyle Schwarber, who’d be working on a 12-year streak with the Cubs, Red Sox and Phillies if not for the 2019 Cubs missing the playoffs. Same with Mookie Betts, ticketed for his 10th postseason in 11 years with the Dodgers and Boston, missing only in ’19 with the Red Sox.
The wild-card format – which began in 1995 and expanded in 2012 and 2022 – makes this list unavoidably modern due to the expanded access it affords. Still, some players from past eras were near-constants in the playoffs.
Mr. October himself, Reggie Jackson, reached the postseason 10 times in 12 years from 1971 to 1982, winning four World Series with the Oakland Athletics and New York Yankees, and then, just for kicks, reaching the 1982 ALCS with the California Angels.
The great Yogi Berra was a 10-time World Series champion, but his longest consecutive streak of playoff runs was five years. Yet reaching the World Series 14 times in 17 years, when only two teams reached the playoffs, remains a stunning feat.
So perhaps Bregman - even with 102 career postseason games, 19 homers, 91 hits and a .791 OPS - has a little more work to do to match some of the legends of October. Yet from Houston to Boston to Chicago, he’s leaving little doubt that wherever he goes, winning follows.
This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Alex Bregman's wild MLB playoff streak has star in rare air – injured face willing

item.dc:creator: Mark W Sanchez
item.description:
Aaron Judge and Aaron Boone agree that the Yankees captain is doing everything he can to get back on the field as soon as he can. They spoke “a little bit,” the manager said Thursday, about the two things they apparently disagreed on:

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge and Aaron Boone agree that the Yankees captain is doing everything he can to get back on the field as soon as he can.
They spoke “a little bit,” the manager said Thursday, about the two things they apparently disagreed on:




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
First, Boone saying Tuesday he did not expect Judge to return in time for the wild-card series before Judge said Wednesday his goal is to be ready for Game 1 of that series; and second, the manager publicly conceding Judge’s calf strain is “moderate,” while the notoriously private — at least on the subject of injuries — Judge said he didn’t “know why [Boone] used those words.”
“I don’t want to get too much into that [conversation with Judge],” Boone said Thursday when asked about the two seemingly not being on the same page. “At the end of the day, we’re all in this together. And in his case, trying to get him right and get him healthy so he can be an option for us here at some point.
“But we’re also going to listen to the injury. I see it as just a passionate player that’s doing all he can to get back for his teammates.”
What others might interpret as annoyance or anger from Judge, Boone said was “passion.”
Boone — who all along has said he is not ruling out Judge returning in time for the postseason (even if it seemed and seems unlikely) — also said the roster decisions for a round that will begin Tuesday may not be made until Tuesday morning.
Thus, the Yankees will give Judge as much time as possible to recover from a calf strain suffered Sept. 16 — which was just seven games after he returned from a rib fracture that cost him more than three months — before declaring him in or out.
“The bottom line is Aaron and I have always had an amazing relationship and still do and will,” Boone said before finishing the series against the Rays in The Bronx. “This is about a player that, again, is pouring everything he possibly can into being ready, and we’re going to support that.
“And when he’s ready, we’ll make a call of when that is based on how he’s doing.”
Both superstar and manager have emphasized this week that Judge is doing everything in his power to build up quickly and be ready for a three-game series that almost certainly will be against the Red Sox, but Judge — who received a platelet-poor plasma injection Monday — is still limited barely a week after suffering the injury.
Notably, he is not swinging yet.
“He’s doing all the things in the training room, all the modalities, that you can take advantage of,” Boone said of Judge, who plans to return as a right fielder and not a DH. “He’s moving on the treadmill, things like that, doing the different exercises to get the calf healed.
“Doing everything he can to make that as speedy as possible.”

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK – Arropado profundamente dentro de una sudadera con capucha, Cam Schlittler se desplazaba por el clubhouse de los Yankees a primeras horas de la tarde del jueves, con una tableta de video afianzada en su mano derecha. Lucía la expresión firme de alguien enfocado en el futuro, no del todo listo para celebrar el final de una campaña con calibre de Premio Cy Young.
Sin embargo, este es un momento tan bueno como cualquier otro para apreciar el panorama. Schlittler le puso los toques finales a sus estadísticas con tres sólidas entradas en la victoria de Nueva York por 6-4 sobre los Rays, terminando con efectividad de 1.95 para ganarse un lugar entre los mejores rendimientos en una sola temporada en la historia de los Yankees.
Solo Spud Chandler (1.64 en 1943) y Ron Guidry (1.74 in 1978) han registrado una mejor efectividad en la historia de la franquicia que Schlittler, quien permitió dos carreras (una limpia) y tres hits a lo largo de tres episodios.
La efectividad de 1.95 de Schlittler es la mejor en la Liga Americana desde que Justin Verlander registró efectividad de 1.75 por los Astros en el 2022.
Los Bombarderos mantuvieron la cuenta de pitcheos de Schlittler a 70 en su 33ra presentación y última de la campaña regular, preparando al diestro para una asignación como abridor en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Aunque algunos anticipaban que fuera una certeza que el favorito al Cy Young abriera el Juego 1, el club de Nueva York está contemplando la idea de que Schlittler en vez lance en el Juego 2. El zurdo Max Fried está recibiendo una fuerte consideración para la asignación del primer compromiso, según el coach de pitcheo Matt Blake.
Schlittler ponchó a cinco bateadores de los Rays, terminando la temporada regular con 239 ponches. Eso lo empata con Jack Chesbro (239 en 1904) en la cuarta mayor cantidad para un jugador de los Yankees en una misma temporada; solo Gerrit Cole (257 en el 2022, 243 en el 2021) y Guidry (248 en 1978) han conseguido más.
Considerado hombro a hombro con Dylan Cease de los Azulejos durante gran parte de la campaña en el debate del Cy Young, Schlittler se apartó con un sólido cierre. Registró efectividad de 1.17 (10 carreras, siete limpias) en sus últimas nueve aperturas, a lo largo de 54 episodios.
Schlittler permitió apenas 27 imparables y 18 boletos a lo largo de ese trecho, que se remonta al 9 de agosto contra Atlanta, ponchando a 68. Se convertiría en el séptimo jugador de los Yankees en ganar el Premio Cy Young y el primero desde Cole en el 2023.

item.dc:creator: Joey Haverford
item.description: The New York Yankees have already confirmed their postseason path with a Wild Card series at home against the Boston Red Sox. Most fans assumed that American League Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler will start Game 1 since he's arguably the best pitcher in all of MLB this season. However, Yankees manager Aaron Boone recently claimed he's unsure of the order with Schlittler and Max Fried starting the first two in some order. MLB insider Bryan Hoch revealed Boone is not lying and transcribed pitchi
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have already confirmed their postseason path with a Wild Card series at home against the Boston Red Sox. Most fans assumed that American League Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler will start Game 1 since he's arguably the best pitcher in all of MLB this season. However, Yankees manager Aaron Boone recently claimed he's unsure of the order with Schlittler and Max Fried starting the first two in some order.
MLB insider Bryan Hoch revealed Boone is not lying and transcribed pitching coach Matt Blake sharing the Yankees are considering Fried over Schlittler for Game 1:
"I think it's more just getting all the information after his last outing here and making sure he's in a good spot to go on five days again. Max is on extended rest, and Cam would be on his third five day in a row. So just making sure he's in a good spot before we make any rash decisions."
Fried having extra rest is one reason given, but it still has Yankees fans on edge. The season has seen Fried hit with injuries for many months and having a shorter pitches limit in recent months. Schlittler is obviously the top pitcher for New York, but many fans trust Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon more than Fried right now.
Another Reason For Max Fried Yankees Won't Admit
One logical reason for Fried starting Game 1 would be the Yankees wanting a fully rested bullpen to enhance their chances. Fried has not thrown more than 100 pitches since May 3rd against the Baltimore Orioles.
Boone could view Fried as a trustworthy arm he may want to pull after 4 or 5 innings to start maneuvering bullpen matchups against top Red Sox hitters like Willson Contreras and Wilyer Abreu. This scenario would see Schlittler saved for Game 2 with fewer bullpen arms ready to go.
The reaction to this potential plan has been overwhelmingly negative in Yankees fan spaces since it feels like overthinking too much. History sees the best pitcher starting Game 1, and Sonny Gray is the expected starter for Boston since he's been the top starter all year. Boone is under fire to make the right decision here.
Yankees Will Likely Still Start Cam Schlittler
The logic of Fried having extra rest means little since Schlittler would be on his normal rest ahead of Game 1. Aaron Boone is expected to manage Schlittler's pitches and remove him after a few innings of limited work.
Game 3 remains the biggest question if the Yankees and Red Sox split the first two to set up a winner takes all scenario. Cole has the track record of being a legendary pitcher throughout his long career with the Yankees, Houston Astros and Pittsburgh Pirates.
Rodon has been on fire and looks better than ever since returning from injury. Boone will likely trust Cole more due to his history in big games. The Yankees must get by the rival Red Sox to enter the real playoffs with teams like Tampa Bay, the Cleveland Guardians and Texas Rangers in their way.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Why Yankees Are Considering Max Fried For Game 1 Vs Red Sox appeared first on HEAVY.

item.dc:creator: Mark W Sanchez
item.description:
Coming up through the Yankees’ system, George Lombard Jr. wowed as much with his athleticism and winning plays as he did with his bat and glove. One of those athletic, winning plays showed up in the majors on Thursday in a fun highlight in a game that did not matter much.

item.content:encoded:
Coming up through the Yankees’ system, George Lombard Jr. wowed as much with his athleticism and winning plays as he did with his bat and glove.
One of those athletic, winning plays showed up in the majors on Thursday in a fun highlight in a game that did not matter much.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
A slide both inventive and impressive helped the Yankees score a run in the seventh inning against the Rays in The Bronx, where the rookie shortstop awakened a crowd that was watching essentially an exhibition after the Rays already had clinched the division.
Lombard was on third base when Tampa Bay’s Brody Hopkins unleashed a wild pitch that bounced off the backstop but right back to catcher Liam Hicks.
Hicks took a few steps toward the ball, spun around and dove to the plate, beating Lombard easily.
But Lombard had begun a feet-first slide that he then abandoned once he saw Hicks, too, was on the ground.
In one motion, Lombard scrambled to his feet, took a step and tumbled over the plate and Hicks, dragging his right hand on the plate to cut the deficit to 4-3.
He then jogged into a Yankees dugout that was filled with smiling faces who had just witnessed a slide and tumble that few had seen before.
Lombard continued his heroics in the eighth inning after belting his seventh home run of the season to left field, giving the Yankees a 6-4 lead.
