item.content:encoded:
The Yankees announced Thursday that they have moved Saturday’s game against the Orioles to Friday because of the forecast for sustained inclement weather.
The postponed game will be played as the first game of a single-admission doubleheader at Yankee Stadium beginning at 4:05 p.m. Friday. The second game will start no earlier than 7:05 p.m. If the opener ends after 6:35 p.m., the second game will begin approximately 30 minutes after the final out.
CC Sabathia’s number retirement ceremony and Monument Park plaque unveiling will also take place Friday before the 4:05 p.m. game.
Only tickets dated Friday, Sept. 25, will be valid for the doubleheader. Tickets for the originally scheduled Saturday game will not be accepted Friday and can be exchanged for a comparable regular-season game, subject to availability.
Yankee Stadium gates will open at 2:30 p.m. Friday.

Chicago's Pete Crow-Armstrong walked to lead off the first inning and promptly stole second base to become the seventh player in MLB history to record at least 40 homers and 40 st
item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

25 Sep 2026, 02:35 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Matt Marton)
Nico Hoerner ripped a go-ahead RBI single in the sixth and Matthew Boyd tossed seven strong innings, helping the host Chicago Cubs clinch a playoff berth with a 2-1 victory over the Miami Marlins on Thursday afternoon.
Chicago's Pete Crow-Armstrong walked to lead off the first inning and promptly stole second base to become the seventh player in MLB history to record at least 40 homers and 40 stolen bases in a single season. Armstrong, who has 45 homers, joined Jose Canseco (1988), Barry Bonds (1996), Alex Rodriguez (1998), Alfonso Soriano (2006), Ronald Acuna Jr. (2023) and Shohei Ohtani (2024) as the only players to reach the 40-40 milestone.
Seiya Suzuki belted a solo homer in the fifth inning to highlight his two-hit performance for the Cubs (88-71), who salvaged the finale of their three-game series with Miami.
Boyd (10-5) allowed one run on five hits to record his second straight victory following a 0-4 stretch over his previous six starts.
Daniel Palencia bridged the gap to Ryan Zeferjahn, who retired the side in order in the ninth inning to secure his seventh save of the season.
Jakob Marsee had an RBI single in the third inning for the Marlins (78-81), who have lost four of their last six games.
With the game tied 1-1, Ian Happ tripled off Jack Ralston (0-2) to lead off the sixth inning and came home on Hoerner's RBI single to left field.
Ralston permitted two runs on three hits in 1 1/3 innings.
Brian Navarreto doubled to lead off the third inning against Matthew Boyd before coming home on Marsee's RBI single to center to open the scoring.
Suzuki forged a tie in the fifth inning, depositing a 1-0 pitch from Ralston over the wall in center field. The homer was Suzuki's 26th of the season and second in his last four games.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [740thefan.com] Pete Crow-Armstrong joins 40/40 club as Cubs clinch wild-card spot

Crow-Armstrong, who is tied for the MLB lead with 45 home runs, joins Jose Canseco (1988), Barry Bonds (1996), Alex Rodriguez (1998), Alfonso Soriano (2006), Ronald Acuna Jr. (2023) and Shohei Ohtani (2024) as the only players to collect at least 40 homers and 4
item.content:encoded:
By Field Level Media
Sep 25 (Field Level Media) – Pete Crow-Armstrong became the seventh player in MLB history with a 40-40 season, as he stole his 40th base of the season Thursday, the same day his Chicago Cubs clinched a playoff berth.
Crow-Armstrong, who is tied for the MLB lead with 45 home runs, joins Jose Canseco (1988), Barry Bonds (1996), Alex Rodriguez (1998), Alfonso Soriano (2006), Ronald Acuna Jr. (2023) and Shohei Ohtani (2024) as the only players to collect at least 40 homers and 40 steals in a season.
The favorite for National League Most Valuable Player walked to lead off the first inning against the visiting Miami Marlins and promptly stole second base.
He was stranded at third that inning, but the Cubs (88-71) went on to beat the Marlins 2-1 to lock in their NL wild-card playoff spot with three games to go.
“Recently here, I really felt how badly people wanted it for me, and I wanted it,” Crow-Armstrong said afterward. “I wanted to put myself in that same conversation as such impressive and great players. But every day I showed up and if I took the right base, it was going to help the team. And that’s how I’ve framed everything this year. I’m so lucky for that and that realization and that approach to (the) game.”
Crow-Armstrong saluted the crowd with his batting helmet in hand as he stood on second base.
“I was pretty emotional, I’m not going (to) lie,” Crow-Armstrong said. “I know I try and play it off sometimes like I’m all cool and s—, but I got a little thrown off when I ran out into the outfield today. … I’ve never felt anything other than love when I’ve been here and that was pretty emotional.”
Crow-Armstrong, 24, has played in all 159 games for the Cubs this season and batted .280 with 107 RBIs. His 45 long balls are tied with Philadelphia’s Kyle Schwarber for the major league lead.
(–Field Level Media)

item.title: [mlb.com] Hall of Fame broadcaster Matthews to be celebrated for 8,000th game of legendary career

item.content:encoded:
KANSAS CITY -- On a cold winter day during this past offseason, a dozen Royals media members gathered in the Kauffman Stadium press box to go through decades of baseball history.
Every single game Hall of Fame broadcaster Denny Matthews has ever called -- starting from the first Royals game in 1969 -- has been preserved through his scorecards, sorted by year, then eventually decade, and separated in manilla folders. Stars from the past fill these lineup cards -- Nolan Ryan, George Brett, Reggie Jackson, Cal Ripken Jr., Rickey Henderson, Ken Griffey Jr. among them -- telling the stories of thousands of games that Matthews has called throughout his legendary baseball career.
A few of those scorecards detail some of the Royals’ most iconic moments, like Kansas City’s two World Series titles or Brett’s 3,000th hit, signed by the Hall of Famer himself, but others are another day at the ballpark -- a single day in one of the 58 years and counting of Royals baseball.
Matthews has been in the booth for every single one. And after counting 86.6% of the total possible scorebooks in Royals history, it was discovered that Matthews will be calling his 8,000th game on Friday night against the Guardians at Kauffman Stadium.
"I don’t think I’ve really accepted that yet. It’s still just a number, and maybe when the season is over and I start thinking about that, it’ll take on a little different tone," Matthews said. "But that’s a lot of foul balls."
Matthews will be honored for his one-of-a-kind career on the television broadcast, as well as a special moment on the field, during Friday’s game in recognition of the achievement. But don’t worry, Matthews is planning to return for his 59th season in 2027.
“There’s so many reasons why I am still in Kansas City and the biggest reason is, I’m going to say organization but that doesn’t mean a lot, because organizations are people. And the reason that I’ve been around this long is because of the people I’ve associated with,” Matthews said.
“It’s the people that count. All in all, that’s why I’m still sitting here instead of being in Chicago or St. Louis -- or Cucamonga.”
That one-liner is a perfect example of the quick wit and humor listeners have come to expect from the longtime broadcaster. But he’s also telling the truth, at least about the first two cities. Matthews grew up in Illinois, between St. Louis and Chicago, and had dreamed as a young broadcaster of eventually moving on to cover one of the teams who he grew up listening to.
When Matthews was 10 years old, he would lay in front of the radio and listen to broadcasters such as Jack Buck and Jack Brickhouse, taking in their every word and falling in love with the game. Like every kid, his real dream was to play, of course, and Matthews did in high school and college before turning to broadcasting -- although he wouldn’t cover baseball until the Royals.
“Listening to those guys, all those summer nights, I was getting a great college education in how to broadcast baseball, and I didn’t have to pay any tuition and I didn’t have to do homework,” Matthews said. “... A lot of that was in my mind when I probably sat down and would describe a play the way that Jack Buck or Jack Brickhouse did. But when I was hearing all those games all those years and it was preparing me, I had no idea what I was eventually [going to do]. That’s pretty cool I think.”
Buddy Blattner and Matthews formed the first Royals radio broadcast duo in club history in 1969, and it was Blattner that helped guide the then-26-year-old Matthews while he settled into the booth and began forming his signature broadcasting style.
“One thing that is really underappreciated about him is not just his ability to describe the game, but his ability to analyze the game,” said broadcaster Ryan Lefebvre, who has worked with Matthews since 1999. “... He has a great feel for the game, which sets him up to see things happen before they actually happen. And it’s not like he has this crystal ball and ability to look into the future, … but I’ve been with him in the booth when he’s predicted things a pitch or two before they happen, and it’s just amazing.
“The feel for the game that he has and his ability to analyze the game hasn’t been part of describing Denny Matthews as much as it should be.”
It wasn’t long before other teams noticed that talent, including large markets like Chicago and New York, but a conversation with Royals founder and former owner Ewing Kauffman left a lasting impression on Matthews after just his third season in the booth.
“[Kauffman] said, ‘I’ll tell you what young man. You’re going to have other opportunities and decisions to make … but I want to tell you one thing, we like the way you do the games and you can stay here as long as you want,’” Matthews said. “... So here we are, 58 years later.
“The Kansas City Royals to me have been family.”
Matthews has in turn been a central part of baseball families in Kansas City, spanning generations of Royals fans as a common voice. He’s just one of four announcers in MLB history to broadcast for the same team for at least 50 seasons, joining Vin Scully (67 with Dodgers), Jaime Jarrín (64 with Dodgers) and Bob Uecker (54 with Brewers).
Matthews called 99.5% of Royals games from 1969-2000, missing only 23 games over 32 seasons (5,061 out of 5,084). He’s been calling games since before Apollo 11 landed on the moon, and even when it did, Matthews called both games of a doubleheader against the White Sox at Comiskey Park on July 20, 1969.
He’s watched the introduction of the designated hitter (1973), the Wild Card (1995), Interleague Play (1997), pitch clock (2023) and much more while providing a stable voice in the booth while the sport and world changed around him for nearly six decades. Matthews has called games featuring the franchises oldest-born (Ted Abernathy, 1933) and youngest-born player (Carter Jensen, 2003) in club history. Matthews even got married last year inside Kauffman Stadium.
“He is a walking, living, breathing encyclopedia of the Kansas City Royals,” Lefebvre said. “There is nobody that comes close as far as being able to, not just know the history of the Royals, but have observed the history of the Royals. … It’s kind of like sitting at the feet of your grandfather and just learning from someone who has experienced so much life. And to be able to turn words into pictures, and turn pictures into words, there’s nobody else in Major League Baseball like him.”
Matthews was inducted into Cooperstown in 2007 following his Royals Hall of Fame induction in 2004. He’s a Ford C. Frick Award winner, one of the highest honors for a broadcaster, and is in the Missouri Sports Hall of Fame.
And he’s still sitting in the Royals broadcast booth in 2026, calling every home game. His road trips have declined in recent years, although he makes occasional appearances at Busch Stadium and Wrigley Field, but his love for the game hasn’t. He returned to Spring Training this season after not traveling to Arizona the past couple of years because in his words, “I missed it.”
Radios across Kansas City have broadcast the words of Matthews for decades during Royals games. It’s been that way literally forever. And on Friday night that impact will be celebrated.
“Denny has always been there. Denny is the constant of Royals baseball,” said broadcaster Jake Eisenberg. “The very first time that they played a game, Denny’s the one who said, ‘Royals win.’ When they win their next game, he’ll be the one that says, ‘Royals win.’
“There is nobody like Denny Matthews that has existed in baseball history, and there is nobody that ever will again. There is nobody that has been the voice of a franchise, since its existence, for as long as he has been … and we should not take that for granted.”

item.title: [marca usa] Aaron Judge vs. Aaron Boone: Crece la tensión en los Yankees
item.dc:creator: Jose Rodriguez

item.content:encoded:
- MLB. Aaron Judge desafía la postura de Aaron Boone y planea superar su lesión para estar listo en playoffs
- MLB. La grave lesión de Alex Bregman podría obligar a la MLB a romper una tradición de larga data: "No tenemos por qué seguir haciendo eso"
Con apenas tres juegos restantes en la temporada regular y los New York Yankees enfocados en su debut en los playoffs, el estado de Aaron Judge sigue rodeado de incertidumbre. Lo que parecía una actualización médica rutinaria ahora se ha convertido en un debate público, después de que el estelar bateador contradijera abiertamente al manager Aaron Boone, una situación que ya llamó la atención de un reconocido analista de MLB.
Judge cuestiona la postura de Aaron Boone
Mientras Judge continúa fuera de acción por una lesión en la pantorrilla, Boone aseguró que el equipo no espera contar con su capitán para la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana y describió la molestia como una distensión de grado moderado.
Sin embargo, Judge rechazó esa evaluación y dejó claro que su objetivo sigue siendo estar listo para el Juego 1 de la postemporada, lo que llevó al veterano periodista Ken Rosenthal a señalar en Foul Territory que este tipo de desacuerdos públicos son poco habituales dentro de la organización de los Yankees.
"La historia de anoche fue Aaron Judge insistiendo en que quiere jugar. Su plan es jugar y, aunque fue sutil, sí contradijo a Boone. Las palabras importan. No me importa cuánto estuviera sonriendo cuando lo dijo", comentó Rosenthal.
El reconocido analista de MLB también destacó otro punto en el que Judge pareció discrepar con su manager: la gravedad de la lesión.
"Judge también pareció cuestionar que Boone calificara la distensión como moderada. Dijo: 'Una distensión moderada para una persona no es igual que para otra'. Entonces, ¿qué está pasando aquí? Porque con los Yankees rara vez se ve este tipo de desacuerdo hacerse público", agregó Rosenthal.
Una situación poco común dentro de los Yankees
Rosenthal considera que no hay duda de que Judge está haciendo todo lo posible por regresar lo antes posible y cree que sus declaraciones reflejan la mentalidad de una superestrella que no quiere perderse el béisbol de octubre. Sin embargo, advirtió que las lesiones en la pantorrilla suelen ser impredecibles.
"Quizá Aaron Judge se recupere de repente, pero las lesiones en la pantorrilla son notoriamente complicadas. No sé cómo terminará esto. Lo que sí sé es que es muy inusual ver a los Yankees mostrando este nivel de desacuerdo públicamente", concluyó Rosenthal.
A pocos días del inicio de la Serie de Comodines, la situación de Judge sigue sin resolverse. Mientras Boone prepara a los Yankees como si no fuera a contar con su máxima figura, Judge mantiene un mensaje firme: su intención es estar en el terreno de juego para el Juego 1 de los playoffs.

item.title: [New York Post] Michael Kay not ‘close at all’ to Yankees retirement after Mets’ Howie Rose steps away from booth

I don’t t
item.content:encoded:
Michael Kay doesn’t think he’s “close at all” to starting to think about his broadcast future, though he joked in a phone interview with The Post on Thursday that “when you reach a certain age, people are going to wonder.”
Kay, 65, has started to hear speculation and the retirement of Mets broadcaster Howie Rose last week likely added more intrigue, but the longtime Yankees sportscaster isn’t looking ahead in that way.
“It’s funny because I worry about that decision whenever I make it. I don’t think I’m close to it at all,” he said. “I love the line, God laughs at those that make plans.”
Kay has been part of Yankees’ radio and TV broadcasts for 35 years and said on Thursday that he still feels good, noting how much health can play into any decision.
He also reiterated a comment he made on the Awful Announcing podcast last month when he was asked if he would follow in longtime Yankees play-by-play radio announcer John Sterling’s footsteps and carry on his career behind the microphone into his 80s.
“I probably can’t even imagine being 80, so I can’t imagine what I’d be doing then,” Kay said.
The Yankees broadcaster also recalled a conversation he had with Rose when the Mets announcer called it “strange” that their colleagues stayed in their jobs as long as they do.
“I said, ‘because it’s a great job. Why would you, why would you give it up willingly,’” Kay recalled saying to Rose. “Obviously, if you lose your skill or you see yourself slowing down, then you probably owe it to your bosses and the audience to consider.
“But I don’t think I’m anywhere near that. I guess other people would have to judge that for themselves, but I think I’m a pretty good judge of myself, so I don’t see retirement anytime in the future.”
Kay won’t be slowing down during the postseason either, as he’s slated to call the national radio broadcast of the Yankees’ Wild Card series on ESPN Radio.
The series will be aired locally on 880 ESPN, and Kay will also be working the pre- and post-game shows on YES Network during the length of the Bronx Bombers’ playoff run.
The Yankees voice added one other reason for not looking too far into what his future holds, joking that his son — a diehard Bronx Bombers fan — is “dead set against it.”
“He knows there’s advantages to your father is the Yankee announcer,” he said jokingly. “Then let’s say that I continue to do it.
“Well, in five years, my daughter’s in college, and six years, my son’s in college, and I don’t know if [Kay’s wife] Jody would want me around that much.”

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 MLB regular season has been a roller coaster ride for the Philadelphia Phillies.
After being as many as 10 games under the .500 mark in April, they managed to claw their way back and are on the cusp of clinching a playoff spot. They are essentially one victory away from being in the National League field because the San Diego Padres and Arizona Diamondbacks, two of the teams they are competing with, are facing off this weekend, so someone has to lose.
Heading down the stretch, and hopefully into the postseason, the Phillies' biggest strength is their starting rotation. Even potentially being without Jesus Luzardo hasn’t taken too much luster off the group because Aaron Nola has found his groove the last few weeks.
After a disastrous start to the campaign, in which he was in the running as the least effective starting pitcher in baseball, he has completely turned his season around since the calendar flipped to July.
Aaron Nola has earned the confidence of Don Mattingly
So much so that interim manager Don Mattingly has the utmost confidence in giving the ball to his veteran righty should the need arise in the postseason.
“What he’s been able to do for us, it’s kind of turned that spot in the rotation to (where) you feel like he’s going to give you a good game every time now,” Mattingly said, via Charlotte Varnes of The Athletic (subscription required). “He’s just like Sanchy and Zeus and Wheels — you just feel like you’re getting a good outing every time.”
Through his first 17 starts of the season, Nola had a 6.04 ERA after a brutal outing against the Pittsburgh Pirates when he allowed eight runs, seven earned, in only 4.1 innings of work. He was failing to execute, leading to short outings.
Only four times in those first 17 outings did Nola pitch beyond the fifth inning, not providing the kind of length the team needed. Lacking options to turn to, the team had to hope their veteran would eventually figure it out, and luckily for them, he did.
In 15 starts since that point, Nola has produced a 3.10 ERA across 89.1 innings with 90 strikeouts.
Aaron Nola has been performing at a high level
On top of that, his efficiency has improved as well. He was working deeper into games, recording more than five innings pitched on 11 occasions. That was a major help, taking pressure off the bullpen to cover so many innings on days that he pitched.
Home runs have remained a bit of an issue, surrendering 17, but he has done a much better job of limiting the damage. For example, he gave up two to the Milwaukee Brewers, but both were solo shots, as self-inflicted wounds aren’t clogging the basepaths.
“I gave up a lot of home runs this year,” Nola said, “but I felt like more solos in the second half rather than the first, (which was) two-, three-run homers a lot. (I was) just not making as quality pitches (then), and pitches were kind of hanging a little bit more than the second half.”
This turnaround feels legitimate, with Nola providing much more than a normal No. 4 pitcher would. He has earned the trust of Mattingly to be the No. 3 starter behind Cristopher Sanchez and Zack Wheeler for however long Luzardo is sidelined.

He was a contributor to HoopsHabit, with work featured on Bleacher Report and Yardbarker. In addition to his work here, he is a reporter for both NBA Analysis Network and NFL Analysis Network, as well as a writer and editor for Packers Coverage. item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – CC Sabathia will enter Yankee Stadium’s Monument Park one day earlier than originally scheduled, with the Orioles and Yankees having postponed Saturday’s contest due to a forecasted nor’easter.
The clubs are now scheduled to play a single-admission doubleheader on Friday, with first pitch set for 4:05 p.m. ET.
The second game will start no earlier than 7:05 p.m. ET. If the first game ends later than 6:35 p.m. ET, Game 2 would start approximately 30 minutes after the end of Game 1.
Tickets for Saturday’s game (Saturday, Sept. 26) will not be valid for the single-admission doubleheader.
Friday also marks a coveted promotional item, a Yankees bobblehead depicting Josh Hart of the NBA champion Knicks. All Yankee Stadium gates will open to fans with valid tickets at 2:30 p.m. ET. The bobbleheads are being distributed to the first 18,000 guests in attendance.
The Yankees are encouraging fans to arrive by 3 p.m. ET for the Sabathia ceremonies.
Fans with paid tickets for Saturday’s game (Saturday, Sept. 26) may exchange them for tickets to a similar regular-season game at Yankee Stadium (subject to availability) as described in the Yankees’ rain check policy, which may be found at www.yankees.com/raincheck.
Tickets can be exchanged online only and cannot be exchanged in person at the Yankee Stadium Ticket Office.
Sunday’s 3:20 p.m. ET game between the Orioles and Yankees currently remains on as scheduled.

item.content:encoded:
CHICAGO (AP) — Pete Crow-Armstrong joined the 40-40 club by stealing his 40th base to go along with his major league-leading 45 home runs, and the Chicago Cubs clinched their second straight postseason berth a 2-1 victory over the Miami Marlins on Thursday.
Seiya Suzuki homered for the Cubs (88-71), who assured themselves of one of the NL’s three wild card berths.
Chicago also was a wild card last year, when the Cubs beat San Diego in the first round and lost to Milwaukee in a Division Series. The Cubs will be making consecutive postseason appearances for the first time since four straight from 2015-18, which in 2016 included their first championship since 1908.
The Cubs clinched their berth shortly after the White Sox earned their postseason trip with a 9-1 win at Kansas City.
Miami (78-81) was assured its third straight non-winning season.
A favorite to win the NL MVP award, Crow-Armstrong became the seventh 40-40 player, joining a group that includes Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani and Atlanta Braves outfielder Ronald Acuña Jr. Jose Canseco was the first with the 1988 Oakland Athletics.
Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th homer during Sunday’s 9-1 win at Cincinnati, extending his career high. The 24-year-old drew a leadoff walk from Tyler Phillips in the first inning and swiped second base on the next pitch to Suzuki for his 40th steal in 47 attempts. Fans chanted “MVP” as the Wrigley Field videoboard proclaimed the feat.
Ohtani was the previous player with a 40-40 season, hitting 54 homers and stealing 59 bases for the 2024 Dodgers. Acuña hit 41 homers and swiped 73 bases for Atlanta in 2023. Alfonso Soriano (2006 with Washington), Alex Rodriguez (1998 with Seattle) and Barry Bonds (1996 with San Francisco) are the other 40-40 players.
Matthew Boyd (10-5) allowed one run, five hits and two walks over seven innings, and Ryan Zeferjahn pitched a perfect ninth for his seventh save to finish a five-hitter.
Ian Happ tripled off Jack Ralston (0-2) to start the sixth and came home three pitches later on Nico Hoerner’s single, breaking a 1-1 tie.
Miami’s Jakob Marsee had an RBI single in the third and Suzuki hit his 26th homer in the fifth, a drive off Jack Ralston.
Up next
The Marlins return to Miami on Friday to begin a season-ending, three-game series against Atlanta.
The Cubs play a day-night doubleheader Friday at Boston. The opener was shifted to Sunday by Major League Baseball because of a forecast for a storm.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] Yankees Sequence of the Week: Carlos Rodón (9/22)
item.dc:creator: Peter Brody
item.description: The Yankees were officially eliminated from the AL East title race by the Rays’ win in the second game of the doubleheader on Tuesday. item.content:encoded:
The Yankees were officially eliminated from the AL East title race by the Rays’ win in the second game of the doubleheader on Tuesday. They managed to temporarily stave off elimination thanks to a dominant performance by Carlos Rodón in the first game of the day’s twin billing. With eight scoreless innings, he equalled his longest outing in a Yankees uniform to lower his season ERA to a sterling 2.67. Given the gravity of the performance and the game, it was a no-brainer to select Rodón for our Sequence of the Week.
We join Rodón facing Liam Hicks to lead off the top of the second. With one of MLB’s best run suppressors in Nick Martinez on the mound for the Rays, the task ahead of Rodón is a tough one. Hicks has proven an inspired pickup from the Marlins by the Rays at the deadline, batting .305 with a 143 wRC+ in 123 plate appearances since making the switch from the Atlantic Coast to the Gulf Coast, which explains why the catcher is batting cleanup for Tampa Bay.
Rodón starts Hicks with a first pitch four-seamer at 93 mph, Ali Sánchez setting a target low and away.
Rodón nails his spot with this fastball, painting the corner for called strike one. Hicks must be looking for something on the inner half, because he watches it go by without a thought of offering.
It appears Rodón is satisfied with the way that pitch felt coming out of the hand, because he goes right back to that pitch-location combo.
Same pitch, even better execution. Rodón paints the bottom edge of the zone with this 93 mph four-seamer for strike two called. It’s obvious at this point that Hicks is hunting something he can pull given the bat has not left his shoulder, and this is the last pitch you want to be trying to get out in front of.
At this point, Hicks has to defend that corner of the strike zone. Establishing the four-seamer for called strikes there has Hicks perfectly set up for the wipeout slider down and away out of the zone as he’s now forced to look away.
It’s the right idea but just without the execution to match. Rodón pulls this slider a hair, bouncing it beyond home plate for ball one. It looks like a ball low out of the hand, making for a pretty easy take from Hicks.
Rodón is still in the driver’s seat with the count 1-2. He’d be well within his rights to try another slider low and away, this time trying to execute it closer to the zone. However, he elects to go back to the four-seamer, if not for the strikeout then to set up a future slider.
Even though Rodón fails to elevate this four-seamer where he wants it and ends up leaving it in a pretty dangerous place, the 19 inches of induced vertical break keep the pitch above Hicks’ barrel, leading to a foul ball rather than a ball in play. What’s more, as we are about to see, this fastball is the perfect setup pitch for a chase slider.
By continuing to prove that he can land his four-seamer on the outer edge of the zone, Rodón keeps the door open for Hicks to chase a slider.
Rodón unleashes a dandy, this slider looking like a strike out of the hand before falling off the table for the swinging strikeout. This kind of slider is so tough to lay off because it remains over the plate for the entire journey toward home, the sharp downward movement carrying it into an unhittable location. Rodón can thank the prior four-seamer for the outcome of this slider.
Look at the way the slider and the four-seamer that immediately preceded it look exactly the same coming out of Rodón’s hand. Rodón landing that four-seamer where he did set a perfect target for him to tunnel the subsequent slider. Hicks really never had a chance at distinguishing the two pitches from each other and goes down with a weak hack.
Here’s the full sequence:
Rodón is hitting his stride just in time for the playoffs. Over his last eight starts he has a 1.67 ERA with less than one home run allowed per nine, allowing two or fewer runs in all eight of those appearances. He really can’t do much more when it comes to making a case for the postseason rotation. The competition is fierce, with Cy Young frontunner Cam Schlittler starting early on and Aaron Boone looking likely to pick 2024 ace Gerrit Cole and 2025 ace Max Fried for the two other Wild Card Series starts. Even with Rodón’s recent excellence, he could be out of luck unless they advance. Still, Rodón has certainly earned the opportunity and is someone I would absolutely feel confident handing the ball.
We’ve written a lot about Rodón’s evolution as a starting pitcher to being a more well-rounded complete package thanks to the mastery of changeup and sinker. I certainly do not want to downplay this transformation and how key it is for his longevity. However, this outing was something of a throwback start for Rodón — a glimpse of the peak version from his days in Chicago and San Francisco. He whiffed over 30-percent of batters on his four-seamer and over 40-percent on his slider, that deadly pitch pairing the hallmark of his earlier years. This AB in particular was vintage Rodón, with each four-seamer exhibiting at least 19 inches of induced vertical break — well above the threshold that is considered elite — and his slider dropping two inches more than its season average. If he can hold onto the feel of this start, the Yankees will have a real weapon in the playoffs, be that out of the rotation or the bullpen.

item.title: [amsterdamnews.com] Can the Yankees take down the Red Sox without Aaron Judge?

item.content:encoded:
This was supposed to be the year the Yankees would win the franchise’s first World Series since 2009. A roster that included all-time greats Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera and Alex Rodriguez, Hall of Famer CC Sabathia, and Series MVP Hideki Matsui, one of the best players Japan has ever produced.
Yet, as the Yankees look towards Tuesday, when they open the playoffs at home against what is virtually certain to be the Boston Red Sox, their longtime nemesis, in a best-of-three wildcard series, the prospects of them navigating an always perilous path to the World Series were reduced when Yankees manager Aaron Boone said this past Tuesday that the reigning American League MVP likely won’t play in the series due to a right calf strain.
“We’re planning on him not being a part of that,” Boone revealed to reporters.
Judge, who has only appeared in 66 games this season, primarily recovering from a right rib stress fracture, which caused him to sit out 84 games from May 31 to Sept. 8, is now on the 10-day injured list, placed there last Friday. The 34-year-old Judge, arguably the best player in the sport over the last decade, isn’t expected back for the divisional round if the Yankees get by the Red Sox.
Last weekend, Boone informed the media the team didn’t have a firm estimate as to when Judge, a three-time AL MVP, three-time AL home run leader, two-time MLB RBI king and last season’s MLB batting champion, would return to the lineup.
“I mean, I have no idea, we’re in the early stages,” expressed Boone, now in his ninth season as the Yankees manager. “We’ll just obviously treat it and see what transpires.”
The Yankees watched Tampa Bay clinch the AL East title on Tuesday at Yankee Stadium when they won the second game of a double-header on Tuesday 6-1. The Yankees shut out the Rays in the opener. Tampa Bay 96-61 going into the third game of the four-game series last night with the finale scheduled for 7:05 tonight. The Yankees were second in the division at 90-67 and the 84-73 Red Sox third.
With Judge unavailable, the Yankees offense will have to be multifaceted — both power and small ball will be required to make a deep postseason run. Designated hitter Ben Rice, who as of Wednesday had 39 home runs and 95 RBIs, both team highs, was the only Yankee with more than 20 homers and 80 runs batted in, so timely power will have to come from sources such as second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. (19 home runs), first baseman Paul Goldschmidt (18), and left fielder Cody Bellinger (17).
But it is pitching that must advance the Yankees, led by leading AL Cy Young Award candidate Cam Schlittler, who is 14-6 with a 1.94 ERA and 234 strikeouts. Schlittler is scheduled to start tonight before taking the mound next week in the wildcard series.
But the prevailing question is: Can the Yankees win without Judge?

Schmidt had hoped to throw on Thursday, but that was nixed as his arm discomfort lingered. He was warming up in the bullpen in Sunday's series finale against the Diamondbacks, but cut it short due to what he described as "bicep cramps." Schmidt told reporters after the game that it was a precautionar
item.content:encoded:
Clarke Schmidt is back on the shelf with another injury.
The Yankees announced Thursday afternoon that the righty is being placed on the 15-day IL with right bicep neuritis, retroactive to Sept. 21. Schmidt had hoped to throw on Thursday, but that was nixed as his arm discomfort lingered. He was warming up in the bullpen in Sunday's series finale against the Diamondbacks, but cut it short due to what he described as "bicep cramps." Schmidt told reporters after the game that it was a precautionary measure.
Schmidt played catch on Tuesday and Wednesday as he tried to shake the bicep troubles, but it did not improve, meaning he will not be an option for the Wild Card Series against the Red Sox, which begins on Tuesday night.
Schmidt had recently returned from Tommy John surgery, and will finish the regular season having made just one appearance in relief, tossing 0.2 innings.
The injury to Schmidt is the latest blow for a Yankee team counting on injured pitchers to return and give their beleaguered bullpen a boost for the postseason. Ryan Weathers, who was having a splendid season before landing on the IL, was seen as a good bet to return in time to make an impact in relief come October, but he is no longer expected to be ready before the end of the regular season, making it hard to imagine he will be on the Wild Card Series roster. Brent Headrick has looked more human of late as his heavy workload continues, and Fernando Cruz is still trying to make his way back from a partially torn UCL.
A potential bullpen option is off the table for the Wild Card Series.

item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday night, the New York Yankees beat the Tampa Bay Rays (at home) by a score of 9-3.
They were led by Ben Rice, as he hit two home runs.
The Yankees wrote (via X): “Last night, Ben Rice became the third Yankee in franchise history to hit at least 40 HR within his first three Major League seasons, joining Aaron Judge and Joe DiMaggio 🙌”
Gerrit Cole Makes Rice Statement
Gerrit Cole got the start on Wednesday.
He allowed two earned runs (with eight strikeouts) in 5.2 innings.
After the game, Cole was asked about Rice (via YES Network).
Reporter: “We’ve seen a lot from Ben Rice over the last year-plus. But 40 and 41 now. What does it say about his continued development and what he really means to this lineup?”
Cole: “Super proud of him. Really exciting season for him. Deserves it too. He works really hard and puts in a lot of work behind the scenes. And had a great night tonight along with Mac. That was great to see along with George. Just keep plugging along. Those homers were huge for us. The offense played well. And we played pretty good defense in a tough environment tonight too. So overall really great, and a nice night for Ben.”
Looking At Rice
Rice was picked in the 12th round of the 2021 MLB Draft.
He is currently batting .263 with 148 hits, 41 home runs, 97 RBIs, 103 runs and three stolen bases in 151 games.
The 27-year-old has spent all three seasons of his MLB career with the Yankees.
Looking At Cole
Cole is in the middle of his 13th MLB season.
He has also had stops with the Pittsburgh Pirates and Houston Astros.
Right now, Cole is 10-9 with a 3.61 ERA in 22 starts.

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees will be operating without Clarke Schmidt again.
New York placed Schmidt back on the IL with right bicep neuritis before Thursday's game.
Because of the IL stint, the right-hander will not be a bullpen option for the Yanks for at least the upcoming Wild Card series.
Schmidt had been warming up to enter Sunday afternoon's series finale against the Diamondbacks when he first started experiencing bicep soreness.
He underwent testing earlier this week, and the team felt he was in a "pretty good spot."
The 30-year-old was set to play catch at Yankee Stadium on Wednesday to determine his availability, but he was unable to do so and now officially lands back on the IL.
Schmidt made just one big league appearance in his return from Tommy John surgery, striking out two of the four batters he faced last Wednesday against the Twins.
In his place, Bradley Hanner has been recalled from Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre.

item.title: [whec.com] Judge hopes to be ready for playoffs and Stanton could return for Yankees after 5 1/2-month absence

item.content:encoded:
Judge hopes to be ready for playoffs and Stanton could return for Yankees after 5 1/2-month absence
NEW YORK (AP) — Yankees slugger Aaron Judge hopes to return from a strained right calf for the playoffs next week and Giancarlo Stanton could be back after a 5 1/2-month absence.
New York manager Aaron Boone repeated he’s not counting on Judge to play in the AL Wild Card Series opener Tuesday. Judge, sidelined since Sept. 16, said he’s trying to do all he can to be in the lineup.
“The Bronx is a magical place in October,” Judge said after Wednesday night’s 9-2 win over AL East champion Tampa Bay. “I don’t want to miss out on that opportunity.”
Judge had a platelet-poor plasma injection Monday. He was sidelined by a fractured rib from May 31 to Sept. 8 and played in just seven games before the latest injury.
“Any injection doesn’t feel too good that day, but I feel a lot better today and we’re going to keep making strides,” he said.
A three-time AL MVP, Judge is hitting .241 with 18 homers, 41 RBIs and an .871 OPS in 66 games this season, including .174 with one homer and three RBIs since coming back from the rib injury.
“We are going to listen to the body and see how he heals,” Boone said. “If he is in a position to do that, obviously we are going to want him. So, no, I haven’t ruled anything out, of course.”
Boone said Tuesday he wasn’t planning on having Judge available for next week’s best-of-three series, likely against Boston.
“Obviously as a player, you don’t want to hear that but that’s out of my control,” Judge said.
Boone said Judge had a moderate strain.
“Everybody’s `moderate’ is a little different,” Judge said.
Stanton, trying to return from injuries to calf muscles in both legs, faced pitchers Wednesday at Double-A Somerset along with center fielder Trent Grisham, sidelined since straining his right hamstring on Sept. 4. Both ran the bases and Stanton homered while taking six or seven at-bats.
“Putting them on the outskirts of the conversation,” Boone, bothered by a cold, said in a raspy voice.
Following the end of the seasons for Yankees farm teams, New York has minor leaguers working out at Somerset in nearby New Jersey.
Stanton hasn’t played since April 24 because of strained calf muscles in both legs after starting the season with a .256 batting average, three homers and 14 RBIs in 24 games. The 36-year-old former NL MVP had 38 homers and 100 RBIs in his first season with New York in 2018 but has missed 500 of 1,194 games since (41.9%), through the end of this regular season.
His other injuries included strains of his right biceps, right knee, left hamstring (three times), left quadriceps and both calf muscles along with right ankle inflammation, left Achilles tendinitis and tendon pain in both elbows.
“You’re looking more at a pinch-hit scenario,” Boone said. “We’ll see if that’s even a realistic option.”
Stanton is owed $25 million next year in the final guaranteed season of a $325 million, 13-year contract that includes a $10 million buyout of a 2028 club option.
Lagrange could be brought up for major league debut
Carlos Lagrange, a 23-year-old right-hander who reached 100 mph with 98 pitches at Triple-A this year, threw to batters at Somerset. He was out between June 28 and Sept. 16 because of a right capsule strain.
Lagrange was shifted to the bullpen at the start of June.
“He’s in the conversation for something,” Boone said.
Clarke Schmidt still out
Right-hander Clarke Schmidt, who returned Sept. 16 following Tommy John surgery in July 2025, played catch but remains sidelined by right biceps cramps. New York had hoped to use him as a reliever in the postseason.
“Today was better than yesterday,” Boone said. “If he’s not a real viable option by tomorrow, then we’ll probably go a different way.”
Postseason rotation
Boone said Cam Schlitter will start Game 1 or 2 of the playoffs. Max Fried appears set to start whichever game Schlittler doesn’t, with Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón available for Game 3.
“Whoever goes 1 or 2 can pitch 2 and 5 in the next series,” Boone said.
Fernando Cruz throws a bullpen
Right-hander Fernando Cruz threw a bullpen this week and is to throw another one Thursday.
He hasn’t pitched in a game since Aug. 25 because of right elbow discomfort caused by a partially torn ulnar collateral ligament.
“I’m in a really good position to be back I will say in the next couple of weeks,” Cruz said.
He took issue with the diagnosis of his injury.
“I had a real good inflammation, real stiffness and irritation,” he said. “People can say it’s a partial tear, but in my heart it’s not a partial tear.”
Volpe will see time at the hot corner
With second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. back from a sprained right thumb, Boone said Anthony Volpe will see time at third.
“I’ll probably get him on there a time or two,” Boone said.
Volpe entered Wednesday hitting .263 with one homer, seven RBIs and four stolen bases over 11 games since his recall from Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre. He played three games at third base for the RailRiders.
“It didn’t feel that bad when I played there, but we’ll see,” Volpe said.
___

The Yankees placed Schmidt on the 15-day injured list Thursday with right bicep neuritis, retroactive to Monday.
Schmidt's move to the injured list will officially rule him out for the AL Wild Card Series and the start of the ALDS, but there's a chance that the Yankees may shut the 30-year-old down for the season and focus on getting him ready for 2027. He appeared in just one regular-season game this year, allowing two hits and recording two strikeouts in two-thirds of an inning Sept. 16 against Minnesota. Bradley Hanner will come up to fill the open bullpen spot.

item.title: [Fox News] Why Yankees ace Cam Schlittler is in the AL MVP conversation and could join an exclusive club
item.dc:creator: Ryan Canfield
item.description: If you shoot for the moon, you will land among the stars. In Cam Schlittler’s case, however, he and his blazing fastball may take him past the stars and straight to the moon. The New York Yankees ace has been nothing short of dominant this season. The swashbuckling 25-year-old is all but a lock to win the American League Cy Young Award. But why stop there? He should win the American League MVP too. Schlittler should become just the 12th player in MLB history to win the Cy Young and MVP in the sa
item.content:encoded:
If you shoot for the moon, you will land among the stars. In Cam Schlittler’s case, however, he and his blazing fastball may take him past the stars and straight to the moon.
The New York Yankees ace has been nothing short of dominant this season. The swashbuckling 25-year-old is all but a lock to win the American League Cy Young Award.
But why stop there? He should win the American League MVP too. Schlittler should become just the 12th player in MLB history to win the Cy Young and MVP in the same season.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
Heading into his final start of the year against the Tampa Bay Rays on Thursday, Schlittler leads all American League pitchers in ERA (1.94) and is tied for first in WHIP with Drew Rasmussen (0.91). He has been durable, making all his starts, and is second in the AL in innings pitched (190 2/3).
With a devastating combination of cutters, sinkers and fastballs, the young right-hander has racked up 234 strikeouts, third in the AL behind Cleveland Guardians ace Gavin Williams (244) and likely Cy Young runner-up Dylan Cease (239).
Schlittler has set a Yankees franchise record by allowing one or no runs in 21 starts this year. He became just the third pitcher age 25 or younger in the live-ball era, which began in 1920, to achieve the feat, joining Dean Chance (1964) and Blake Snell (2018).
Schlittler also leads the AL in bWAR with 7.0, ahead of other MVP contenders such as Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez (6.6), Kansas City Royals star Bobby Witt Jr. (6.5) and Rays phenom Junior Caminero (5.6).
The numbers for Schlittler are outstanding, but they don’t tell the full story.
Schlittler has been the pillar of the Yankees' pitching staff, which leads all of baseball with a 3.21 team ERA.
While the pitching staff has been fantastic, it has have dealt with plenty of injuries to the starting rotation.
Gerrit Cole didn’t make his season debut until May 22, as he was recovering from Tommy John surgery. Carlos Rodón began the season on the IL after undergoing surgery to remove a bone spur and loose bodies and didn’t debut until May 10. That was just his first stint on the IL. He returned to the IL on July 3 and didn’t come back until Aug. 18.
Rodón was not the only Yankees ace to land on the IL twice, as Max Fried did as well. Fried first went on the IL with a left elbow bone bruise on May 13, right after Cole returned, and was activated on July 22. He went on the IL for a second time on Aug. 17 with the same injury and returned Aug. 29.
Ryan Weathers, who had been key in stepping up during the absences of Cole, Fried and Rodón, went on the IL on Aug. 23 with a left forearm flexor strain.
For the Yankees, not only was it paramount that Schlittler make every start, but it was also essential that he remain dominant to help keep the rotation afloat.
Adding to the pressure on Schlittler and the pitching staff as a whole, the Yankees’ offense cratered after Aaron Judge was placed on the IL at the beginning of June. Since June 1, the Yankees have hit a paltry .229 with a putrid .297 on-base percentage.
The Yankees’ offensive ineptitude put further pressure on Schlittler and Co. to win games without Judge.
In 2023, the Yankees’ season went off the rails when Judge suffered a torn ligament in his toe. They went 25-31 without the captain and missed the postseason. The Yankees’ pitching staff in 2023, led by Cole, who won the AL Cy Young Award that season, had a 3.97 ERA, which was not enough to save the Yankees from finishing 82-80.
In 2026, the Yankees went 48-41 without Judge in the lineup, buoyed by the pitching staff’s excellence. Carried by the Schlittler-led pitching staff, the Yankees made the postseason and secured home-field advantage in the American League Wild Card Series.
While the Yankees didn’t catch the Tampa Bay Rays and win the American League East, they might have missed the postseason entirely if it weren’t for Schlittler.
By the award’s definition, Schlittler has been the most valuable player on his team.
Alvarez has been dominant in his own right. The hulking left-handed hitter, with a .316 batting average, 41 home runs and 102 RBI made a bid for the Triple Crown, but that seems out of reach.
Alvarez has been primarily a designated hitter, filling that role in 131 of the 154 games he played this season. Shohei Ohtani is the only player to win an MVP as a primary designated hitter, and he did so after becoming the first player to hit 50 home runs and steal 50 bases in a season.
Unless Alvarez surges to win the Triple Crown, nothing he is doing this season is unprecedented or historic.
Alvarez’s Astros, who are 78-80, might miss the postseason despite playing in the American League West, a division that has been historically bad.
Bobby Witt Jr. has been his usual superstar self but missed 11 games due to injury and has also taken a slight step back from last season while playing for the AL Central-worst Kansas City Royals.Caminero, the linchpin of the AL-leading Rays’ lineup, trails Schlittler in bWAR by more than a full win. Still, his .274 average and 41 home runs leave him in the thick of the AL MVP race.
Despite the excellence of Alvarez, Witt and Caminero, Schlittler should become the first pitcher since Justin Verlander in 2011 to win the American League MVP.
Verlander, like Schlittler this year, led the American League in bWAR with 8.6.
Without Schlittler, the Yankees do not survive Judge’s absence. When the Yankees could hardly scrape together three runs a game in the dead of summer, Schlittler made sure it was enough to hold on.
Without Schlittler’s dominance and durability, the Yankees do not have the second-best record in the American League (91-67).
Without Schlittler, Yankees fans are in a complete state of panic because they might still be trying to secure a Wild Card berth in a weak American League.
At the sportsbooks, Schlittler is a long shot to win the American League MVP. But odds be damned, the award should be his. He has landed on the moon.

item.title: [MLB.com] ¡De locura! Dieciséis datos asombrosos de la temporada del 2026
item.dc:creator: Anthony Castrovince
item.description: En el Día Inaugural de este año, los Cardenales y Rays jugaron un partido en el que cada uno anotó seis carreras o más en la sexta entrada. Apenas llevábamos unas horas en la temporada del 2026, y ya los investigadores del Elias Sports Bureau estaban buscando en los libros de récords para encontrar que un juego del 19 de abril de 1890 entre los Boston Beaneaters y los Brooklyn Bridegrooms marcó la última vez que dos escuadras habían anotado tantas rayitas en un solo inning en un partido inaugura
item.content:encoded:
En el Día Inaugural de este año, los Cardenales y Rays jugaron un partido en el que cada uno anotó seis carreras o más en la sexta entrada. Apenas llevábamos unas horas en la temporada del 2026, y ya los investigadores del Elias Sports Bureau estaban buscando en los libros de récords para encontrar que un juego del 19 de abril de 1890 entre los Boston Beaneaters y los Brooklyn Bridegrooms marcó la última vez que dos escuadras habían anotado tantas rayitas en un solo inning en un partido inaugural.
Así comenzó nuestra dosis diaria de estadísticas de locura en el béisbol.
Ahora que la campaña del 2026 está a punto de terminar, revisemos esos libros para ver cuáles números extraños de todo el año la han hecho tan especial.
(Todas las estadísticas son hasta los juegos del martes. Como de costumbre, ¡gracias a la investigadora Sarah Langs, que es increíble en el mejor de los sentidos, por su ayuda en la recopilación de esta lista!)
.673
El OPS de Pete Crow-Armstrong al llegar al primer tercio de la temporada de los Cachorros. Esto, de un muchacho que terminó registrando una temporada de 10 de fWAR (la versión de FanGraphs de Victorias por Encima del Reemplazo) y que probablemente se lleve fácilmente el premio a Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Nacional.
Nunca ha habido un giro similar. Entre los 56 jugadores anteriores en tener una campaña de 10 de fWAR, éstas fueron las marcas de OPS más bajas en el primer tercio:
Eddie Collins, Atléticos de Filadelfia de 1909: .826
Mike Trout, Angelinos del 2012: .835
Honus Wagner, Piratas de 1908: .894
Trout, Angelinos del 2013: .920
Wagner, Piratas de 1905: .924
Como pueden ver, nadie se había acercado a un OPS tan bajo como el de PCA en el primer tercio de la campaña de camino a un total de WAR tan extraordinario. PCA sólo valía 1.4 de fWAR en ese momento. Ahora, podemos decir que ha tenido posiblemente la mejor temporada individual en la historia de la no tan joven franquicia de los Cachorros. Un repunte en plena campaña para el recuerdo.
200+
Tanto Jacob Misiorowski de los Cerveceros (223) como Cam Schlittler de los Yankees (217) tienen EFE+ por encima de 200, lo que significa que han sido más del doble de buenos que el promedio de la liga. Por eso son los presuntos favoritos para los Premios Cy Young.
En primer lugar, es inusual contar con dos lanzadores con una EFE+ de al menos 200 en una sola campaña. Eso sólo ha ocurrido dos veces en una temporada completa en este siglo: En el 2015 (Jake Arrieta y Zack Greinke) y en el 2018 (Jacob deGrom y Blake Snell).
Pero lo doblemente asombroso aquí es que tanto Misiorowski como Schlittler están apenas en su segunda campaña en las Mayores. Los únicos otros monticulares en la Era de la Bola Viva (desde 1920) en tener una EFE+ de al menos 200 en su primera o segunda temporada fueron Dwight Gooden en su legendaria campaña de 1985 (229) y Paul Skenes en su año del Cy Young en el 2025 (226).
81
Victorias para los Medias Blancas. Eso es por mucho la mayor cantidad para un equipo después de tres temporadas consecutivas de 100 derrotas o más. El récord anterior había sido de 70, logrado por los Astros del 2014, los Senadores de Washington de 1965 y los Bravos de Boston de 1925.
Ningún equipo ha clasificado para los playoffs después de siquiera dos campañas seguidas de 100 derrotas. Los Patipálidos podrían convertirse en los primeros.
106
Bases por bolas para el cañonero cubano de los Astros, Yordan Álvarez -- la mayor cantidad en las Mayores.
Si Álvarez de alguna manera puede conseguir la Triple Corona de la Liga Americana en estos días finales (necesita superar a Pete Alonso por el título de impulsadas), no sólo sería el primero en lograr esa hazaña en cualquiera de las ligas desde el venezolano Miguel Cabrera en el 2012. También sería apenas el segundo jugador en ganar una Triple Corona y a la vez liderar la liga en bases por bolas. Ted Williams lo hizo en 1942 y 1947.
Para los niños que nos leen: Ustedes quieren batear como Ted Williams. Eso es algo bueno.
16
El número de jugadores esta temporada que han dado jonrón en su debut en MLB. Es un nuevo récord, tres más que el tope anterior establecido en el 2022.
2
Salvamentos para el as dominicano de los Marlins, Sandy Alcántara, quien además es el líder en entradas lanzadas en las Grandes Ligas (213.0). Desde que el rescate se convirtió en una estadística oficial en 1969, la única vez, según Elias, que un lanzador registró un salvamento en una campaña en la que lideró Grandes Ligas en entradas lanzadas fue cuando Phil Niekro lo hizo en 1978.
2
El número de equipos para los cuales Jo Adell ha conectado el cuadrangular más largo de la campaña. Dio un bambinazo de 449 pies para los Angelinos el 10 de mayo y luego, tras un cambio a mitad de año, conectó uno de 455 pies para los Guardianes el 18 de agosto. Ningún otro jugador en la Era Statcast ha dado el vuelacercas más largo de su club en múltiples equipos en la misma temporada.
3.98
La proporción de ponches por cada base por bolas del novato de los Guardianes, Parker Messick. Messick podría ser finalista al Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, gracias a un comando que es sumamente inusual para alguien con tan poca experiencia en Grandes Ligas. El único otro novato en la Era Moderna (desde 1900) con al menos 180 entradas y una mejor proporción K/BB fue el miembro del Salón de la Fama Don Sutton (4.02), con los Dodgers de 1966.
6.7
El bWAR (modelo de Victorias Sobre Reemplazo de Baseball-Reference) de la sensación novata de los Tigres, Kevin McGonigle. Es el más alto de todos los tiempos para un jugador en una temporada de debut en la que pasó la mayor parte del año con 21 años o menos. La marca anterior era de 6.6, conseguida tres veces: Por el dominicano Albert Pujols en el 2001, Frank Robinson en 1956 y aquel tal Ted Williams que mencionamos anteriormente, en 1939.
1.16
La efectividad de Cam Schlittler como visitante. Es la tercera mejor en la Era de la Pelota Viva para un lanzador con al menos 100 episodios fuera de casa. Las únicas mejores cifras pertenecieron a los miembros del Salón de la Fama Bob Gibson (0.81) en 1968 y Greg Maddux (1.12) en 1995. (Cabe destacar que ninguno estaba en su segunda temporada de Grandes Ligas en ese momento).
235
El EFE+ de Shohei Ohtani en 85.2 innings lanzados.
Es demasiado fácil acostumbrarse a lo que hace Ohtani e incluso restarle importancia a su campaña como jugador de dos vías, dado que los problemas de lesiones lo obligaron a dejar de lanzar a principios de julio. ¡Pero esto no es normal! En la Era Moderna, apenas otros ocho abridores de las Ligas Americana/Liga Nacional han registrado un EFE+ de al menos ese nivel con un mínimo de 85 entradas lanzadas:
Jacob deGrom, Mets de 2021: 373
Pedro Martínez, Medias Rojas de 2000: 291
Greg Maddux, Bravos de 1994: 271
Maddux, Bravos de 1995: 260
Bob Gibson, Cardenales de 1968: 258
Clayton Kershaw, Dodgers de 2016: 237
Clay Buchholz, Medias Rojas de 2013: 237
Obviamente, es inherentemente más impresionante registrar un EFE+ de ese nivel lanzando durante una temporada más completa. ¿Pero saben qué más es impresionante? Conseguir un EFE+ tan alto mientras también registras OPS de .902 en casi 600 visitas al plato.
De nuevo, no es normal. Ni siquiera para Ohtani.
47
La cifra de bases robadas, líder de las Mayores, del segunda base de los Nacionales, el dominicano Nasim Núñez, quien por lo demás está teniendo dificultades ofensivas esta temporada. Núñez tiene OPS de .529. El único otro jugador en la Era Moderna con OPS inferior a .550 que aun así logró robarse 40 bases fue Rollie Zeider (OPS de .548, 49 robos) de los Medias Blancas de 1910.
.374
El porcentaje de slugging de Cal Raleigh. El mismo Cal Raleigh que disparó 60 cuadrangulares la temporada pasada. De las nueve ocasiones anteriores en las que un jugador tuvo una campaña de 60 bambinazos, el porcentaje de slugging más bajo en la campaña siguiente había sido el .485 de Roger Maris en 1962. Eso sigue siendo más de 100 puntos superior al de Raleigh, quien pasó de ocupar el tercer lugar entre los bateadores calificados de MLB en SLG el año pasado (.589) a estar ahora entre los últimos 25.
42
Salvamentos desperdiciados por los Nacionales, un nuevo récord de Grandes Ligas. La marca anterior era de 36, establecida por los Medias Blancas en el 2024, cuando perdieron 121 juegos. Se podría decir que los Nacionales hicieron “volar” ese récord.
217, 28
Totales de ponches de los compañeros de los Filis Kyle Schwarber y el venezolano Luis Arráez, respectivamente. Schwarber está compitiendo por el liderato de ponches de MLB, mientras que Arráez (quien llegó procedente de los Gigantes en un cambio durante la Fecha Límite) terminará de último en ponches entre los bateadores calificados de la Gran Carpa.
Según Elias, sólo ha habido cuatro ocasiones en la Era de la Expansión (desde 1961) en las que el líder de MLB en ponches y el jugador con la menor cantidad de ponches (nuevamente, entre los bateadores calificados) terminaron la campaña en el mismo equipo… ¡y dos de ellas también involucraron a los Filis!
Medias Blancas de 1963: Dave Nicholson (más ponches), Nellie Fox (menos ponches)
Filis de 1965: Dick Allen (más), Octavio “Cookie” Rojas (menos)
Filis de 1976: Mike Schmidt (más), Dave Cash (menos)
Angelinos de 1982: Reggie Jackson (más), Tim Foli (menos)
0.8
Terminemos con la recta. Éste es el porcentaje de todos los pitcheos en MLB este año que han sido registrados a 100 mph o más. No se trata sólo de que sea el porcentaje más alto de la era de seguimiento de pitcheos (que se remonta al 2008), sino de que ni siquiera está cerca. ¡La cantidad de pitcheos de 100 mph o más ha aumentado en un 43.5%… tan sólo desde el año pasado!
Una razón más para que tengan nuestro permiso de ignorar a cualquier veterano que intente decirles que antes los lanzadores tiraban igual de duro.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Cam Schlittler is one start away from joining Ron Guidry in Yankees history
item.dc:creator: Tate Mosher
item.description: After his electric performance in Game 3 of the American League Wild Card series versus the Boston Red Sox last season, expectations for New York Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler suddenly grew for 2026. The 25-year-old was a seventh round selection in the 2022 draft by New York, but nonetheless rocketed through the minor leagues to make his debut in July 2025. Over that regular season, he made 14 starts with a 2.96 ERA. With the season he had plus that exceptional showing against Boston in a
item.content:encoded:
After his electric performance in Game 3 of the American League Wild Card series versus the Boston Red Sox last season, expectations for New York Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler suddenly grew for 2026.
The 25-year-old was a seventh round selection in the 2022 draft by New York, but nonetheless rocketed through the minor leagues to make his debut in July 2025. Over that regular season, he made 14 starts with a 2.96 ERA.
With the season he had plus that exceptional showing against Boston in a winner-take-all playoff game, anyone could have said he would be a good pitcher. However, Schlittler's performance this season has somehow blown expectations out of the water.
Potential Yankees history
Ahead of his 33rd and final start of the regular season Thursday versus the Tampa Bay Rays, the All-Star can make some franchise history. Per Gary Phillips of NY Daily News, Schlittler can become the third Yankee starting pitcher ever to finish a season with an ERA below 2.00.
Across 32 starts, Schlittler is 14-6 with a 1.94 ERA. He has pitched 190 ⅔ innings, striking out 234 and walking 47. He had a splendid half-season in 2025, but has impressively toned down the walks and upped the strikeouts this year.
With the way things look currently, Schlittler will win the AL Cy Young Award when it is announced in November. If so, he will become the seventh Yankee to win the award, and would join his teammate Gerrit Cole (2023) in the honor.
Looking ahead to the postseason
Aug 28, 2026; Bronx, New York, USA; New York Yankees pitcher Cam Schlittler (31) pitches against the Boston Red Sox during the first inning at Yankee Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Tom Horak-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
New York is locked into their current position of the No. 4 seed in the AL. They will host the No. 5 seed in the Wild Card round, with the winner advancing to take on the Rays in the Division Series starting Oct. 3.
In all likelihood, it will be a rematch of last year's Wild Card with the Red Sox traveling to the Bronx for a best-of-three. Including that series, Schlittler is 3-1 with a 0.56 ERA and 39 strikeouts against his hometown team in his brief career.
With the Massachusetts native taking the mound Thursday versus Tampa Bay, he likely will not pitch Game 1 against Boston next Tuesday. A normal rest schedule would have him in line for Wednesday's Game 2.

item.content:encoded:
El número 41 apareció en la pantalla del Yankee Stadium y, por un instante, los Yankees volvieron a mirar hacia 1961.
Ben Rice conectó dos cuadrangulares el miércoles ante Tampa Bay para llegar a 41 en la temporada. El segundo puso al primera base de Nueva York en el mismo escalón de jonrones que Pete Alonso, Junior Caminero y Yordan Álvarez en la Liga Americana.
Pero el verdadero alcance de la noche va más allá de una carrera por el liderato de cuadrangulares. Rice acaba de entrar de lleno en la conversación por el MVP de la Liga Americana en la última semana del calendario. Sus números de temporada, después de 162 partidos para Nueva York, son 41 jonrones, 97 carreras anotadas, 148 hits, .263 de promedio, .362 de porcentaje de embasarse y .899 de OPS.
Al otro lado del clubhouse está Cam Schlittler.
El derecho de 25 años se convirtió en el brazo alrededor del cual gira la conversación por el Cy Young de la Americana. Después de 32 apariciones suma 14-6, 1.94 de ERA, 190.2 innings, 234 ponches y 0.91 de WHIP.
Pareja que entraría a los libros de historia de Yankees
Si Rice terminara conquistando el MVP y Schlittler el Cy Young, los Yankees volverían a tener en una misma temporada a los ganadores de los dos premios individuales más importantes de la Liga Americana. La última vez ocurrió en 1961.
Ninguno de los dos llegó a Nueva York con la etiqueta de fenómeno inevitable.
Rice fue elegido por los Yankees en la ronda 12 del Draft de 2021, con la selección 363, procedente de Dartmouth. Schlittler fue seleccionado en la séptima ronda de 2022, con el pick 220, después de jugar en Northeastern.
No fueron elecciones de primera ronda. No fueron nombres destinados desde el Draft a cargar con el uniforme de los Yankees.
Hoy, sin embargo, Rice es un bateador de 41 jonrones y Schlittler es el líder de una rotación que tiene al resto de la industria hablando del Cy Young. MLB describió recientemente la transformación de Schlittler como la de un séptima ronda convertido en All-Star y candidato al premio.
Y mientras Aaron Judge pasó buena parte de 2026 fuera por lesión, Rice terminó ocupando el espacio ofensivo que quedó abierto. Judge apenas disputó 66 encuentros y bateó .241 con 18 cuadrangulares.
¡Qué sucedió en 1961 para los Yankees!
Roger Maris y Whitey Ford escribieron una de las temporadas más reconocibles en la historia de la franquicia.
Maris bateó 61 cuadrangulares, rompió el récord de 60 que Babe Ruth había establecido en 1927 y terminó como MVP de la Liga Americana. En 161 partidos produjo .269/.372/.620, con 141 carreras impulsadas.
Ford, mientras tanto, tuvo una temporada que parecía diseñada para acompañar semejante hazaña: 25-4, 3.21 de ERA, 283 innings y 209 ponches. Ganó el Cy Young.
Los Yankees ganaron 109 juegos, conquistaron la Liga Americana por ocho juegos y después vencieron a Cincinnati en cinco partidos para ganar la Serie Mundial.
Existe además una precisión histórica importante. En 1961 todavía había un solo Cy Young para toda MLB. El premio comenzó a entregarse por separado en cada liga en 1967. Ford fue, por tanto, el ganador absoluto del Cy Young de 1961.
Rice no necesita batear 61 para entrar en esta conversación. Schlittler tampoco necesita reproducir exactamente los números de Ford.
Lo extraordinario sería que dos Yankees seleccionados fuera de las primeras rondas terminaran colocando sus nombres junto a Maris y Ford en la misma fotografía de premios.
¿Hay otros equipos con Cy Young y MVP en la misma temporada?
Antes de 1967, cuando el Cy Young era único para toda MLB, ocurrió con los Braves de 1957 —Hank Aaron y Warren Spahn—, White Sox de 1959 —Nellie Fox y Early Wynn—, Pirates de 1960 —Dick Groat y Vern Law— y Dodgers de 1962 —Maury Wills y Don Drysdale—.
Después de la división del premio por liga, la lista continuó con casos como Boston en 1986, Milwaukee en 1981, Oakland en 1990, Atlanta en 1991, Chicago White Sox en 1993, Oakland en 2002, St. Louis en 2005 y Minnesota en 2006. MLB registra 18 ocasiones en las que dos jugadores de un mismo equipo consiguieron MVP y Cy Young en la misma temporada hasta ese último caso.
También existe otra variante. Un mismo jugador ganó ambos premios en una temporada. Justin Verlander lo hizo en 2011, mientras Clayton Kershaw lo consiguió en 2014. En total, 11 pitchers han ganado Cy Young y MVP en el mismo año.
Por eso el último tramo de 2026 tiene una particularidad para Nueva York.
Today in 1961, Roger Maris of the @Yankees surpasses Babe Ruth’s record with his 61st homerun of the season. ⚾️
(📽 “61” released in 2001)#TodayInSports #PinstripePride
https://t.co/QJYClMw96G
Ben Rice y Cam Schlittler están en carrera por estos dos prestigiosos premios y también están intentando devolver a los Yankees a una fotografía que no aparece desde que Roger Maris y Whitey Ford hicieron historia hace 65 años.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Could New York shut Clarke Schmidt down amid injury concern? appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
As the New York Yankees prepare for the playoffs, they are also trying to manage some of the injuries they're dealing with. One of those players is Clarke Schmidt, who has been working through a biceps injury. He's been going through testing, and though it seems like he's progressing, there's a chance that the Yankees consider shutting him down, according to MLB.com.
"Sept. 22 was a 'better' day for Schmidt, who felt discomfort while warming up Sept. 20 at Arizona. If Schmidt is unable to pitch Sept. 24, the Yankees may shut him down," MLB.com wrote.
That's not the best news for the Yankees, as Schmidt is an important part of the team. Especially with it being the playoffs, they want to be as healthy as possible. Right now those chances are looking slim, but it all depends on whether he's able to pitch in their final game of the series against the Tampa Bay Rays.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
The Yankees are already going to be without Aaron Judge for their first playoff series as he deals with a calf injury. He is still hoping to come back at some point, but the goal is to be as healthy as possible.
"My goal is to come back as soon as I can," Judge said. "That's what we're doing right now. If [Boone] says I'm not gonna be ready, I've got no control over that. I've got control over what I can do to try to get back."
It'll be interesting to see what the Yankees' lineup looks like by the time they get to the playoffs.
