item.content:encoded:
Major League Baseball’s postseason is rapidly approaching, with the Los Angeles Dodgers seeking a third-straight World Series title. It remains to be seen how much some of the game’s biggest stars will be able to participate come October, though.
The Dodgers are once again among the best teams in the big leagues, and they’ll have several challengers in October, including the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays. All three teams could finish the regular season with 100 wins or more. Los Angeles is there even though four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani’s health is a concern.
The New York Yankees, Boston Red Sox and Atlanta Braves have also clinched spots in the postseason. The Yankees’ three-time MVP Aaron Judge is dealing with a right calf strain that will keep him on the injured list until at least the final day of the regular season.
The regular season ends this Sunday, and while the 12-team playoff field appears mostly set, there are a few long-shot contenders for the postseason, and specific matchups are in flux.
Here’s some of what to watch as the season comes to a close.
Here’s who can clinch a playoff spot Monday
No team can clinch a playoff spot on Monday with most of the league getting a day off.
There is one important game in the American League, where the Toronto Blue Jays travel to face the Baltimore Orioles. The Blue Jays are hanging on the fringe of the AL race, starting the day three games back of the final wild-card spot.
AL race is murky while NL is more defined
There’s quite a bit of mediocrity in the AL Central and West divisions this season, which has led to some fascinating pennant races and could lead to a sub-.500 team making the postseason.
The Cleveland Guardians (81-75) have a narrow advantage over the Chicago White Sox (80-76) in the AL Central while the Texas Rangers (78-78) are just ahead of the Houston Astros (77-79) in the AL West.
Over in the National League, the playoff bracket is close to set.
The Chicago Cubs (87-69), San Diego Padres (87-69) and Philadelphia Phillies (86-70) are jockeying for position in the wild-card race but will almost certainly make the postseason. The only team within shouting distance is the Arizona Diamondbacks (82-74), who are four games back.
MVP races, stats to watch
MLB’s major awards probably won’t have much drama this season.
Both MVP races have strong favorites with Chicago’s Pete Crow-Armstrong running away with the NL honor while Houston’s Yordan Alvarez is the probable choice in the AL, though Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero has also had a fantastic season. Alvarez still has a shot at a rare Triple Crown. He leads the AL in batting average at .313 but his 40 homers are one behind Caminero and his 99 RBIs are six back of Baltimore’s Pete Alonso.
For the Cy Young Award, Milwaukee flame thrower Jacob Misiorowski and New York ace Cam Schlittler are the favorites in the NL and AL, respectively.
The Rookie of the Year races also look set with Cincinnati’s Sal Stewart and his 110-RBI season the leader in the NL and Detroit’s Kevin McGonigle the favorite in the AL.
What is the MLB playoff format?
There are 12 teams that qualify for MLB’s postseason, including six teams from both the AL and NL. The three division winners in each league get seeds No. 1 through No. 3, ranked by win-loss record. Then the three wild-card teams get seeds No. 4 through No. 6, also ranked by win-loss record.
The top two teams with the best record in both the AL and NL automatically advance to the Division Series. The other eight teams play in the Wild Card Series, which is a best-of-three format beginning on Tuesday, Sept. 30. In both the AL and NL, the No. 6 seed will travel to face the No. 3 seed while the No. 5 seed goes to No. 4. The higher seed hosts all three games.
The winners then advance to the best-of-five Division Series, followed by the best-of-seven League Championship Series and a best-of-seven World Series between the winners of the AL and NL.
What is the MLB postseason schedule?
Wild Card Round: Sept. 29-Oct. 1 (NBC/Peacock)
Division Series: Oct. 3-10 (AL on TBS, NL on FOX/FS1)
Championship Series: Oct. 11-20 (AL on TBS, NL on FOX/FS1)
World Series: Oct. 23-31 (FOX)
Who are the favorites to win the World Series?
The Dodgers (+220) are the favorites to capture a third straight World Series title while the Brewers (+600), Yankees (+800) and Rays (+800) are viewed as the top contenders.
___
See AP’s full MLB coverage here
David Brandt, The Associated Press

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Aaron Judge Injury: Yankees Impact in Shifting AL Playoff Race
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: Over the last few days, Aaron Judge has been the talk of Major League Baseball. Judge is back on the Injured List after returning from the IL for a brief seven-game stint. Judge has played in just 66 games this season and the biggest question in baseball is whether he will be able to return during the postseason. If Judge is Judge, then the Yankees are built to make a run to the World Series. If Judge doesn't return, all of a sudden the Yankees look like a team that could have a short playoff ru
item.content:encoded:
Over the last few days, Aaron Judge has been the talk of Major League Baseball.
Judge is back on the Injured List after returning from the IL for a brief seven-game stint. Judge has played in just 66 games this season and the biggest question in baseball is whether he will be able to return during the postseason. If Judge is Judge, then the Yankees are built to make a run to the World Series. If Judge doesn't return, all of a sudden the Yankees look like a team that could have a short playoff run. On Monday, Joel Sherman of the New York Post gave an update that will could certainly impact the race.
"There's some strong possibility he doesn't play anymore," Sherman said. "Calf strains are notorious for when they heal, let them heal more because it is a re-injury area of the body."
At this point, the vibes aren't high or pointing towards a return for Judge. Calf injuries are tough. Jim Bowden of The Athletic reported that Judge is dealing with a soleus strain. The playoffs begin in eight days. On Sep. 29, the Yankees will begin a three-game Wild Card series, very likely against the Boston Red Sox.
If Sherman is correct and Judge doesn't return, it completely changes the calculus of the American League playoffs. A healthy Judge balances New York's lineup. Without him, the Yankees are lefty-heavy. Outside of Ben Rice, no other member of the Yankees has hit more than 20 homers as a member of New York this season. Luis García Jr. has 30 total homers, but has hit just seven in a Yankees uniform. The power threat isn't the same without Judge.
The Tide Is Shifting In the American League
New York will have to face off against the Red Sox in a three-game Wild Card series, barring something shocking happening. Even if the Yankees were to win, they would then have to go against the American League-leading Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Division Series. A brutal one-two punch, to say the least.
Without Judge, that arguably should make the Red Sox the favorites in a three-game set. New York's lineup is lefty-heavy. The Red Sox happen to be loaded from a left-handed pitching standpoint. The Red Sox could roll with Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez in two out of three games. Plus, Garrett Crochet is close to returning in a bullpen role. Imagine a scenario in which the Red Sox start either Tolle or Suárez in a game and then get multiple innings out of a healthy Crochet afterward? That's the worst-case scenario for a Yankees lineup that is full of lefties.
If Boston advances, it would be a toss-up between the Red Sox and the Rays in an ALDS series. Then, either would be the favorite in the American League Championship Series over the Chicago White Sox, Cleveland Guardians or the Texas Rangers. Arguably, the Red Sox should be the favorites in the American League in general right now with Judge out, although it would be close. The Red Sox have been the best team in baseball since the end of June and now the path is a little clearer.
The American League runs through the American League East. If Judge was fully healthy, New York would be the favorites. The Yankees' rotation is electric and this team can seriously put up runs when Judge is at his best. Judge is the most impactful right-handed hitter in baseball. This is a guy who three out of the last four AL MVP awards, including the last two years in a row. When he's on the field, he moves the needle. Without him, the Yankees are still good, but they're not as big a World Series threat.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick also received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Fastball On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.title: [si.com] The Brewers Are About to Test the Limits of Power Pitching
item.dc:creator: Tom Verducci
item.description: This article is a part of Verducci’s View, a new weekly baseball newsletter from Sports Illustrated senior writer Tom Verducci. Every Monday, Tom empties out his notebook over email and covers MLB’s hottest topics, provides in-depth analysis through both text and video breakdowns, looks forward to what’s worth watching during the week and more. If you want to be featured in his new mailbag, please email newsletters@si.com with any questions about MLB or his decades in the sport. Can an old-schoo
item.content:encoded:
This article is a part of Verducci’s View, a new weekly baseball newsletter from Sports Illustrated senior writer Tom Verducci. Every Monday, Tom empties out his notebook over email and covers MLB’s hottest topics, provides in-depth analysis through both text and video breakdowns, looks forward to what’s worth watching during the week and more. If you want to be featured in his new mailbag, please email newsletters@si.com with any questions about MLB or his decades in the sport.
Can an old-school, fastball-based power pitching staff win the World Series? As spin has overtaken the game, recent history says no. None of the past 17 full-season champions ranked among the top five teams in fastball usage. Eleven of the 17 champions ranked in the bottom half in fastball use:
2008-25 World Champions Fastball% MLB Ranks (Full Seasons)
| Rank | Champions |
|---|---|
| 1–5 | 0 |
| 6–10 | 3 |
| 11–15 | 3 |
| 16–20 | 3 |
| 21–25 | 3 |
| 26–30 | 5 |
As the game has moved away from fastballs as the foundation of pitching, three teams are out to prove you can still win it all by throwing heaters more than half the time: the Brewers, Red Sox and Yankees, the only three playoff teams (and among only six overall) that throw more than 50% fastballs (cutters not included).
The Brewers are the ultimate test of how far power pitching can take a team. We have never seen a pitching staff like this in the postseason.
Milwaukee will have the highest average fastball velocity in postseason history (95.9 mph), the most pitches clocked at 100 mph in recorded history by a 62% margin over any other staff and as many as six pitchers on their postseason roster who have hit 100. In Jacob Misiorowski and high leverage relievers Abner Uribe, Aaron Ashby and Trevor Megill, manager Pat Murphy can use nothing but 100-mph arms to win a game.
Most Pitches 100 MPH in MLB History
| Team | Pitches |
|---|---|
| 1. 2026 Brewers | 1,141 |
| 2. 2026 Padres | 703 |
| 3. 2018 Padres | 673 |
| 4. 2026 Dodgers | 565 |
| 4. 2024 Athletics | 565 |
Milwaukee should avoid the temptation to follow the industry trend of throwing fewer fastballs in the postseason. Last season, in getting swept by the Dodgers, Brewers pitchers Freddy Peralta (down 10.3%) and Misiorowski (down 13.3%) typified how Milwaukee went away from its usual rate of fastballs (down 3.8% overall).
Since 2018, the Brewers have played .573 baseball in the regular season, fourth best in MLB, but .355 baseball in the postseason (11-20).
Here are the facts about fastball use to keep in mind entering playoff baseball:
- Fastball use is at an all-time low (47.1%).
- Fastball average velocity is at an all-time high for a sixth straight year (94.6 mph).
- Batting average on fastballs in the last decade has dropped from .280 to .261, the second lowest mark in recorded history (since 2008).
- Fastball use in the postseason typically declines from the regular season, falling to an all-time low last postseason (46.5%).
Here is a look at regular season and postseason fastball use over the past 18 years. You will notice how 1) how the pitch-tracking boom in 2015 accelerated the decline of the fastball and 2) how teams generally throw fewer fastballs in the postseason:
The experience of former manager Joe Maddon is that the more important the games become the more people in the front office want to get involved in game planning. Everybody wants to pull from their own silo of information to find the incremental edge that is sure to turn a series. Reinvent at your own risk.
The overriding aim of game planning is to pitch away from slug, especially as hits become more infrequent in the postseason. One swing can change a game. That’s the quick reason why fastball use goes down in October. MLB hitters slug .424 against fastballs and .381 against non-fastballs.
But the Red Sox (52.1% fastballs, only Seattle throws more), Brewers (51.8%) and Yankees (51.2%) should stick to their strengths. There is no need to reinvent Peyton Tolle of Boston, Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler of New York, who rank 1-2-3 in fastball use among pitchers with 1,400 pitches.
Last postseason was the postseason of the splitter, with more than double the rate of splitters (6.7%) ever seen in a regular season or postseason The champion Dodgers cut their fastball use from 45.9% in the regular season to 43.8% in the postseason—the lowest ever by a World Series winner—and the Blue Jays cut their fastball use from 45.7% to an incredible 37.9%—the lowest ever by a World Series loser.
Maybe, just maybe, this will be the postseason of the fastball. Only one potential playoff team ranked in the bottom 10 this year in fastball use, the Rangers. And if this October is a return to old-fashioned hardball, the Brewers must be the team leading the way.
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. He also is the only writer to be a game analyst for World Series telecasts. He lives in New Jersey with his wife, with whom he has two children.

item.title: [marca.com] Yogi Berra, New York Yankees legend: “It ain’t over ’til it’s over”
item.dc:creator: Jose Victor Escobar Rodriguez
item.description: - World News. Confucius, Chinese philosopher: "It does not matter how slowly you go as long as you do not stop" - Chicago Bulls. 'Michael Jordan: "I have failed over and over and over again in my life. And that is why I succeed"' There are certain phrases that become immortal, and without a doubt, the one attributed to Yogi Berra, the New York Yankees legend, is one of them. Not only because of the context in which it emerged, but also because of how relevant it remains whenever an athlete or te
item.content:encoded:
- World News. Confucius, Chinese philosopher: "It does not matter how slowly you go as long as you do not stop"
- Chicago Bulls. 'Michael Jordan: "I have failed over and over and over again in my life. And that is why I succeed"'
There are certain phrases that become immortal, and without a doubt, the one attributed to Yogi Berra, the New York Yankees legend, is one of them. Not only because of the context in which it emerged, but also because of how relevant it remains whenever an athlete or team is trying to complete a comeback in sports.
It was during his managerial career that Berra shared his most famous quote with the media:
It ain't over 'til it's over
Those words are still used today in situations where an athlete or team is facing elimination or is up against the odds and needs a comeback.
Berra's famous phrase came while he was managing the 1973 Mets and is actually a misquote.
Berra said those words midway through the season, when his Mets were sitting in last place in the standings, although he always clarified that his actual words were: "It isn't over until it's over." He even credited Rocky Bridges, another former Major League player, as the inspiration behind the expression.
What seemed like a simple motivational phrase ended up becoming a prediction. Berra's Mets rallied to win the division, stunned the Cincinnati Reds — the legendary "Big Red Machine" led by Pete Rose, Joe Morgan, Johnny Bench and Tony Pérez — in the National League Championship Series, and pushed the powerful Oakland Athletics all the way to Game 7 of the World Series.
Yogi Berra became one of the greatest legends in New York Yankees history, helping the franchise reach 14 World Series during his 18 seasons in the Bronx.
His legacy was defined by an extraordinary career: he played in more World Series games than any other player in Major League Baseball history, won three American League MVP awards, was selected to 15 All-Star Games, and received baseball’s highest honor when he was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 1972.

He’s now on the IL with a calf strain and is eligible to return with just a couple of games left in the regular season, but it’s unclear if the Yankees will go that route. Either way, with a postseason berth already locked up, the Yankees’ judgment day is rapidly approaching, and rather shortly they will have to make a decision on Judge. Well, Yankees pundit
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees were forced to place Aaron Judge back on the IL just a week after he returned from the 60-Day IL with a fractured rib.
He’s now on the IL with a calf strain and is eligible to return with just a couple of games left in the regular season, but it’s unclear if the Yankees will go that route.
Either way, with a postseason berth already locked up, the Yankees’ judgment day is rapidly approaching, and rather shortly they will have to make a decision on Judge.
Well, Yankees pundit Joel Sherman isn’t too optimistic that Judge will even play again this season, regardless of how far the Yankees advance.
More MLB on Heavy: Los Angeles Dodgers Josue De Paula Shares Honest Message
Joel Sherman Thinks Aaron Judge May Not Play Again This Season
Joel Sherman recently said (about Judge):
“There’s some strong possibility that Aaron Judge doesn’t play anymore this season”
It’s a very vague statement by Sherman, but certainly a major warning for Judge and the Yankees.
The good thing for New York is they’ve been without their star slugger for so long this season, and while their World Series chances take a significant hit without Judge, it’s not like this currently constructed roster isn’t used to not having him in the order (for this season at least).
There is growing belief that Aaron Judge may be so hurt that it’s not worth sending him out to play if he’s less than 50%.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Face Major Free Agency Choice on All-Star Pitcher
More on Aaron Judge’s Importance
If the New York Yankees are going to be without Aaron Judge for the rest of the MLB season, it will be all hands on deck for the rest of the squad.
Things tend to be magnified in the MLB playoffs, so there will need to be big swings from other contributors if the Yankees are going to make a deep run behind perhaps the best pitching staff in the playoffs.
With that being said, even if Judge’s playoff numbers don’t necessarily match his regular-season pace, his being in the batting order completely changes the complexity of how the opposing pitching staff targets the Yankees batters.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Mets Trade Pitch Offloads Mark Vientos to Pirates

item.title: [purplerow.com] Monday Rockpile: TJ Rumfield & Gabriel Hughes reflect on their rookie seasons
item.dc:creator: Samantha Bradfield
item.description: Gabriel Hughes and TJ Rumfield are two very different players. Hughes was drafted by the Rockies in the first round of the 2022 MLB Draft and has worked his way up through their minor league system. Rumfield was acquired from the Yankees in an offseason trade. Rumfield made the Opening Day roster; Hughes debuted mid-season. And, of course, Hughes is a pitcher coming off Tommy John surgery while Rumfield is a position player. But both have made an impact for the Rockies this year in different way
item.content:encoded:
Gabriel Hughes and TJ Rumfield are two very different players.
Hughes was drafted by the Rockies in the first round of the 2022 MLB Draft and has worked his way up through their minor league system. Rumfield was acquired from the Yankees in an offseason trade.
Rumfield made the Opening Day roster; Hughes debuted mid-season.
And, of course, Hughes is a pitcher coming off Tommy John surgery while Rumfield is a position player.
But both have made an impact for the Rockies this year in different ways.
TJ Rumfield
TJ Rumfield is making a case for NL Rookie of the Year. Through Saturday, he is slashing .302/.392/.454 with a 23-game on-base streak, the longest in the Majors and the longest single-season on-base streak by a rookie in franchise history.
But how would Rumfield sum up his rookie season?
“A lot of learning experiences,” he said. “I think a lot of the team stuff – trying to gel together with guys and make conversations with new people, and even when you have new faces in here, trying to make them feel comfortable because I know how I felt when I first got in the locker room. It’s just small things like that, and ultimately just learning every day.”
And those learning experiences have paid dividends for the rookie, as he ranks among all qualified rookie leaders in average (.302, 1st), OBP (.392, 1st), OPS (.846, 1st), hits (159, 3rd), and multi-hit games (41, T-2nd). Rumfield ranks among NL qualified rookies in doubles (29, 1st), RBI (70, 2nd), extra-base hits (47, 2nd) and total bases (239, 2nd). And he ranks among Major League leaders in OBP (.392, 3rd) and average (.302, 5th).
He and Yordan Alvarez (.312/.429) are the only qualified players in all of MLB with a batting average of at least .300 and an OBP of at least .309.
Not too shabby.
Rumfield has also been a defensive stalwart for the Rockies at first base — something they’ve been sorely lacking since Todd Helton retired in 2013. He’s made plenty of jaw-dropping plays, but one stood out to him in particular on May 18 against the Texas Rangers at Coors Field.
“I just remember the ball going up in the air and like, ‘Okay, this is one where I can maybe go over the dugout. Like this could be cool,’” he recalled. “And you get closer and closer, and you’re like, ‘Uh oh, it’s about to happen!’ And the momentum taking me over – it was just everything you dream of. Nobody caught me, but it was fine. It’s baseball. You dream of making plays like that and just trying to make a little difference in the game.”
He’s also been leaning on his teammates, especially Troy Johnston.
“(He’s given me) more golf advice,” Rumfield chuckled. “But the boy’s a great teammate. I would actually go to him when I’m feeling down. And he can attest to this – I’ll go to him and I’ll be like, ‘Troy, you’ve got to give me something. Tell me something good about myself.’ And he always does. We’re currently 3-for-3 on that one.”
Manager Warren Schaeffer has also helped his fellow Virginia Tech alum get settled from day one.
“Schaeff was unbelievably welcoming on the first day in spring training,” Rumfield recalled, “calling me into his office and letting me know, ‘Hey, you’re welcome here. I just want you to come and compete.’ It didn’t feel like anything was given to me. I just had to go out and earn it, and I’ve wanted to do that. That’s what I’ve done my whole entire career. It was nice to have the front office be so welcoming – Schaeffer be so welcoming – and just everything kind of working out.”
Gabriel Hughes
The former 10th-overall pick had a long way to the majors that included Tommy John surgery in 2023. But he didn’t let that slow him down, making his long-awaited MLB debut on July 3.
Hughes made his last start on September 18 — his 13th of the year — and took yet another no decision. In 14 appearances (13 starts), Hughes is 0-8 with a 6.33 ERA. The only other Rockies pitcher in franchise history to begin their career with zero wins through their first 13 starts was Jon Gray in 2015-16.
But like Rumfield, Hughes said his rookie year has been “a learning experience.”
“It’s been very different from every level I’ve played at so far, and I think learning how to manage that schedule is part of being a professional,” he said. “But it’s been wonderful, too, being able to travel to so many different places, play so many different places, experience so many different things. It’s been really special being able to see so much of the country in such a short amount of time.”
For example, Hughes was able to pitch at Yankee Stadium — somewhere he’d always dreamed about as he grew up as a huge fan of Mariano Rivera. And he had to navigate the New York City Subway System to get there:
But like all of the other pitchers, Hughes noticed a difference pitching at Coors Field versus the road. But not necessarily in the way one would think.
“I think it’s an experience that Albuquerque has prepared me for, where you go from elevation to non-elevation every week,” he said. “I think here, the biggest difference is that you do it every three to four days instead of every week.”
In addition to his body preparation, though, Hughes has made some adjustments to his pitching.
“I think one of the things I’ve really learned is that I have to have different starting points for a lot of my pitches when I’m here versus on the road,” he said. “It’s not something I’ve thought about too much in the past when I was in Albuquerque. But here, where the margin for error is so low, I think it’s extremely important. So that’s something I’ve continued to work on. But that’s probably the biggest thing I’ve noticed because the margin for error is so low, so you have to be sharp here and on the road.”
And the coaching staff have given Hughes a lot of good advice and a lot of good ideas, which he has enjoyed.
“It’s been awesome. They’re all young and full of ideas,” he said.
“And working with Alon (Leichman) and Gabe Ribas and Matt Buschmann has been really cool because there’s always some new idea, and it’s always, ‘Hey, take it or leave it. If it works for you, great. If not, no worries.’ There’s no ego there. But I think it’s really cool because if I have ideas, I can bounce them off them. They have great ideas that they bounce off me, too.”
He also had high praise for his manager.
“I think Schaeff’s been really cool, too,” he continued. “He’s been a great manager so far because he’s been willing to give praise when you need it and to give you tough words when you need it. And I have no doubt that all the coaches would go to war for us.”
There have been a lot of up-and-down moments for Hughes during his rookie season, but one stands out in particular:
“Striking out Shohei (Ohtani) on three pitches at Dodger Stadium was pretty cool,” he said. “I think it was to lead off an inning, and it was a fastball up, a curveball that he fouled off, and a fastball above the zone for a swing and miss. That was a pretty cool feeling.”
Hughes was optioned to Triple-A Albuquerque on September 19 to finish his rookie year, but still finished with 1.1 fWAR — leading the Rockies’ rotation.
Looking to the future
Rumfield and Hughes represent the Rockies future. Both have been bright spots in different ways, and it will be exciting to see what they are able to do in their sophomore campaigns.
In the meantime, there are six games left in the Rockies 2026 campaign and hopefully they are able to finish strong.

item.title: [blogs.fangraphs.com] Ben Clemens FanGraphs Chat - 9/21/26
item.dc:creator: Ben Clemens
item.description: Ben Clemens Hey everybody, welcome to the chat. We're testing out a new chat interface today, one that we'll hopefully roll out more broadly in the weeks to come. So come on, let's run it through its paces. Kevin In a weekly transactions H2H league, would you risk rolling with Aroldis this week? I don't see why the Bosox would rush him back into action. Ben Clemens Yeah, I would not. For exactly the reason you said. It just feels like you're opening yourself up to some risk without enough upside
item.content:encoded:
Ben Clemens
Hey everybody, welcome to the chat. We're testing out a new chat interface today, one that we'll hopefully roll out more broadly in the weeks to come. So come on, let's run it through its paces.
Kevin
In a weekly transactions H2H league, would you risk rolling with Aroldis this week? I don't see why the Bosox would rush him back into action.
Ben Clemens
Yeah, I would not. For exactly the reason you said. It just feels like you're opening yourself up to some risk without enough upside back for it. You're going to feel REALLY bad if they ease him back in and you're playing him. And on the flip side, what if he's not right immediately? Can't have a 0% chance of that.
SPArn
Any favorite random MLBers as we wind down the stretch, or little hopeful glimpses? I still don't believe Scott Bandura is real, even though Mo'Ne Davis went to his debut, and I nearly shed a tear during Josiah Gray's return
Ben Clemens
I mean, this guy is definitely very real, but David Freese is my all-time favorite good but not great guy who stuck around long enough for me to have fond memories of them.
Ben Clemens
Many of mine are Cardinals themed because that's when I was most strongly a fan of a single team. Pete Kozma. Bo Hart.
Ben Clemens
If we're talking current guys, well, how about Trent Harris, who I've grown inordinately fond of very quickly this year
SPArn
Your piece(s) on Cade Cavalli are excellent, much more thorough and better reasoned than this. But, I think the extension boils down to: 4/47 is low risk enough it doesn't hurt if he regresses or breaks, and if it turns into 5/70, it must have worked out great for the Nats. All reporting seems like he's a truly excellent leader too. We came a long way from "sit down, boy" and we can all be grateful for that
Ben Clemens
Yeah, I think that's basically the risk management part of mine. It's a good bet even if you know he gets hurt some of the time, because on average you get a nice amount of value out of signing him. I leave the leadership stuff aside – I agree with you that it's widely reported that way, I just think that those types of things are extremely subjective and don't hold over long periods of time anyway.
aldrinbatistarocks
A while ago, I remember listening to a BP podcast in which they were talking about christopher morel, the gist of the discussion being "it's okay to acknowledge when a guy is probably having their career year." Are there any candidates in 2026 for guys you think hit their apex production this season?
Ben Clemens
Love this one. Some easy ones for me: Otto Lopez. PCA. Gabriel Moreno. Randy Arozarena. Jake Bauers.
Ben Clemens
I don't mean any of them ill by that. But I just think a ton of stuff broke well for those players in their years, and that it feels hard to have all of that plus more hit right in a future year for them to eclipse it. You can still be a very good player after hitting your apex production
smoothio
Does Tatis have an MVP season in him?
Ben Clemens
Whether he actually wins one? who can say. Whether he has the capability to? Clearly yes. He's played at an MVP level for half of this year, for example. The talent is definitely there. Winning an MVP is tough because you have to have it hit for a whole year when no one else hits their even better outcome.
oaktownblues
Think the A's can hold onto a winning record against every AL west team this season? Just need to not lose series vs Angels and Astros
Ben Clemens
I do. I think that'd be a pretty cool footnote on what was just a real bummer of a season. Kind of a hilarious one, too. The AL is a mess this year.
bosoxforlife
The Red Sox should start Tolle in game 1 in The Bronx. The reality is that the Red Sox look outmatched and his personality fits the occasion perfectly and a few quick K's could change the mood.
Ben Clemens
I like the idea of starting Tolle game one. I feel crazy saying this, but I kind of like the idea of just starting three lefties and daring the Yankees to play their righty platoon bats, kind of gambling on Judge being less than 100%
Anonymous Member #46
Holy crap, I dig the new chat interface so far. No login issues!
Ben Clemens
Great to hear. Sean and team are still working on adding functionality (polls, images, that kinda thing) but I have been liking the clean look and it gives us more flexibility on our end
Ben Clemens
a little more legible and the scroll bars are nicer. Setting up the chat has more options. Basically this just has more options across the board. Oh, and I love the little FanGraphs icon by my name, so fun
oaktownblues
How does the new chat interface differ on your end? Are questions organized differently than before?
Ben Clemens
so, there's something I'm still getting used to, published those two out of order
riceball
where does Yordan rank among unlikely batting title winners? (assuming he holds on)
Ben Clemens
Nowhere near the top. He has a career .300 batting average! Among big league regulars, only Luis Arraez, Chandler Simpson (small-ish sample), and Jose Altuve are better
bosoxforlife
I can't get over the fact that either the Guardians or the White Sox will, most likely, receive a bye in the first round while whoever wins the AL West plays the team that finishes second but gets the home field against a team with a better record. I don't want to pour cold water on the new interface but the submission box is too small to handle more than two lines of copy.
Ben Clemens
Great feedback on the submission box. That sounds like an easy fix to me, I'll let Sean know.
As to the playoff system, yeah, I agree that this is a problem. I really like the bye system we have at current. It gives a reward for teams that have great regular seasons. But I agree that the divisional system interacts awkwardly with it. What if they handed out playoff spots the way they do now but pre-reseeded, ordering teams by record? I'm totally with you that it's a good idea that feels obviuosly unfair in practice.
SPArn
Pitchers having their best year: Nick Martinez, Luzardo, Messick, Louis Varland, Martin Perez some candidates that leap to mind. (Don't say the Miz, don't say the Miz, don't say the Miz)
Ben Clemens
I don't think the Miz counts. Like, yes, he's having an extremely good year. But he could throw more innings. the strikeouts don't look crazy unsustainable. it COULD be a career year but it doesn't feel like a blow-off top (a finance term I love and have been trying to use more of late) in the way that, say, Otto Lopez does
didace
Submission box – The default seems small, but click/hold and drag the little thing in the bottom right corner and you can make it very large.
Sean Dolinar
We are going to fix that once this chat is over. Thanks everyone for the feedback! – Sean
Ben Clemens
Martinez doesn't count because this isn't even his best year! He had his career year in 2024 in Cincy. Luzardo, same kinda deal, he's basically repeating last season. probably not 'career year' territory. I definitely agree with you on Varland, don't think Messick is really fair since he's a rookie, and Martin Perez got a qualifying offer once!
Ben Clemens
My own list would have: Reid Detmers, who I think is good but not this good. Sean Burke, though without much conviction there. And Foster Griffin.
Michael De Vivo
will spencer jones be overmatched by playoff level pitching?
Ben Clemens
If by overwhelmed you mean he'll strike out a lot, absolutely yes. He's a high-strikeout guy and the octane of pitchers ramps up int he playoffs. But it's not like he hasn't faced hard pitches in the regular season or in the minors. His game is tons of strikeouts and sometimes the ball leaves the yard. One playoff homer or so and we'llb e like man, this guy has it. And since homers are pretty rare events, it feels like Jones could be basically the same hitter and based on whether he happens to run into one or not we'll say he just didn't have it or performed as expected.
ado64
Who do you think starts Brewers playoff game 3, and how many innings do they get? 3 innings of Gasser or Drohan, maybe? Does May ever start a game with his recent inconsistency?
Ben Clemens
I think that some kind of piggyback situation is reasonable here. Like, three of Drohan with May backing him up? Or some other lefty/righty switch of that style. I'm extremely curious to see how they deploy Harrison.
Ben Clemens
I really don't know what you do with Harrison. Like, he's been so bad recently! But he has such high highs. The test in relief hasn't gone all that well so far. It's not like they can afford to just not have him pithc, he was a big part of their run prevention this year.
Ben Clemens
Sorry, I missed an answer before messing around iwth the interface. I meant to say that Harrison is the highest-unceratinty question in the entire playoff picture for me. The Brewers were the best team in baseball this year and Kyle Harrison was a ton of that. What are they going to look like with less good pitching? Can they figure out what ails him in time? I have no clue but I'm very excited to find out.
Anon21
Maybe dumb question. When Team A is one game ahead of Team B in the standings and also holds the tiebreaker on Team B, it's often said that they effectively have a two-game lead. But is there a similar way of describing the situations of the Astros and White Sox, who are one game back in the standings but hold the tiebreaker over the team ahead? Like are they effectively 0.8 (or something) games back, rather than one? (I know this is accounted for by magic numbers, just wondering if there's a simple way to describe this situation.)
Ben Clemens
I'd say they're one back with the tiebreaker. Or alternately that they're 'effectively only a half game back' because of the breaker. I agree with you that the wording is kind of tricky, though. You can't say they're 'effectively tied', that's not true. If they hvae the same records they won't make the playoffs
Nomar6666666
No question really. Just a frustrated fan with few places to vent. If the owners lock out the players next season, and we miss one single game, I will not go to a single game next year, nor will I buy the MLB TV package. I Wii continue to support this site
Ben Clemens
Nomar, we appreciate your continued support, of course. That's very kind. And honestly, I feel pretty similar. I think the owners are more to blame than the players for the upcoming fight we're sure to have. I don't feel great about anyone's role in this though. There's so much freaking money in baseball. Work it out between yourselves like adults so that we the fans, who pay a ton of money to enjoy your product, can still get it. No one is on our side in this negotiation, and that makes it feel bad
Braydon Roberts
Thoughts on the NL RoY race? Seems like everyone gave it to Sal Stewart when JJ went on the IL, but Stewart has had a rough September. fWAR is 4.4 to 2.2 in JJ's favor.
Ben Clemens
So, I've had JJ all along. I just don't really buy the arguments that some counting numbers matter so much that they're more important than the overall picture. I'm not saying Stewart's homers don't matter or anything. Obviously they do. But eh, the RBI's, I'm not as convinced by, because a stat like RE24 (which cares about driving in runs, but also cares about how many opportunities you had to drive in runs) says Stewart was about 10 runs better with the bat than Wetherholt this year so far.
Ben Clemens
That's not a ton of runs better. And again, that accounts for the RBI and the homers and all. And if you care about win probability – as in how important those RBIs were – Wetherholt actually has a BETTER bat than Stewart
Ben Clemens
Also he's a plus defender at an important position instead of a first baseman who defensive metrics aren't fond of
Ben Clemens
Like, I get the sentiment. And I get wanting to push back against WAR and be like 'no the old stats we love still matter'
Ben Clemens
There are times where I think that's true! I'd vote for Yordan by a mile for AL MVP, and it's because I think that his offensive value is so high that WAR is overly penalizing him for his defense. no one cares when you hit that well. BUt that's not Sal Stewart's case.
war2d2
Don’t like the new interface, all my questions are still poorly thought out and badly edited. Thought it would have fixed that.
Ben Clemens
That's coming in FanGraphs 2.0 🙂
Greg Simons
Regarding last week's lack of any questions about lunch, I think we all figured someone else would ask. Of course, when that happens, you make a "fig" out of "u" and "re," or something like that. Whatever the case, I hope you have a good lunch planned today.
Ben Clemens
Why thank you. It's like House said once, I think: That's what happens when you make a presumption. You make a pres out of you and some guy named umption.
As for lunch, leftovers from a very nice salmon dish that a friend of ours cooked this weekend.
WonderWall
Piggybacking on Nomar's comments, why do you think that both the owners and the Union seem to pretty much refuse to let the situation continue. Why do both sides feel like something needs to change?
Ben Clemens
Many possible answers to this. I think the most important, for me, is that they'd act this way even if they thought that 'no change' was acceptable, because that's how bargaining well in advance of a deadline works. So I'm hopeful that when the rubber meets the road, both sides will cave simultaneously.
Barbaro Garbey
Thank you for the chat Ben. The Tigers have to feel good about former top prospects Kevin McGonigle and Max Clark thriving in their first big league action this year. Wondering though if you have any thoughts on any of the "other" Tigers rookies who have been getting run down the stretch? Personally, I have loved watching the energy guys like Hao-Yu Lee and Eduardo Valencia have brought; and Ben Malgeri and Brett Callahan have at least looked like quality defensive outfielders (at least compared to some of the butchers the Tigers have put out there). Do you think any of this group could succeed/thrive in closer to a full time role next year?
Ben Clemens
Truthfully I don't think I've seen enough of any of them to be all that sure, but I do think that they did enough that if I'm the Tigers, I'm interested in leaving some space for the minor leaguers to have bigger roles next year. Like, leave an outfield hole perhaps?
Phil
Are we sure the Sox' best option, with Rafaela back, isn't Anthony in right and Gasper/Jones at DH? I'm not really believing in Duran right now.
Ben Clemens
This seems like possibly the best option, but their behavior year to date basically tells me they won't be doing this. Or, well, assuming you mean Anthony in left, I like Abreu in right.
PC1970
Would you even put Harrison on the roster if you were Milwaukee? He looks unplayable at the moment. Maybe overreaction, but, you also can't just punt a playoff game like they can a regular season game.
Ben Clemens
I mean, I would. If I thought playing Harrison was punting a game, I wouldn't put him on there. But I kind of think that you need to give yourself chances to have your best possible team. And c'mon, if he's awful for two innings and you yank him, I think that's short of punting the game. I think that not rostering him would basically be playing too conservative. You should try to hit your high-upside outcomes to win in the playoffs, imo
Anon21
Following up more on the lockout question…I think implicitly I'm assigning the probability of missing any games to be low, definitely less than 10%. Commentators throwing around the possibility of losing the whole season seem nuts to me–isn't that obviously suicidal from a business perspective? Where do you stand on probabilities of losing any games/a significant number of games/the whole season?
Ben Clemens
I'm at least close to you on this one. I think I have the odds of missing games very low and the odds of missing a season at pretty close to zero. I just don't think the owners have the collective will. I don't think the players do either, when push comes to shove.
Robert Stewart
After the Bregman injury, should MLB enforce the rule that on deck hitters should be in the on deck circle? I remember a few years ago when they did that and the batter (I think it was Beltre) moved the actual circle to where he was standing. He may have been ejected.
Ben Clemens
No, because clearly this enforcement wouldn't stick and no one likes feeling either like a nanny or like they're being nanny stated by the umpires. The Beltre thing was a while ago at this point I think? But a specific umpire told him to get back in the circle so he moved it. It wasn't at the same time as an enforcement push or anything, if I'm remembering correctly.
wheelhouse
Boston’s about to sail to the WS, no? Easy opponent after easy opponent ahead of them
Ben Clemens
A jinx? A stealth insult? Who knows, let's hit publish.
Vee
i would be very happy if this is not Pete's peak. I dream of 12 war PCA.
Ben Clemens
Haha right? That one was kind of a gimme just because it's SO hard to imagine a better season.
HappyFunBall
Is Kyle Harrison at risk of not even making the playoff roster?
Ben Clemens
Didn't realize that this was less of a fringe opinion and more of a 'thing people are thinking'. I guess that I underestimated it. I don't really think that it's likely because he's good! Clearly capable of dominance. But the Brewers have a lot more granular data and maybe they really do think he's cooked for the moment. I just…. c'mon, the guy was so good earlier this year, and if you leave him off the playoff roster in the NLDS, you're never bringing him back on, you're accepting that you're just playing without this big important piece. I just hate settling like that.
Tim Tebow's Thunder Thighs
Dider Fuentes is rolling as a mid-reliever, but do you think the Braves should stretch him back out into a starting role next year a la Strider?
Ben Clemens
I think they'll try, realize that he's better in this current role, and move him back. They should try even if they don't think it'll work. The odds of it working are obviously not zero and he'd be more valuable by a lot if it stuck
appayipyip
If you had to sit down and name every baseball player you can think of how many names could you get to?
Ben Clemens
Oh man. Hundreds. Probably a thousand? I think I'd get tired before I ran out of names. Playing OOTP for many years, and Perfect Team in particular (Paul Sporer curates the sets over there and does an incredible job of finding fun old players) has given me a big memory bank of names
Tim Tebow's Thunder Thighs
Holy crap, am I able to submit a question as a logged in FG member? That's the first time in months.
What you do suspect the Braves will do with Profar's contract after two long term suspensions with one year remaining (which isn't far off from a qualifying offer)? I can't imagine AA getting much of anything for him
Ben Clemens
Oh yeah…. I think they'll either cut him or trade him eating all the money for a lottery ticket.
Ben Clemens
Tebow sighting yesterday btw! At the Broncos Jags game. Florida man with Denver connections, makes sense.
Phil
Yes, by right I meant left, sorry, and thanks. Also, Sean, can we bring back the thing where your own question is blue? That was both pleasurable and, particulalry when illicitly following the chat on a phone at work, useful.
Ben Clemens
putting this in the log so Sean can see it too. I didn't even know about that feature. See, this is why it's good to test things.
jonmberra
Do you think the Mariners can fix their defense this offseason? Seems like they hit a little worse than expected, and the team imploded because their defense is terrible.
Ben Clemens
I do think this is fixable. I think it might kind of fix itself, to be honest. Their worst defenders by FRV are Crawford and Arozarena, both FA's. Luke Raley was bad in right before he got hurt, but he was also just not great overall, they're surely looking for better options. TO me, it looks like they're set up to improve on defense without even focusing on it specifically, just from the change in team composition.
draftdingers
Do the Cardinals test the trade market for Herrera this offseason and could they even get a good return? Burleson seems to be the First Basemen for the next few years and I can't see Herrera staying behind the plate with his subpar defense and the glut at catcher coming through the system.
Ben Clemens
I think that they'll test the trade market, and I think they will definitely get a good return if they decide to trade him. I think that zero-ish other teams see him as a catcher, though. I see him as a 1B/DH who can maybe be an emergency catcher, I didn't like the way the Cards kept tring him at catcher even after the writing was on the wall, at least to me.
Ben Clemens
But when I was bouncing players off of my sources this summer and talking about Herrera as a fringy name, probably not top 50 trade value but surely top 100, people didn't have much to say about that eitehr way, which suggests to me that it's roughly right. Good plus bat, might benefit from not having to play catcher so often, cost controlled for a while. Teams would be interested in this for sure. He has a batting line 20% above average for his career and doesnt' cost much; the pitch sells itself.
kingkash7788
how much has nimmala rose post trade deadline
Ben Clemens
This is really more of a question for the prospect guys than for me but his stock is clearly up, impressive performance in Double-A at 20. I am not sure he's their starting shortstop on opening day next year because Neto is awesome and I'm not sold on a move to third base being inevitable. But I think that he's clearly arrow up from what we thought of him at the deadline. Good trade for the Angels. Might be a win-win, I think Soriano is gonna play well in Toronto next year, but the Angels have 100% done well there.
HappyFunBall
re: Dider Fuentes. The question to ask is not whether or not he'll be better as a reliever. MOST pitchers are. That's why they get put there in the first place. The question to ask is will Fuentes be able to thrive in a 5+ innings role or not.
Ben Clemens
Concur with this. And my thinking there is that if you're being honest with yourself, it's not certain whether he'll thrive in a 5+ inning role but he certainly hasn't ruled it out with his performance. Particularly if the Braves feel good about his feel for the splitter, which he's basically been able to mothball in relief but would surely need to add back in as a starter, I think it'd be crazy NOT to try. He's 21 and destroying major league hitting and came up as a starter.
sloejoe
Thanks for the chat! Is Robert Gasser a starter next year? According to Roster Resource he is their 5th starter. Has he shown to have the stuff to move up?
Ben Clemens
Yeah, the Brewers always use a bunch of starters interchangeably throughout the year but I have no reason to think he won't be one of them.
appayipyip
If you were the Jays would you try to extend Soriano?
Ben Clemens
I would. The weird part is the timing – like, if they haven't started on it now, I doubt they're getting it done before the lockout unless both sides really want it. So is it a next year post lockout kinda thing? Maybe. But I am generally a fan of trying to sign contract extensions when it makes even a little sense, and this one clearyl makes some sense.
fincampbell05
What are the Red Sox going to do? They're going to have some money to spend, but there really isn't a clear hole on the roster except for SS, where they surely would not sign someone that blocks Arias, if there were even any good free agent shortstops.
Ben Clemens
This isn't a great year to spend money, it's looking like. But that suits them just fine – like you said, there isn't a super clear hole on the roster aside from shortstop. And for me, backup at 3B because I dno't quite believe Durbin's torrid stretch. But I think I'd just be willing to keep some powder dry, basically. I think we've discussed their payroll situation some in recent weeks; it's really well set-up for next year, very few players leaving. Maybe they try to work out another year of Sonny Gray, maybe they just top up on pitching, but this is a great year to not need a bunch of players in FA, because the FA class is not good. I don't think they need to overcomplicate things too much – they went hard last winter, they can cool it this winter.
Rayball
Who do you have emerging in this final week between TEX and HOU?
Ben Clemens
Houston because they're like the bogeyman, they always seem to keep coming even when you think they're done. But no strong lean
drplantwrench
Also another note: it would be nice to make `Your questions awaiting the host` collapsible
Ben Clemens
Noted.
randomname1234
If you're the Red Sox, do you tank this week and hope to get WC#3 instead of WC#2? Almost certainly not catching NY for WC#1, and road games against AL West and AL Central winners sound much better than road games against Yankees and Tampa.
Ben Clemens
A few people asked versions of this earlier, I happened to like this phrasing most. But I'm answering all of your questions. No. I'd be happy if that happened, but I would not mess with wanting my good players to play well a week before the playoffs, for marginal gain. Matchups matter, but only so much, and there's no guarantee.
bosoxforlife
I do not understand why teams don't see players like Herrera as a potential career DH and as a very valuable third catcher. Mickey Gasper is presently showing just how valuable that type of player is even if doesn't keep hitting at this level. When a team has two catchers it really only has one but with three all can be used freely.
Ben Clemens
Oh I 100% agree. I think this is a leak among teams. And Herrera hits well enough, or at least projects to hit well enough, that you're not sacrificing offense anywhere, it's just free-ish value.
Phillip Denny
Do you think Luzardo's injury means he's just a glorified opener (or maybe gives you 2-3) in the WC/DS? If so, is there an argument for turning him into a late inning fireman instead?
Ben Clemens
I am unsure, but I am leaning towards him having very short starts, at which case yes, I'd prefer him as an impact reliever. I don't know if he is ready to warm up and play in that role, though, and given his at-times-injured past and his contract, if I'm the Phillies, I want him to give me a strong sign that he's interested in this role and thinks he'd do well at it
Ben Clemens
Okay everyone, this was a wonderful chat, but now I'm going to go have that aforementioned salmon and start working on an article for tomorrow.
Ben Clemens
Thanks for all the great questions, and for helping us test out the new chat interface. May the last week of the regular season be delightful for you, and let's get ready for the playoffs.
Ben is a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @benclemens.

item.title: [blogs.fangraphs.com] Untying the Tiebreaker Scenarios, One More Time
item.dc:creator: Jay Jaffe
item.description: With one week to go in the regular season, the playoff field is nearly set in the National League, though it’s anything but settled in the American League, with two of the three division leaders — two different ones since I last checked in — ahead by just one game and those races spilling over into the battle for the third and final Wild Card spot. We’re not going to get any tiebreaker games due to the fun police and the playoff format change put into effect by the 2022 Collective Bargaining Agr
item.content:encoded:
With one week to go in the regular season, the playoff field is nearly set in the National League, though it’s anything but settled in the American League, with two of the three division leaders — two different ones since I last checked in — ahead by just one game and those races spilling over into the battle for the third and final Wild Card spot. We’re not going to get any tiebreaker games due to the fun police and the playoff format change put into effect by the 2022 Collective Bargaining Agreement, but it’s entirely possible a playoff spot — and perhaps even a division title — will be decided on the basis of MLB’s tiebreaker procedures.
Since the situation is simpler in the NL, I’ll start there. The Brewers (98-58) lead the Dodgers (96-60) in the race for the top seed, and own the tiebreaker there on the basis of a 4-3 season series advantage. According to our Playoff Odds, as of Monday at 9 AM, the Braves (92-64) have just a 0.9% chance of bypassing either Milwaukee or Los Angeles. The Brewers — who have a magic number of one to clinch a first-round bye — finish out with a visit to the Phillies (86-70) before coming home to face the Cardinals (76-80), while the Dodgers host the Padres (87-69) for three and then travel to the Giants (62-90), with the Braves hosting the Reds (72-84) and then visiting the Marlins (76-80).
The Padres have taken advantage of a soft spot in their schedule — series against the sub-.500 Nationals, Giants, Rockies, and Marlins, after taking two out of three from the Yankees — to win 13 out of their last 14 games. Not only did that push them past the Diamondbacks (now 82-74), whom they trailed by half a game before the start of the surge, but they’ve tied the Cubs (87-69) for the top NL Wild Card spot, with the Phillies a game behind them. The Phils have been phlailing lately, going 8-10 in September and failing to win a series since beating the Diamondbacks at the start of the month. Their slide gave the Braves enough room to clinch the NL East title on Sunday.
Before turning to the grid involving the four NL teams battling for three Wild Card spots, here’s another look at the tiebreaking procedures:
- Head-to-head records: This is self-explanatory when it comes to two-team tiebreakers, and if they played an odd number of games against each other, which is currently the case if they’re in the same division, then no other steps will be necessary. If more than two teams are involved and they have identical records against each other, then the team with the best combined winning percentage against the other teams within the tie wins the tiebreaker. If it’s still relevant, the remaining two teams are untied by head-to-head records and on down the line.
If more than two teams are involved and they do not have identical records against one another, but one team won its season series against each of the other teams, then that team takes the tiebreaker. Otherwise, it goes in order of combined winning percentage against the other teams they’re tied with, as above. One additional point to add in the event of a tie involving more than two teams: If it has implications for both a division race and a Wild Card race, the division tiebreaker is settled first, on the basis of head-to-head records. For example, if the Rangers and Astros tie atop the AL West and the White Sox finish with the same record but behind the Yankees and Red Sox, the Texas/Houston tiebreaker is settled first.
- Intradivision records: This one is relevant only for two situations — multi-team scenarios where the teams all have the same head-to-head records within the group, or for two Wild Card teams in different divisions. In the latter case, there’s still a good chance they played seven games against each other instead of six.
- Intraleague records: A team’s record against all three divisions in the same league.
- Last half of intraleague games: If a team has played 48 interleague games, then this would be decided based on their winning percentage over the last 57 (half of 114) games against teams in their own league. And if that doesn’t work…
- Last half of intraleague games plus one… or more, as needed: Under the above scenario, this would be decided based on their winning percentage over the last 58 intraleague games, then 59, 60, 61… as many as it takes.
And now, the big board:
| Team | W-L | CHC | SDP | PHI | ARI | Intra |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CHC | 87-69 | — | 5-1 (0,0) | 6-1 (0,0) | 4-2 (0,0) | 26-26 |
| SDP | 87-69 | 1-5 (0,0) | — | 0-6 (0,0) | 5-5 (3,0) | 28-18 |
| PHI | 86-70 | 1-6 (0,0) | 6-0 (0,0) | — | 3-3 (0,0) | 28-24 |
| ARI | 82-74 | 2-4 (0,0) | 5-5 (0,3) | 3-3 (0,0) | — | 28-18 |
The Cubs have a leg up on all of the other contenders here when it comes to the battle for the top Wild Card spot because they took the season series from each one. If they end up in any kind of tie, that advantage will be the difference between them playing the entire best-of-three series at Wrigley Field versus going on the road. The Padres are already on the short end of things with regards not only to the Cubs but also to the Phillies, with their series against the Diamondbacks hanging in the balance. San Diego hosts the Snakes at Petco Park over the regular season’s final weekend to determine who has the upper hand, though by then it may not matter.
Since they split their season series, a Phillies-Diamondbacks tie would be based on intradivision records. Philadelphia doesn’t have any more games against NL East rivals remaining; they host the Brewers and Rays for three-game sets starting on Tuesday. The Diamondbacks, who travel to both Colorado and San Diego, need one more win to clinch the intradivision tiebreaker advantage, but realistically they need a lot more than that to improve their chances. Their Playoff Odds are down to 5.6%.
Back to the Cubs, who host the Marlins for three and then visit the Red Sox (84-72). In the event of a four-team tiebreaker, Chicago would win because they beat all three other teams, and likewise for any three-way tiebreaker that involves them. If there’s any need to go further than that — say, if there were a three-way tie for the top Wild Card spot — after the Cubs it would come down to head-to-head and then intradivision records. A three-way tiebreaker not involving the Cubs would be decided first on combined head-to-head records within the group. Based on current records, the Phillies (.750, 9-3) would have the advantage over the Diamondbacks (.500, 8-8) and Padres (.313, 5-11), and once they’re untied from that knot, an Arizona-San Diego tiebreaker would still come down to head-to-head records.
Turning to the American League, the Rays (95-60) own a six-game lead over the increasingly banged-up Yankees (89-66) — who will be without Aaron Judge for the rest of the regular season due and possibly longer, due to a right calf strain — in the AL East. The two teams have a four-game series in the Bronx starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday. Tampa Bay leads the season series 6-3; a single win would not only seal a potential tiebreaker, it would clinch the division title. Nobody’s going to catch the Rays for the number one seed, either. The Guardians (81-75) took two out of three from the White Sox (80-76) this past week in Cleveland to take over first place in the AL Central. That said, Chicago owns the 7-6 season series advantage for tiebreaking purposes and has the softer schedule ahead; the White Sox visit Kansas City (67-89) for three and then host Colorado (57-99), while Cleveland travels to Boston and then Kansas City for a pair of three-game series. Whichever team wins the AL Central will likely grab the second first-round bye; between the Guardians and White Sox, their odds of doing so are 97.3%.
Meanwhile, the Rangers (78-78) are clinging to a one-game lead over the Astros (77-79), and yes, it’s entirely possible that the winner could be the majors’ first full-season sub-.500 playoff team. Houston won the season series 9-4 and therefore has the tiebreaker in the AL West, but for both teams, it’s all scoreboard-watching the rest of the way. The Astros are on the road against the Mariners (73-83) and A’s (61-95), while the Rangers host the Mets (71-85) for three before finishing with three in Minnesota (73-83).
As for the AL Wild Card, we don’t need to mind the Yankees and Red Sox since they’ve clinched playoff berths and are more or less locked into their spots; one Yankees win or one Red Sox loss will sew up placement as the fourth and fifth seeds, with a rematch of last year’s Wild Card Series slated for the Bronx. For the big board below, I’m including the Guardians and Rangers since it won’t take much to bump either of them into a position where their tiebreakers matter.
| Team | W-L | CLE | CHW | TEX | HOU | TOR | Intra |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CLE* | 81-75 | — | 6-7 | 2-4 | 2-4 | 2-4 | 27-22 |
| CHW | 80-76 | 7-6 | — | 4-2 | 2-5 | 5-1 | 31-18 |
| TEX* | 78-78 | 4-2 | 2-4 | — | 4-9 | 6-1 | 23-29 |
| HOU | 77-79 | 4-2 | 5-2 | 9-4 | — | 3-3 | 22-24 |
| TOR | 77-79 | 4-2 | 1-5 | 1-6 | 3-3 | — | 25-24 |
Alas, with the Rangers and Blue Jays finishing their season series on Sunday, none of these teams will face each other again until October, so we’re left with the same four scenarios I outlined a couple of weeks ago, but with the division leads having changed hands.
Scenario 1: Guardians and Rangers win their divisions
If both division leaders maintain their spots, leaving the other three teams vying for the sixth seed, the Astros would have the advantage over the White Sox in a tiebreaker because they won their season series. Because the Astros and Blue Jays split their series, a tie between them would be broken based on intradivision records; right now, the Blue Jays have the advantage, but they have fewer such games remaining (three in Baltimore from Monday to Wednesday, with their final three at home against the Reds), while the Astros, as noted, have six to play against AL West rivals. If the two teams end up with the same intradivision records, the next step would be intraleague records; currently the Astros have the edge, with a .519 winning percentage (56-52) to the Blue Jays’ .495 (55-56).
In the case of a three-way tie, the Astros would prevail, because they went 8-5 (.615) against the other two teams, while the White Sox went 7-6 (.538) and the Blue Jays 4-8 (.333).
Scenario 2: White Sox and Rangers win their divisions
This one would leave a three-team fray between the Astros, Guardians, and Blue Jays. The Astros won their season series against the Guardians, and a potential tie with the Blue Jays would be settled by intradivision or intraleague records as noted above.
In a three-way tie involving combined head-to-head records, the Astros and Blue Jays would tie at .583 (7-5), leaving the Guardians (.333, 4-8) in the dust. The Astros/Blue Jays tiebreaker would then be settled as outlined above.
Scenario 3: Guardians and Astros win their divisions
If the Guardians hold onto their narrow one-game lead, the White Sox would still be in decent shape, as they took the season series from both the Blue Jays and Rangers, so in the event of a three-way tie, Chicago would claim the remaining Wild Card berth.
Scenario 4: White Sox and Astros win their divisions
The Rangers remain sandwiched between the Guardians and Blue Jays record-wise, but they have the tiebreaker advantage over both teams. Because they won their season series against both Cleveland and Toronto, in a three-way tie, they would come out on top.
Undeniably, the situation in both leagues still leaves room for some suspense with regards to who will advance to October. Still, we can hope that as the players and owners hammer out the next CBA during what is likely to be a frigid winter on the labor front, they think long and hard about what’s been lost with the elimination of tiebreaker games. It’s much more fun rooting for chaos than for math.
Brooklyn-based Jay Jaffe is a senior writer for FanGraphs, the author of The Cooperstown Casebook (Thomas Dunne Books, 2017) and the creator of the JAWS (Jaffe WAR Score) metric for Hall of Fame analysis. He founded the Futility Infielder website (2001), was a columnist for Baseball Prospectus (2005-2012) and a contributing writer for Sports Illustrated (2012-2018). He has been a recurring guest on MLB Network and a member of the BBWAA since 2011, and a Hall of Fame voter since 2021. Follow him on BlueSky @jayjaffe.bsky.social.

item.title: [blogs.fangraphs.com] FanGraphs Power Rankings: September 14–20
item.dc:creator: Jake Mailhot

item.content:encoded:
We’ve made it to the final week of the regular season. There are still two divisions in the American League up for grabs, a couple of long-shot playoff hopefuls looking to make a last-minute run, and playoff seeding to fight over. It should make for a dramatic end to a great season.
Our power rankings use a modified Elo rating system. If you’re familiar with chess rankings, you’ll know that Elo is an elegant ranking format that measures teams’ relative strength and is very reactive to recent performance. To avoid overweighting recent results during the season, we weigh each team’s raw Elo rank using our coin flip playoff odds (specifically, we regress the playoff odds by 50% and weigh those against the raw Elo ranking, increasing in weight as the season progresses to a maximum of 25%). The weighted Elo ranks are then displayed as “Power Score” in the tables below. As the best and worst teams sort themselves out between now and October, they’ll filter to the top and bottom of the rankings, while the exercise remains reactive to hot streaks and cold snaps. If you’re looking for a visual representation of the ups and downs of your team throughout the season, look no further than the brand new Power Rankings Board in the FanGraphs Lab.
First up are the full rankings, presented in a sortable table. Below that, I’ve grouped the teams into tiers with comments on a handful of clubs. You’ll notice that the official ordinal rankings don’t always match the tiers — there are times where I take editorial liberties when grouping teams together — but generally, the ordering is consistent. One thing to note: The playoff odds listed in the tables below are our standard Depth Charts odds, not the coin flip odds that are used in the ranking formula.

| Team | Record | Elo | Opponent Elo | Playoff Odds | Power Score |
