item.content:encoded:
We know what you’re thinking: The New York Yankees cannot realistically replace Aaron Judge.
Unfortunately for Aaron Boone and Brian Cashman, they have no choice. Judge landed back on the injured list with a right calf strain, and the earliest that he could return is next Sunday’s regular-season finale against the Orioles. The Yankees have not committed to the three-time AL MVP potentially being ready for the AL Wild Card Series.
“I usually deal with calf stuff all year long,” Judge told reporters on Saturday. “It usually doesn’t get to [the media], and I usually don’t miss any games. So that was kind of the same thing I was feeling. I was working my way back, and then something kind of grabs you at a strange time.”
So, who will man right field in Judge’s absence? Will it be Spencer Jones, who has flashed as a rookie? What about Cody Bellinger, who could shift over from left field?
As it turns out, the answer might be speedy utilityman José Caballero. Seriously.
José Caballero could start in the Yankees’ outfield following Aaron Judge’s latest injury
The 30-year-old Caballero drew the start in center field on Saturday night, hitting two singles and drawing the walk in a 5-3 loss. He's played 20 of his 130 games in the outfield, with most of that action coming in the corner spots.
For what it’s worth, we’ve always liked Caballero enough that we repeatedly advocated for the Yankees to consider naming him the full-time shortstop and trading Anthony Volpe. So we’re not opposed to the thought of him playing right, with Bellinger starting in center and Heliot Ramos taking over in left field.
The 5-foot-9, 190-pound Caballero's calling card has always been his legs, and he's stolen at least 26 bases in each of his first four seasons. This year has been no exception, with him swiping a team-leading 32 bases in 43 attempts. But to his credit, Caballero has added some power to his game, recording a career-high 14 home runs in nearly 450 plate appearances.
Bellinger has played 118 of his 127 games in left field, though he has extensive experience in both center and right. The reigning All-Star Game MVP is also one of the Yankees' most reliable hitters, even as his OPS has dropped from .813 to .781.
Objectively speaking, the Yankees can afford to have an outfield consisting of Caballero, Bellinger, and either Ramos or Jones. Trent Grisham remains out with a right hamstring problem, though Boone has hinted they’d get the two-time Gold Glove winner back in time for the playoffs. As things stand, the Yankees would host the rival Red Sox in a first-round rematch of last year’s Wild Card Series.
Ideally for the Yankees, they’ll have Judge batting second and playing right field next Tuesday night. But if you’re looking for a dark horse candidate to shine this postseason, you could do far worse than the versatile Caballero.

item.title: [fansided.com] MLB Power Rankings: Playoff stakes rise as October contenders make their move
item.dc:creator: Chris Landers; Mark Powell
item.description: The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series. "Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not
item.content:encoded:
The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series.
"Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not only grabbing hold of a Wild Card spot but now pushing for home-field in the first round if things break right. The latter, meanwhile, has once again snatched the AL Central while no one was looking. And they're not the only ones making serious moves in our latest MLB power rankings.
But who are we buying as serious title contenders, and who still has work to do? Read on to find out.
30. Colorado Rockies
The Rockies have admittedly let go of the rope of late, well on their way to yet another 100-loss season. There are at least some promising young hitters in this organization, which represents something to build upon moving forward. Of course, the pitching staff remains a mess, and no one's been able to crack that nut yet in Colorado.
–Chris Landers, FanSided.com editor
29. Los Angeles Angels
In Reid Detmers, Walbert Urena and Ryan Johnson, the Angels have at least some sort of foundation upon which to build for the future. Well, OK, maybe not Detmers, who will almost certainly be dealt this offseason. But still, L.A.’s pitching staff has been a real bright spot of late. The offense … well, that’s another question. Things are going to get worse before they get better under John Mozeliak. At least Arte Moreno is no longer around to meddle in it.
–CL
28. Athletics
The A’s are playing out the string of a lost season, although the contributions they’ve gotten from young bats like Henry Bolte, Max Muncy (not that one), Lawrence Butler and Zack Gelof down the stretch have been notable. None of that will matter, though, until the team fixes its pitching staff. We know we sound like a broken record, but it really is that simple, and no potential answers have emerged in the second half.
–CL
27. San Francisco Giants
Rafael Devers' injury, which figures to cost him at least some of next season as well as the end of this one, is a fitting if unfortunate end to what's been a miserable season by the Bay. Devers had been one of the few bright spots on this Giants team down the stretch alongside Bryce Eldridge; now, it's unclear how San Francisco will rebuilt its offense for 2027 in addition to finding reinforcements for a pitching staff that simply hasn't been good enough.
–CL
26. Kansas City Royals
The Kansas City Royals have been eliminated for quite some time now. If there is one clear goal for Kansas City this winter, it's to build a roster around Bobby Witt Jr. that is capable of making a postseason run. That is every team's goal, but the Royals are so far away from contention despite featuring such a prolific player, Witt Jr.'s career is closer to becoming Mike Trout's than Derek Jeter's.
-Mark Powell, FanSided.com MLB director
25. Minnesota Twins
At one point not all that long ago, the Twins had a realistic chance to make the playoffs as the third AL Wild Card spot. Then, the bottom fell out. Byron Buxton underwent successful hip surgery just last week that will keep him out until spring training, whenever that may be. The Twins once again experienced the roster flaw of building around an injured star.
-MP
24. New York Mets
This week couldn’t have been more awkward for the New York Mets when Pete Alonso hit his 300th home run in his return to Citi Field, much to the delight of many Mets fans in attendance, but once Alonso left town, the Mets began to play better, winning two games in a row against the Phillies. Those wins, headlined by more quality play from youngsters like Carson Benge, Zac Thornton and Christian Scott, show why Mets fans should be somewhat enthusiastic for what’s to come.
–Zach Rotman, FanSided.com staff writer
23. Cincinnati Reds
In the American League, the Reds likely wouldn't be the worst team in their division. But the NL Central has been a gauntlet all year long, and the Reds couldn't keep up. Despite breakthrough seasons from Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart, Cincinnati still has a long way to go on the starting pitching front. Can they rely on Hunter Greene and Chase Burns moving forward?
-MP
22. Seattle Mariners
Going 3-3 against the Angels and Rockies this week just about sums up this season in Seattle. The good news is that youngsters like Michael Arroyo and Lazaro Montes have helped to key an offensive turnaround. The bad news is that the starting rotation hasn’t held up its end of the bargain of late, and there are still tons of long-term questions about this lineup — especially with Randy Arozarena set to hit free agency. Jerry DiPoto will need to find some answers this offseason after a year in which just about everything went wrong.
–CL
21. Washington Nationals
The Washington Nationals deserved a better fate in 2026. Even with their offense falling off a bit of late, they’re still third in the majors in runs scored. The dynamic duo of CJ Abrams and James Wood is as good as any in the National League. Recently extended Cade Cavalli is a budding ace. Andrew Alvarez has thrown the ball incredibly well and looks like a future rotation stalwart. If it weren’t for a historically bad bullpen, we’d be talking about this team in Wild Card contention.
–ZR
20. Detroit Tigers
The Tigers have the best run differential in the AL Central and a pythagorean record of an AL playoff team. None of it matters. Scott Harris and the Tigers front office gave up on their team's postseason hopes at the trade deadline. Then, they proceeded to get fans' hopes up with a late August run, only to play like the team Harris assumed they'd become when it mattered most. The Tigers have some work to do, though the emergence of young stars in the lineup like Hao-Yu Lee and Kevin McGonigle, paired with Riley Greene's consistent play, give them some building blocks.
-MP
19. St. Louis Cardinals
The Cardinals are ahead of schedule, but not a postseason team. Make no mistake about it, St. Louis came crashing back down to earth in September, and has been eliminated from playoff contention. There are questions about the long-term future of Masyn Winn, especially with JJ Wetherholt as the de-facto shortstop of the future. But these are all good problems to have. Now, if only Bloom could find an ace burried in that farm system of his.
-MP
18. Baltimore Orioles
A series against league-best Milwaukee came at the worst possible time for the O’s, which now find themselves needing to hit an inside straight to snatch the final Wild Card spot. Pete Alonso’s heroics at Citi Field aside, Baltimore’s bats simply have not been good enough. Heck, no part of this team has; they’re hovering around .500 for a reason, after all, and there’s no reason to think they have the consistency required to get hot over the final week and overtake the White Sox, Blue Jays and Astros.
–CL
17. Miami Marlins
The Miami Marlins tried to do what they could to stick around in the NL postseason hunt, even using Sandy Alcantara on one day of rest in a save opportunity, but they were eliminated following Friday’s loss in San Diego. As disappointing as that is, the Marlins could finish above .500 for just the third time since 2009. That’s a sign that things are heading in the right direction for Miami.
–ZR
16. Toronto Blue Jays
The Jays have lost three of four series now, and news that Dylan Cease will have his next start bumped due to shoulder fatigue makes it even less likely that Toronto can sneak its way into the playoffs. With Trey Yesavage and Shane Bieber already on the IL, the rotation has begun leaking oil, and that’s not something this power-starved lineup is equipped to handle. The Jays still have a path to the final Wild Card spot, but it’s becoming an increasingly tenuous one, and it’s hard to see them making much noise even if they did get in.
–CL
15. Houston Astros
Getting swept at home by the Braves this weekend might well wind up costing the Astros a playoff spot. The closing schedule isn’t too tough, with trips to Seattle and Sacramento on tap. Still, if Houston doesn’t figure out where its high-powered offense went before it’s too late — and if Joe Espada can’t stop his bullpen from blowing late leads — Yordan Alvarez’s MVP season may well be for nought. As it stands, this looks like a team with fatal flaws that will spoil what could have been a deep run in a wide-open AL.
–CL
14. Chicago White Sox
Reality hit the White Sox real quick. Chicago has lingered around .500 for longer than they'd care to admit, and it was only a matter of time before the rest of the Central caught up to them. Munetaka Murakami has been dreadful since the trade deadline, and thus any contract extension talks have been put on hold. If the White Sox can hold on to a playoff spot, they'll be one of the best stories in October. If not, this season could all be for naught.
-MP
13. Texas Rangers
All of a sudden, the Rangers find themselves back in control of the AL West and home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs. Of course, that says more about the West than it does about Texas; this is still a .500 team, one without a ton of depth on either side of the ball. The interesting thing, though, is that this lineup has finally started to show signs of life of late. Take care of business against the Twins and Mets this week, and no one’s going to want to face a team with Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi in the rotation plus an offense featuring Corey Seager, Wyatt Langford and Josh Jung.
-CL
12. Pittsburgh Pirates
The narrative Pirates fans are spinning these days is the same web every National League non-playoff team will get caught in this week; if only we played in the American League! Yes, the disparity between leagues is easy to blame for the Pirates shortcomings, but the front office also fell short in acquiring bullpen arms last winter, which could've kept Pittsburgh from blowing an extraordinary number of leads in the season's first half. That'll haunt these Pirates forever.
-MP
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
It's not Arizona's fault that their primary competition for a Wild Card spot, San Diego, has become one of the hottest teams in baseball over the last few weeks. Either way, though, Arizona has simply run out of bullets, especially in a rotation that hasn't gotten the boost from Corbin Burnes' return that they were hoping for. Eduardo Rodriguez has turned back into a pumpkin, and there's just not enough depth to keep pace with what's become a beast of an NL playoff chase.
–CL
10. Cleveland Guardians
Here we go again with the Guardians. Cleveland is a legitimate threat in a weak American League. Much like last season, the Guards are taking advantage of a fellow contender floundering down the stretch. This is when Cleveland plays its best baseball, so it should be no surprise they've won five straight games heading into Monday's potential postseason preview against the Red Sox.
-MP
9. Boston Red Sox
Dropping consecutive series to the Rangers and Rays won’t do much to Boston’s postseason outlook — they’ve been more or less locked into a Wild Card series in the Bronx for a while now — but it still doesn’t inspire confidence in this team’s ability to make a run come October. This offense is once again mired in a power outage, and while getting Willson Contreras and others back from the IL figures to help, who knows when that might actually be. And there’s still just a real dearth of power here that even this pitching staff might not be able to make up for.
–CL
8. Philadelphia Phillies
I don’t know what to think of the Philadelphia Phillies. On one hand, a rotation led by Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sanchez, a healthy Jesus Luzardo, a rejuvenated Aaron Nola and a much-improved Andrew Painter should will them to wins. On the other hand, Luzardo is not healthy, the lineup is top-heavy and the bullpen, outside of Jhoan Duran, is an utter disaster. The Phillies are almost certainly going to make the playoffs, but their losses in New York this week ruined any last hope they had at a division title. And with how they’re playing right now, I don’t know if I’d pick them to get beyond the Wild Card Round.
–ZR
7. Chicago Cubs
The Cubs playoff parade was put on hold Sunday as Alex Bregman was struck in the face by a foul ball. Bregman was taken to the local hospital, and it's unclear how much time he will miss as of this writing. Chicago's postseason hopes may hang in the balance, as their one clear advantage over every other NL team is their lineup. The Cubs have scored the most runs in baseball this year.
-MP
6. San Diego Padres
Yes, the schedule has helped, particularly series against Miami, Colorado, Washington, San Francisco and Cincinnati. But no matter who they've played, the Padres look like a different team from the one we saw for much of the year, with their big bats finally mashing and their rotation coming into focus with Nick Pivetta now back in the fold. San Diego is now dead even with Chicago and Philly in the Wild Card race, and no one will want to face this lineup and this bullpen in a short series.
–CL
5. New York Yankees
Just when it seemed like New York was getting ready to make a move, with Aaron Judge finally back in the lineup after months on the shelf, the reigning AL MVP landed right back on the IL — this time with a calf strain that could well jeopardize his entire postseason. It’s been that sort of year for the Yankees, which have the pitching to keep believing in them as contenders but just haven’t been able to put it all together enough to take command of their own playoff destiny. And with a Judge-less offense and a penchant for mistake-filled baseball, winning three series in a row feels like a tough ask even in this AL.
–CL
4. Atlanta Braves
The Atlanta Braves punched their ticket to the playoffs this week, and thanks to the Phillies’ struggles, they’re on the cusp of winning the NL East — ensuring a top-three seed in the National League. Tyler Mahle pitched another gem, and Ronald Acuña Jr. is hitting his stride at the perfect time. There’re still some concerns with the team, like the No. 3 spot in their rotation and struggling stars like Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies, but getting to the playoffs is a big deal, and the Braves can take pride in checking that box.
–ZR
3. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays may well have sewn up the AL East this week, taking two of three from the Red Sox over the weekend to stretch their lead over the Yankees ahead of an all-important four-game set in the Bronx beginning on Tuesday. Even if New York were to sweep all four, though, Tampa would still have the inside track to the division and the No. 1 overall seed. This pitching staff continues to thrive beyond all expectation even with some recent injuries, and the hitting has done just enough. Whether that recipe will withstand the postseason is the only question now.
–CL
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Don't look now, but L.A.'s lineup has begun to stir, with Kyle Tucker looking like the player the Dodgers thought they were paying for this offseason. They also got Edwin Diaz back this week, and he's suddenly looking like the star closer of old — potentially answering this team's biggest question entering October. We know the rotation will be there; if they have Tucker at the height of his powers and a one-two punch in Diaz and Tanner Scott at the end of games, the three-peat march might be back on.
–CL
1. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers set a franchise record with 98 wins on Sunday. They still have a full week to go to add to that mark, and appear likely to reach the 100-win plateau. That's a great accomplishment, but it won't mean squat if Milwaukee falls to the Los Angeles Dodgers — or any other NL team for that matter — on their way to that elusive NL pennant. The Brewers are the favorites, but the Dodgers are lingering right behind them.
-MP

item.content:encoded:
You know that the Pittsburgh Pirates’ offseason has officially arrived when we’re talking about a potential Paul Skenes trade.
It’s been a bit, hasn’t it? The Pirates remained in NL Wild Card contention throughout the second half, which ordinarily would be enough to halt the annual speculation. But Skenes has looked nothing like his Cy Young self, and he could realistically end the year with an ERA above 4.00. This is the same pitcher who had a 1.96 ERA through his first 320.2 innings and looked unhittable most nights.
In the grand scheme of things, nothing has changed. Skenes hasn’t publicly requested a trade, and the Pirates have insisted they won’t trade the three-time All-Star. Objectively, we imagine he’ll be toeing the mound on Opening Day 2027, whenever that might be.
Bleacher Report’s Zachary D. Rymer nonetheless pitched (pun intended) two possible Skenes trades, one involving the Yankees and another featuring Mets. Needless to say, we have plenty of thoughts.
Yankees send Ben Rice, Spencer Jones, and two pitchers to the Pirates for Paul Skenes and Bryan Reynolds
Pirates grade: C+
Yankees grade: C-
Those who spend much of their free time scrolling X/Twitter (hey, we know the feeling all too well) are likely familiar with the meme of Bugs Bunny squinting his eyes and saying “No.” That’s exactly how we felt upon initially seeing this trade offer.
Let’s start with the obvious: the Yankees aren’t trading Rice. At no point did we hear his name floated amid the Tarik Skubal rumors, and his left-handed power makes him a perfect fit for Yankee Stadium’s short porch. He’ll either open next season as the starting first baseman or designated hitter, depending on what Giancarlo Stanton’s future looks like; the 2017 NL MVP has one year left on his deal, and he’s been an injury liability since the start of 2019.
We’re skeptical that Jones would be moved unless the return involves an MVP-caliber outfielder. Trent Grisham is a pending free agent, and we’re genuinely unsure what Jasson Domínguez’s future in New York looks like, especially after his recent demotion to Triple-A. When a team doesn’t want you on the big-league roster ahead of the playoffs, what does that say?
Reynolds has had a fine year, and he entered Sunday leading the league in doubles. But if you’re the Yankees, do you really want to give up Jones and Lagrange for an outfielder who turns 32 in January? Reynolds is under contract through 2030 (with a $20 million team option for 2031), and that’s a significant commitment to someone who, at his best, is a mid-3 bWAR player.
We must also note that Rymer claimed that Rodríguez ranked No. 82 and Lagrange placed No. 100 on MLB Pipeline, which is simply untrue. Shortstop Dax Kilby is the only Yankees player on the most recent MLB Pipeline list, and he placed No. 83. So the Pirates wouldn’t even be landing a top-100 prospect? Hard pass.
That said, we’ll give the Yankees a C- for their return, because an elite Skenes ranks among the game’s best pitchers. But will we see him regain that 2024-25 form? That we’re even asking the question should say enough.
Mets give up Carson Benge and two prospects for Pirates teammates Paul Skenes and Bryan Reynolds
Pirates grade: D
Mets grade: C
At least the proposed Pirates-Yankees trade made some sense. We can’t say the same about Pittsburgh theoretically shipping Skenes and Reynolds to the Mets for Benge, Rojas, and Tong.
First off, why would the Mets only need to give up three players rather than the Yankees’ four? Rymer listed Rojas as the No. 79 prospect and Tong at No. 88, neither of which is accurate; Rojas is No. 73, and MLB Pipeline no longer lists Tong among its top 100 prospects, for reasons we don’t understand. Mariners lefty Kade Anderson has thrown 25.1 big-league innings, and he's still ranked No. 5, but Tong and his 39.2 innings over two seasons no longer qualify. Huh?
Benge has quietly enjoyed a solid rookie season, hitting .276 with 19 home runs, 61 RBIs, 22 steals, and a .760 OPS through his first 149 games. But for him to be the centerpiece of a deal involving both Skenes and Reynolds is absurd. Oh, and Benge turns 24 in January, so he’d be a slightly older second-year starter.
As for the Mets, adding yet another long-term contract isn’t the answer to putting their disastrous 2026 season behind them. As we’ve said before, Bo Bichette would be foolish to exercise his opt-out clause and leave $42 million in guaranteed money on the table. Marcus Semien has two years and $46 million left on his deal, and we’re not even factoring in Francisco Lindor’s contract.
That said, we’ve seen enough positives from Benge thus far to hold off on giving the Pirates’ theoretical return an “F” grade. But both teams should pass on even contemplating such an offer.

September 21 Notes
Falling off: Aaron Judge (ninth), Dylan Cease (40th), Alex Bregman (43rd), Andrés Muñoz (71st), Jesús Luzardo (93rd), Troy Melton (117th), Bryce Eldridge (140th) and 36 other players.
- It’s a fool’s errand, but here’s one last update for the final week of the season. I tried emphasizing two-start starters unless they’re particularly dangerous, but I also tried to take into account that some of the guys currently in line to start twice are going to end up being scratched or making only brief appearances next weekend.
- With no updates yet on Alex Bregman (face) and Andrés Muñoz (knee), I’ve dropped both from the rankings. Pedro Ramírez, who was set to fall off the list with Dansby Swanson back, reclaimed a spot in Bregman’s place. Seranthony Domínguez seems like the likeliest choice for saves in Seattle in Muñoz’s place, so he comes in at No. 166.
- Thank you so much to everyone who has followed along all season. Anyone interested in the full spreadsheet of where players have ranked start to finish, reach out to my gmail at matthewpouliot. I’ll be back in mid-October with the first (or second) go at a 2027 Top 300.
September 14 Notes
Falling off: Shohei Ohtani DH (eighth), Rafael Devers (41st), Jazz Chisholm Jr. (58th), Bryce Miller (177th), Gleyber Torres (183rd), Hayden Wesneski (206th), Royce Lewis (214th), Kyle Bradish (222nd), Michael McGreevy (243rd), Brandon Pfaadt (246th), Braxton Ashcraft (250th) and 21 other players
- I don’t have much of a notes section for you right now, since it’s after 3 am and I’d like to get some sleep. Still, the rankings are updated for the final 14 days of the season. A lot of the pitcher movement this week is elevating guys with three starts remaining and dropping those with only two. I also gave Rockies hitters a nice boost, as they play 10 of their remaining 13 games at home. Padres hitters also got a little lift from that, as they’ll be starting a four-game series in Coors Field on Monday.
September 7 Notes
Falling off: Kyle Harrison (101st), Shane McClanahan (125th), Luis Robert Jr. (163rd), Trent Graham (180th), Joe Musgrove (192nd), Byron Buxton (202nd), Cam Smith (219th), Brendan Donovan (227th), JJ Wetherholt (236th), Eric Lauer (243rd), Jesús Sánchez (247th), Xavier Edwards (254th), Sean Manaea (261st), Samuel Basallo (262nd), Nathan Eovaldi (265th), Connor Norby (268th), Chase Burns (273rd), Shohei Ohtani SP (280th), Tommy White (282nd), Daniel Palencia (285th), Colton Cowser (286th), Taylor Ward (289th), Ezequiel Tovar (290th), Alek Thomas (292nd), Willi Castro (294th), Elvis Alvarado (295th), Brandyn Garcia (299th)
- With three weeks to go, nearly every injured player is off the rankings at this point, with the exception of a few guys hopefully returning before the end of this week. Also, I’m paying a lot more attention to matchups, particularly this week’s. So, some starters with multiple starts this week who wouldn’t normally be in the top 300 make the cut. Also, Athletics hitters have moved up, since they’ll be at home for six games this week. Rockies hitters have dropped off as that team goes back on the road after a week of home games.
- Rafael Devers gets an overdue late bump. There really was good reason for concern early on with his strikeout rate up and his bat speed down, but he bounced back nicely in both categories. Amazing is the consistency in his wOBAs since 2021: .373, .373, .359, .364, .365 and .365. His xwOBAs, on the other hand, still show a little decline: .391, .365, .380, .366, .367, .340. Still, it’s been a really impressive season, and getting to 100 runs scored (maybe) and 100 RBI (almost certainly) on the moribund Giants offense is one heck of an accomplishment.
- The Orioles getting swept by Red Sox over the weekend, dropping their postseason odds at Fangraphs to just three percent, would seem to greatly increase the chances that Kyle Bradish gets shut down with a week or two to go. He’s up to 152 innings in his first full year back from Tommy John, and he’s not exactly doing his best work at the moment.
- Kyle Harrison might have lost his rotation spot with his performance Sunday against the Reds, though I thought about keeping him on the list anyway, since he could be well set up for wins in middle relief if moved to the pen. In the end, he didn’t quite make the cut. It will be really interesting to see how the Brewers play things the rest of the way. I imagine both Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson will make a couple of shorter starts in an attempt to save bullets for October.
- It’ll be nice to see Corbin Burnes back on a major league mound Tuesday, but given that he threw just two innings in his lone rehab start after Tommy John, so I couldn’t see including him here just yet. San Diego’s Nick Pivetta, on the other hand, at least made it up to 4 1/3 innings in his last rehab start as he returns from an elbow injury. That gets him a spot on the bottom of the list, even if he’s a long shot to get a win Monday in his return.

The update comes just four days after he returned to the Yankees following a len
item.content:encoded:
Clarke Schmidt downplayed the latest issue involving his right arm after the New York Yankees' 8-4 loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks on Sunday.
Schmidt was unavailable to pitch because of biceps cramps, according to Bob Nightengale of USA TODAY. The right-hander described the decision as precautionary and is expected to see a team doctor in New York.
Schmidt does not have any diagnostic tests scheduled at this point. The update comes just four days after he returned to the Yankees following a lengthy recovery from Tommy John surgery.
Yankees pitcher Clarke Schmidt, who had biceps cramps and couldn’t come into the game, described it as precautionary.
He will see a doctor back in NY but no testing is planned
The Yankees activated Schmidt from the 60-day injured list on Sept. 16. He made his return against the Minnesota Twins, throwing two-thirds of an inning and recording two strikeouts.
Schmidt underwent surgery in July 2025 after tearing the UCL in his right elbow. The procedure kept him out for roughly 14 months and limited his time to a short late-season return.
Rather than immediately returning to the starting rotation, Schmidt was expected to work as a multi-inning reliever. The Yankees planned to manage his workload carefully while evaluating how he could contribute during the postseason.
The latest issue adds another layer of uncertainty, although Schmidt's own description suggests the team is not treating it as a major setback at this stage.
The Yankees entered Sunday with an 89-66 record and had already secured a postseason berth. They remain six games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East with the regular season nearing its conclusion.
Schmidt's availability could become increasingly important as New York prepares for October. For now, the Yankees will wait for his evaluation in New York before determining whether the biceps issue will affect his return to the bullpen.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Latest Clarke Schmidt injury scare yet another reminder of Yankees' insane trade deadline strategy
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib
item.description: More than almost any other New York Yankees playoff run, this October's edition will provide either immediate vindication for Brian Cashman's trade deadline strategy or all-new reasons to directly blame him for the team's failure. It should be fascinating to watch, if you don't actually have much emotional energy invested in the team's well-being. Clarke Schmidt's postgame note on Sunday evening was just another reason to be anxious about the way this bullpen was constructed and the amount of va
item.content:encoded:
More than almost any other New York Yankees playoff run, this October's edition will provide either immediate vindication for Brian Cashman's trade deadline strategy or all-new reasons to directly blame him for the team's failure. It should be fascinating to watch, if you don't actually have much emotional energy invested in the team's well-being. Clarke Schmidt's postgame note on Sunday evening was just another reason to be anxious about the way this bullpen was constructed and the amount of variables therein.
Trade deadline predictions for the Yankees' haul this year were astoundingly easy to make. A catcher, first and foremost. An impact bat, that was obvious. And then two bullpen arms to help save their late-inning core from running aground before the year ended. Maybe one would be a certified ace, a tier below Mason Miller, but still devilish. Maybe another would be a bounce back candidate or a never-was, someone who Matt Blake could unearth. Either way, the choices were many, but the outcome was obvious: CashGod would be trading for some relievers. Plural.
But then the deadline came and went. We weren't disappointed by the quality of the haul, but rather in a whole new way. No catcher? No relievers? Was this a mistake? Is the deadline tomorrow?
Nope. Cashman went all in and decided that either the prices were too high or not commensurate with the talent available. Instead, he would look the other way and ignore the rising cost of wear-and-tear in August and piece together some bullpen reinforcements using alternate levers. The waiver wire became his friend. His rotation became a plucking ground, as did his own Injured List. Will Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Weathers, Luis Gil, Will Warren, John Schreiber and Michael Fulmer be more valuable together than any names he could've added on Aug. 3? That's the bet. We'll see. I have my doubts, but he has his agenda.
And, in case you weren't already lacking confidence, Schmidt's bicep barked on Sunday and prevented him from entering the game, a game that ace reliever Brent Headrick lit on fire with an average fastball that dipped about a mile and a half below his standard velocity on the season. Hmm. If only he could've been rested during the dog days of summer.
Clarke Schmidt's worrisome postgame comments, Brent Headrick outing vs. Diamondbacks tell the same Yankees story
So, for the record, that's Schmidt - after one MLB outing this year - admitting that, out of precaution, he stopped warming up when his arm barked. His rehab was also halted along the way when he felt forearm cramping on Aug. 4, just one day post-trade deadline. The Yankees getting him back to the MLB level after a summer 2025 Tommy John surgery is remarkable. This is not someone a team should be relying on to cover meaningful postseason innings. And yet.
Headrick's stumble comes in an otherwise phenomenal year, and even as he's lost some gas down the stretch, he's still managed to mostly make things work. He's an expert at limiting inherited runners from scoring, and he's alternated spotless outings with troublesome ones post-deadline. No one knows for certain whether bringing on an experienced seventh-inning guy or two in early August would've prevented the effects of overuse from piling up on Headrick's left arm, but we do know having a viable alternative now could help them deemphasize Headrick if he's struggling to recapture his former glory. Batters hit .345 off him in 15 August games.
That group of alternatives probably doesn't, or shouldn't, include Schmidt, who's hanging on by a thread. Again, it'll be Cashman's crew - Schreiber, Fulmer, Warren, and maybe Weathers, who won't be rehabbing in a regular season game - vs. the field to see who's better equipped for October. Fascinating, if it weren't so presumptuous.

item.content:encoded:
Why Aaron Boone could be in postseason 'hell' with Yankees originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees are looking to end a 17-year World Series drought.
Aaron Boone has completed eight of those years as Yankees manager.
This could be a crucial postseason for Boone's future with the AL East club, but New York's ownership and front office have always shown confidence in the skipper.
If three-time MVP Aaron Judge is unable to play in the postseason due to his calf strain, the Yankees will face a difficult task to end their World Series-less streak.
Elsewhere on the diamond, Bleacher Report's Kerry Miller believes Boone will have to hit the right buttons with the infield alignment.
"However, Aaron Boone is about to be in second-guessing hell in October as it pertains to when and where to deploy George Lombard Jr., Anthony Volpe, José Caballero, Amed Rosario and Ryan McMahon at shortstop and third base," Miller wrote.
Second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. would complicate things further if he returns from the injured list before the playoffs.
Volpe has been playing well at second base, but Chisholm offers a higher offensive ceiling.
Boone could consider moving Volpe or Chisholm to third base to keep both players in the lineup. If so, does Caballero become limited to pinch-running duties?
McMahon is Boone's best defensive third baseman, but he offers little (.208/.275/.343, .618 OPS) with a bat in hand.
It seems likely Lombard will stick at shortstop, but Boone and his coaching staff have to be racking his brain trying to figure out what's best for the team.

item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, the New York Yankees finished their series with the Arizona Diamondbacks in Phoenix.
The Yankees lost by a score of 8-4 (and dropped two out of three games in the series).
36-Year-Old Will Be A New York Yankees Free Agent
With the regular season nearly over, it’s worth noting that Tim Hill will be a free agent this winter.
The 36-year-old has gone 5-2 with a 4.71 ERA in 65 games this year.
It will be interesting to see if the Yankees look to bring him back for the 2027 season.
Looking At Hill’s Career
Hill was picked in the 32nd round of the 2014 MLB Draft.
He spent the first two years of his career with the Kansas City Royals.
Following Kansas City, Hill went on to have stints with the San Diego Padres, Chicago White Sox (and Yankees).
With the Yankees, Hill has been very solid over his three-year tenure.
During the 2024 season, he went 3-0 with a 2.05 ERA in 35 games.
Hill has also appeared in 13 MLB playoff games for the franchise.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Los Yankees se fueron del Chase Field con el tipo de derrota que hace que un solo lanzamiento parezca más importante que todo un fin de semana.
Una ventaja de 4-1 se esfumó en la quinta entrada del domingo. La culpa recayó sobre Brent Headrick, el caballo de batalla de los Yankees y cuyo brazo había estado impecable hasta entonces.
Nolan Arenado conectó el golpe que selló la remontada. Su grand slam puso a Arizona por delante y contribuyó a que Nueva York cayera por 8-4 en su último partido fuera de casa de la temporada regular.
La entrada empezó con Will Warren aún defendiendo una ventaja de tres carreras. Arizona llenó las bases con un out antes de que Aaron Boone recurriera al bullpen. Los Yankees ya habían anotado jonrones en la tercera entrada gracias a Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. y Spencer Jones, una racha que sacó del partido a Corbin Burnes y puso el partido brevemente bajo el control de Nueva York.
Headrick entró con las bases llenas. Eliminó a Geraldo Perdomo por strikeout para conseguir el segundo out y, a continuación, concedió una base por bolas a Corbin Carroll, lo que permitió que entrara una carrera. Arenado mandó la siguiente bola fuera por la línea del campo izquierdo. Un lanzamiento después, la bola se quedó dentro del campo.
Ese jonrón de cuatro carreras cambió el marcador de 4-2 a una ventaja de 6-4 para Arizona. Headrick se llevó la derrota y no se le atribuyó ningún salvamento.
La cifra detrás del Grand Slam es motivo de gran preocupación para los Yankees
El problema más grave salió a la luz tras el partido. La bola rápida de Headrick tenía una velocidad notablemente menor que la que había tenido durante la mayor parte de esta temporada en la que ha destacado. El zurdo alcanzó una media de 92,9 mph con ese lanzamiento el domingo, según una publicación del periodista especializado en los Yankees, Brendan Kuty. Baseball Savant sitúa el promedio de la bola de cuatro costuras de Headrick en 94,2 mph para 2026.
Esa diferencia de 1,3 mph no significa que haya una lesión, y no se ha informado de que Headrick esté lesionado. Pero llega al final de una carga de trabajo como ninguna otra que haya tenido que afrontar como relevista de las Grandes Ligas. Headrick ha jugado 79 partidos y ha lanzado 77 entradas. La MLB lo registra con un balance de 7-4, una efectividad de 2,10, 96 strikeouts, 25 bases por bolas y un WHIP de 1,18.
La publicación de Kuty puso en perspectiva el cambio de velocidad tras la salida más desastrosa de Headrick esta temporada.
«La velocidad media de la bola rápida de Headrick esta noche en Arizona contra los Diamondbacks fue de 92,9 mph», escribió Kuty.
Headrick ha lanzado dos días seguidos en Arizona, lanzando dos tercios de entrada el sábado y otra vez el domingo. Ha sumado 10 ponches en 8 1/3 entradas en septiembre, hasta el domingo.
Headrick se acerca a un hito que pocos Yankees han alcanzado
Lo que diferencia esta temporada de una carga de trabajo habitual como relevista es la frecuencia. Headrick ha lanzado en 79 de los 155 partidos de los Yankees, algo más de la mitad del calendario. La MLB informó el domingo de que solo un lanzador de las Grandes Ligas ha salido al campo más veces esta temporada.
La historia del equipo le da aún más peso a esa cifra. Paul Quantrill estableció el récord de la franquicia de los Yankees con 86 apariciones en 2004. Scott Proctor jugó 83 partidos en 2006. Las 79 de Headrick ya igualan el total de Mike Stanton en 2002 y el de Tom Gordon en 2005. A falta de siete partidos, ya está protagonizando una de las temporadas más intensas en el bullpen que ha vivido la franquicia.
El cambio respecto a 2025 es considerable. Según los datos de la MLB, Headrick lanzó 23 entradas con los Yankees y 24 en la Triple A la temporada pasada. Sus 77 entradas en las Grandes Ligas este año ya superan ese total combinado en 30 entradas.
Este bajón de final de temporada es importante, ya que los Yankees necesitan la mejor versión de octubre .
Las estadísticas de Headrick en toda la temporada siguen convirtiéndolo en una de las piezas más sólidas del bullpen de los Yankees. Solo ha cedido cinco jonrones en los 318 bateadores a los que se ha enfrentado. Ha mantenido a los bateadores diestros en un promedio de .205, según los datos actuales de la MLB sobre estadísticas por tipo de bateador, lo que le ha ayudado a evitar quedarse relegado a un papel de relevo específico para determinados enfrentamientos.
Sus últimas actuaciones no han sido tan buenas. En sus últimas siete salidas, Headrick tiene una efectividad de 4,76 en 5 2/3 entradas. Es una muestra pequeña, pero el momento es clave porque Boone va a necesitar opciones fiables en el bullpen para respaldar a la rotación de la postemporada.
Los Yankees prepararon a Headrick para que tuviera una carga de trabajo más intensa durante el invierno. El entrenador de lanzadores, Matt Blake, ya había identificado la recuperación como el principal reto hace meses, cuando Headrick ya se encontraba entre los relevistas más utilizados de la MLB. La pregunta ahora es si los Yankees podrán reducir su tiempo de juego durante la última semana sin que pierda esa precisión que lo ha convertido en indispensable.
Los Yankees tienen ahora que tomar una decisión sobre el descanso en plena lucha por el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana
Para los Yankees, esta derrota ha puesto las cuentas de la División Este de la Liga Americana al límite. Nueva York tiene un balance de 89-66 y está a seis partidos de Tampa Bay, cuando quedan siete partidos por disputar. Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero ahora empiezan una serie de cuatro partidos en casa contra los Rays con muy poco margen en la lucha por el título de la división.
El domingo también se cerró un balance de 47-34 como visitantes, uno de los mejores registros fuera de casa del béisbol.
Nueva York termina con tres partidos contra Baltimore después de enfrentarse a Tampa Bay. Como ya no hay que viajar después de Arizona y el mes de octubre ya está asegurado, la última semana sirve también para decidir qué lanzadores están listos para la postemporada. Por eso, el estado del cuerpo de lanzadores es casi tan importante como la propia clasificación.
La serie contra los Rays complica esa decisión. Mientras la división siga matemáticamente abierta, los Yankees tienen motivos para usar a sus mejores relevos disponibles en partidos reñidos. Si Tampa Bay se asegura el título, la situación cambia rápidamente. Proteger el brazo de Headrick y que recupere su bola rápida habitual podría llegar a ser más importante que otra entrada decisiva para la clasificación.
El grand slam del domingo seguirá siendo el error más evidente porque decidió el partido. Lo que pasa más desapercibido es lo que los Yankees tienen que vigilar ahora. Headrick ha llevado el peso del bullpen durante seis meses, y su bola rápida llegó a Arizona en su momento más flojo, justo cuando octubre está a la vuelta de la esquina.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Siete jugadores y managers de la MLB que enfrentan presión en el cierre de temporada
item.dc:creator: Ryan Phillips
item.description: El cierre de la temporada regular de MLB ya está en marcha, con poco más de una semana por delante antes de que comience el beisbol de playoffs. Las carreras por los puestos de postemporada están llegando al límite y la presión aumenta en toda la liga. Para algunos jugadores y managers, las últimas semanas de la temporada podrían definir cómo serán recordados sus años. Algunos intentan llevar a sus equipos a la postemporada, mientras que otros luchan por consolidar sus roles de cara a octubre. I
item.content:encoded:
El cierre de la temporada regular de MLB ya está en marcha, con poco más de una semana por delante antes de que comience el beisbol de playoffs. Las carreras por los puestos de postemporada están llegando al límite y la presión aumenta en toda la liga.
Para algunos jugadores y managers, las últimas semanas de la temporada podrían definir cómo serán recordados sus años. Algunos intentan llevar a sus equipos a la postemporada, mientras que otros luchan por consolidar sus roles de cara a octubre. Incluso algunos puestos podrían estar en juego.
Te puede interesar: MLB: 12 hitos y récords que podrían establecerse en las últimas semanas de la temporada
Con poco tiempo para cambiar la manera en que terminan sus temporadas, las siguientes siete figuras de MLB son quienes enfrentan mayor presión y tienen más en juego durante el cierre de campaña.
Gerrit Cole, SP de los Yankees
Los Yankees siguen siendo uno de los favoritos de la Liga Americana y eso se debe en gran medida a su cuerpo de pitcheo de élite. Nueva York lidera a MLB en ERA (3.19) por un amplio margen, y la rotación abridora también encabeza la competencia con una ERA de 3.26. Gerrit Cole alguna vez fue el as del cuerpo de pitcheo, pero existen dudas sobre cuál será su papel en octubre debido a sus actuaciones irregulares recientes y al buen nivel que ha mostrado el resto de la rotación.
Después de perderse todo 2025, Cole regresó de una cirugía Tommy John el 22 de mayo y ha tenido una temporada de altibajos. Antes del enfrentamiento del viernes contra los Diamondbacks, tiene marca de 8–9, con una ERA de 3.67, WHIP de 1.13 y 117 strikeouts en 115 ⅓ entradas. Lo preocupante es que en sus dos últimas aperturas, contra los Padres y Mets, permitió siete home runs en 11 ⅓ entradas. Como resultado, su ERA de septiembre se disparó a 6.48 en tres aperturas.
Cam Schlittler ha sido el mejor pitcher de la Liga Americana esta temporada y debería ser el abridor de los Yankees para el Juego 1 de la postemporada. El veterano Max Fried no está muy lejos y también tiene argumentos gracias a su trayectoria y a su ERA de 2.63 esta temporada. Carlos Rodón (6–3, ERA de 2.95) podría colocarse por encima de Cole como el No. 3, tomando en cuenta sus actuaciones recientes, lo que incluso podría dejar a Cole fuera del roster de los Yankees para una serie de wild card de tres juegos.
Después de su apertura del viernes contra Arizona, a Cole solo le quedará una apertura en la temporada regular. Estará bajo una enorme presión para demostrar que merece una apertura garantizada en la postemporada.
Manny Machado, 3B de los Padres
Machado es el capitán de facto de los Padres y, junto con Fernando Tatis Jr., es el rostro de la franquicia. Con San Diego con una ventaja de cuatro juegos sobre los Diamondbacks por el último lugar de wild card de la Liga Nacional al entrar al penúltimo fin de semana de la temporada, si el equipo se queda fuera de los playoffs, Machado cargará con una gran parte de la responsabilidad, tomando en cuenta su estatus y lo mal que bateó al comienzo del año.
Hasta el 30 de junio, Machado estaba teniendo la peor temporada profesional de su carrera. Bateaba para .189/.274/.399, con 16 home runs, 46 carreras impulsadas y un wRC+ de 86. Fue una actuación brutal para un jugador que representa $31.8 millones contra la nómina del impuesto de lujo. En los 61 juegos posteriores, batea para .257/.349/.427, con 12 home runs, 39 carreras impulsadas y un wRC+ de 119, apenas un par de puntos por debajo de su promedio de carrera.
Está volviendo a parecerse a sí mismo en el momento indicado pero, sea justo o no, ha adquirido la reputación de no responder en los partidos importantes. Machado tiene un OPS de .682 de por vida en postemporada y se fue de 1-de-10 con tres strikeouts en la breve aparición de San Diego en los playoffs del año pasado. Necesita revertir esa tendencia y calentarse en el cierre de la temporada.
Don Mattingly, manager de los Phillies
Mattingly asumió como manager interino de los Phillies el 28 de abril, después de que el equipo comenzara el año con marca de 9–19. Desde entonces, Philadelphia tiene récord de 74–49, en una de las remontadas más marcadas que hemos visto en los últimos años. Sin embargo, todavía queda trabajo por hacer.
Los Phillies son considerados dueños de una de las mayores ventajas de localía de todo el beisbol en los playoffs y llegan al fin de semana empatados con los Cubs por el primer lugar de wild card, lo que les permitiría recibir una serie de wild card. Jugar lo suficientemente bien durante el cierre para superar a Chicago —y a San Diego, que acecha justo detrás de ambos equipos— sería de gran ayuda para las posibilidades de Philadelphia de avanzar a la NLDS.
Persisten los rumores de que los Phillies buscarán contratar a Alex Cora como su manager esta temporada baja, pero Mattingly podría obligar al equipo a cambiar de decisión con un buen cierre de temporada. Si la franquicia está decidida por Cora, Mattingly necesita hacerlos cambiar de opinión. Llegar tambaleándose a la meta no es la manera de conseguirlo.
Vladimir Guerrero Jr., 1B de los Blue Jays
Los Blue Jays de alguna manera siguen en la pelea por el último lugar de wild card de la Liga Americana a pesar de una larga lista de lesiones y de que su jugador estrella está atravesando la peor temporada de su carrera. Después de una postemporada extraordinaria en 2025, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. ha estado jugando como si los Monstars le hubieran absorbido todo su poder. Con su equipo peleando por un lugar en los playoffs, los reflectores estarán sobre el jugador de 27 años durante las próximas semanas.
En 138 juegos, Guerrero batea para .262/.334/.360, con apenas nueve home runs, 56 carreras impulsadas y un wRC+ de 97, el peor de su carrera. Su porcentaje de slugging es el más bajo de su carrera por más de 70 puntos, su porcentaje de embasado es casi 50 puntos menor que su registro de 2025 y su OPS (.694) es casi 100 puntos menor que la peor marca de su carrera. Tuvo que esperar hasta el 13 de septiembre, en el juego 75 de Toronto como local, para conectar su primer home run de la temporada en el Rogers Centre. Como referencia, conectó home runs en cada uno de los dos primeros juegos de los Blue Jays como locales en los playoffs del año pasado.
Toronto comenzó la temporada con aspiraciones de ganar la World Series después de quedarse corto en siete juegos ante los Dodgers el año pasado. El equipo se reforzó durante el offseason, esperando tener un gran año. Ha sido un fracaso y, como su jugador de $500 millones, Guerrero es simultáneamente la cara de la franquicia y el principal símbolo de ese fracaso. Tiene unas cuantas semanas para cambiar las cosas.
Joe Espada, manager de los Astros
Espada era el bench coach del equipo de Houston que ganó la World Series de 2022 y fue promovido a manager cuando Dusty Baker se retiró después de la temporada 2023. Los resultados no han sido buenos durante sus tres temporadas al frente.
Los Astros ganaron la AL West en 2024 con marca de 88–73 (.547). Pero fueron barridos por los Tigers en la serie de wild card. En 2025, Houston se quedó fuera de los playoffs después de terminar con 87–75 y perder un desempate ante Detroit. El dueño de los Astros, Jim Crane, considera que su equipo debería competir por títulos todos los años, pero los equipos de Espada se han quedado muy lejos de esos objetivos, y este año no ha sido diferente.
Houston ha estado con marca de .500 o por debajo durante la mayor parte de la temporada, pero de alguna manera llegó al viernes con una ventaja de un juego en la AL West. Quedarse fuera de la postemporada por segundo año consecutivo pondría el puesto de Espada en serio peligro. De hecho, incluso si clasifican, hay una posibilidad considerable de que se vaya si no consigue una carrera profunda en los playoffs, tras el despido del GM Dana Brown el mes pasado.
José Ramírez, 3B de los Guardians
Al igual que Guerrero, Ramírez está atravesando una de las peores temporadas de su carrera y, hasta ahora, el último mes no ha sido amable con él. Con los Guardians en una cerrada batalla tanto por la AL Central como por un lugar de wild card, el bate de Ramírez será clave si esperan no solo llegar a la postemporada, sino también hacer ruido una vez que estén ahí.
En 117 juegos, Ramírez batea para .230/.319/.364, con un wRC+ de 90, todas ellas sus peores cifras desde 2015. Solo tiene 11 home runs y su poder aislado ha caído de .258 en 2024 a .134 este año.
Desde que se sometió a una cirugía para reparar un hueso ganchoso fracturado en junio, el jugador de 33 años ha bateado como una sombra de sí mismo. En 45 juegos desde su regreso el 22 de julio, Ramírez registra un OPS de .567 y su slump se ha profundizado en septiembre (.140 de promedio de bateo, .345 de OPS).
La piedra angular de la franquicia de Cleveland está llegando a la tercera base de los últimos años de su mejor etapa. No sabemos cuántas oportunidades más tendrá para disputar una World Series.
Dan Wilson, manager de los Mariners
Al igual que Espada y Mattingly, Wilson podría estar dirigiendo para conservar su puesto durante el resto de la temporada.
Después de llegar a la ALCS en 2025, Seattle mantuvo buena parte del mismo roster, pero ha obtenido resultados muy diferentes. Wilson también les ha dado suficientes argumentos a sus críticos con su cuestionable manejo del bullpen, algo que viene desde antes de este año. Los aficionados de los Mariners todavía no olvidan que Wilson recurrió a Eduardo Bazardo en lugar del cerrador Andrés Muñoz en un momento clave del Juego 7 de la ALCS, solo para que Bazardo dejara escapar la ventaja. Después de eso, Seattle simplemente no ha jugado buen beisbol este año. La defensa ha sido pésima y los Mariners ocupan el último lugar de MLB en Outs Above Average, con -51.
Muchos de los problemas de Seattle simplemente se deben a que jugadores clave no están rindiendo a la altura de su potencial. Cal Raleigh es el principal responsable, pero Julio Rodríguez y Josh Naylor también deberían asumir parte de la culpa. Los Mariners tienen prácticamente asegurado quedarse fuera de los playoffs —y ya aseguraron un récord perdedor—, pero es posible que Wilson reciba otro año incluso si eso ocurre. Un buen cierre de temporada contribuiría mucho a asegurar ese puesto.
Publicado originalmente en www.sportsillustrated.com el 19/09/2026, traducido al español para SI México.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Yankees Monday Mailbag 9/21: State of the Bullpen, Aaron Judge's World Series Window, and More
item.dc:creator: Joseph Randazzo; Unknown
item.description: The New York Yankees won't win the American League East after dropping two out of three games to the Arizona Diamondbacks and are now looking at another Wild Card series against the Boston Red Sox. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees won't win the American League East after dropping two out of three games to the Arizona Diamondbacks and are now looking at another Wild Card series against the Boston Red Sox. The rest of this season will now be about figuring out their roster heading into October, and this Rays series won't mean much.
There are plenty of questions from fans about what the roster should look like in the final week of the season. And if you're curious about that, reach out to Joseph Randazzo on X or Instagram at @YankeeLibrarian. Fans can ask anything, from questions about bullpen trust trees to what to do with Jazz Chisholm Jr. when he's activated.
The state of the bullpen
Who do you trust in the bullpen outside of Paul Blackburn, Brent Headrick, and David Bednar?@Mattmann1199 on Instagram
At this point, the two best names behind them are Will Warren and John Schreiber. It's likely that they'll be without Ryan Weathers, and that is the name I would have gone with. Now it's probably Schreiber, but I'm not too convinced about this answer.
Since Luis Gil has been blowing 100 out of the bullpen, they can see what they have in him as a pen arm heading into October. None of these answers inspire much, but they have somehow been one of the best bullpens in baseball.
A returning bat
Where should Jazz Chisholm Jr. play when they activate him@theezratakeshita on Instagram
Chisholm should probably go to second base. Volpe has been okay, but since his big debut against the Colorado Rockies, he has gone 7-for-33. He has two doubles, three stolen bases, and two RBI.
Since Boston has a ton of lefty starters, they can probably start a game with Volpe and then go to Chisholm later. That feels like what the Yankees will do, and it's probably the case if Volpe is scorching the ball. Of course, there is still time for Volpe to make things interesting here.
Judge's World Series dreams
The World Series window for Judge is closing. Might he go without ever winning one?@_not_mikeee on Instagram
That is absolutely on the table. There are some great players who have never won a championship. Dan Marino, Barry Bonds, and Henrik Lundqvist never got their ring. Granted, the Scott Hunter character in Heated Rivalry feels like it's loosely based on mid-2010s Lundqvist, but that might only half-count since it's a work of fiction.
A wild storyline would be the Yankees winning a World Series this year without Judge. Imagine the chaos of his legacy talks if that happens.
Job statuses
Is there a scenario that gets Cash or Boone fired this year?@kirby.phillips7 on Instagram
These questions are always easy to answer. Probably not this year. Cashman will probably go out on his own accord. Boone is the most likely candidate to get fired, but there aren't many teams that are going to axe a manager who kept their team afloat and in postseason contention with the amount of injuries they had. When baseball comes back after the lockout, those two will probably still be here.
Missing the playoffs again might do it for them, but the last time that happened, they stayed. It does feel like they have unlimited security in New York.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] Spencer Jones just made the Yankees' October call harder
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson

item.content:encoded:
Spencer Jones went 1-for-4 with a homer in Saturday’s loss to Arizona, and the hit was not some isolated late-September blip. He has a .279 average, a .343 on-base percentage and a .475 slugging percentage this month.
The catch is sitting right next to it. Jones has struck out 27 times in 68 September plate appearances. That creates a lot of empty trips for a team that may have to win tight games in October, especially with every at-bat getting picked apart.
Still, I do not see how the Yankees can act like the power is optional. Jones has three homers and 14 RBIs this month, and his season line sits at 11 homers with a .759 OPS in 81 games. He is making the hard part of this decision harder, which is a decent place for a young player to be.
The Yankees need to make the power count
Jones gives the lineup something it cannot manufacture with a safer bench piece. The ball comes off his bat differently, and opponents have to respect the damage even when the at-bat is not clean.
That matters because New York does not have the luxury of building an October group around players who merely look tidy. If the games turn into three-run affairs, one Jones homer can change an inning before a manager reaches for a pinch hitter.
The strikeouts will decide the rest
Jones does not get a free pass because he is young or because the homers are fun. The strikeout rate is real, and postseason pitching has a way of exposing loose at-bats quickly.
But there is a useful middle ground here. The Yankees do not need to hand him a permanent everyday role, and they do not need to bury him because the whiffs are ugly. They need to decide whether the power is worth carrying in the spots where it can do the most damage.
The October call is not simple. Jones has made it impossible to treat as a simple yes-or-no question.
More about:New York Yankees

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — Los Yankees se han pasado casi todo septiembre organizando a los lanzadores para la fase de octubre.
Gerrit Cole está en la lista para ser el lanzador titular en la Serie de Comodín. Cam Schlittler se ha ganado un sitio en esa misma conversación.
Max Fried vuelve a la rotación, mientras que Carlos Rodón y Will Warren están en la lista para lanzar como relevos una vez que empiece la postemporada. Estas decisiones han dejado poco margen para que algún aspirante de última hora se cuele de nuevo en el grupo de titulares.
Eso limitó las opciones de Clarke Schmidt incluso antes de que volviera a incorporarse a la plantilla. Su regreso tras una segunda operación de Tommy John nunca se planteó con el objetivo de volver a alcanzar el volumen de trabajo de un lanzador titular en las dos últimas semanas.
Los Yankees lo incorporaron al plantilla el 16 de septiembre para aportar duración, lanzamientos certeros y una variedad de lanzamientos propios de un abridor desde el bullpen. No había jugado en las Grandes Ligas desde el 3 de julio de 2025, y solo había lanzado siete entradas en las ligas menores durante su rehabilitación.
Schmidt volvió esa noche en Minnesota y consiguió dos outs, permitiendo dos sencillos de rebote y ponchando a dos. Fue su primera aparición en las Grandes Ligas en 14 meses y medio. Y lo más importante para los Yankees es que supuso el inicio de una prueba para un papel que requiere una rutina diferente.
En lugar de un día fijo de salida y una larga preparación previa al partido, Schmidt ahora tiene que entrar en calor rápidamente, salir al campo en medio de la acción o en una entrada limpia, y recuperarse siguiendo el horario de un relevista.
La situación de la plantilla ya no dejaba margen para que volviera a la rotación. Según las previsiones actuales de la MLB para la postemporada de los Yankees, Cole, Schlittler y Fried figuran como titulares, mientras que Schmidt, Rodon y Warren están entre las opciones de relevo.
Aaron Boone ha confirmado que Cole será el lanzador titular en una posible serie de comodín. Warren tiene prevista una última salida como titular en la temporada regular antes de pasar al bullpen. La posibilidad de que Schmidt volviera a ser titular se había convertido en algo más teórico que práctico para este octubre.
Un problema en el bíceps interrumpe la única prueba que le quedaba a Schmidt
Esa diferencia se hizo aún más evidente el domingo en Arizona. Clarke Schmidt estaba calentando para lo que habría sido su segunda salida desde la operación cuando notó un calambre en el bíceps derecho durante la derrota de los Yankees por 8-4 ante los Diamondbacks en el Chase Field. Dejó de lanzar y no llegó a salir al campo.
Los Yankees dijeron que las pruebas de fuerza no indicaban ningún problema en el hombro ni en el codo. Se espera que Schmidt vea a un médico del equipo en Nueva York, sin que, por el momento, se hayan previsto más pruebas.
Schmidt explicó por qué se negó a seguir adelante a pesar de esa sensación tan pronto después de la operación. Respondía a la pregunta de si ese episodio sugería un contratiempo estructural.
«No es nada estructural, fue más bien por precaución», dijo Schmidt. «Obviamente, dadas las circunstancias, al estar recuperándome de una operación, no quiero forzar nada. Todas las pruebas salieron bien, ni el hombro ni el codo presentan problemas. Era más bien una sensación parecida a un calambre. No he tenido ningún problema al atrapar la pelota hoy por la mañana y en los últimos días me he sentido muy fuerte. Así que fue algo muy, muy leve, solo por precaución».
Boone dijo que Schmidt no pudo terminar su calentamiento a pesar de haber superado las pruebas iniciales.
«Espero que no sea nada grave, pero sí lo suficiente como para que no entre en el partido», dijo Boone. «Ya veremos qué pasa».
En su lugar, Tim Hill lanzó la sexta entrada. Los Yankees habían conseguido una ventaja de 4-1 gracias a los jonrones de Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. y Spencer Jones en la tercera entrada, antes de que Arizona anotara cinco carreras en la quinta, coronadas por el grand slam de Nolan Arenado ante Brent Headrick. Justin Martínez se llevó la victoria, Headrick la derrota y no se acreditó ningún salvamento.
Un historial de 67 partidos como titular se enfrenta a un futuro repleto de jugadores en los Yankees
Schmidt ya ha demostrado que puede ser titular en las Grandes Ligas. Según los registros de la MLB, 67 de sus 97 partidos como profesional han sido como titular. Tiene una efectividad de 3,82 en 393 1/3 entradas y registró una efectividad de 3,32 en 14 partidos como titular en 2025, antes de que un problema en el codo le obligara a dar por terminada la temporada.
La pregunta es si los Yankees todavía tienen un hueco real en la rotación de titulares para él. Según los registros públicos de contratos, Cole y Rodon tienen contrato hasta 2028 y Fried hasta 2032. Schlittler se ha consolidado como lanzador titular de primera línea, mientras que Warren sigue bajo el control del club. Schmidt podrá acogerse al arbitraje en 2027 y podrá convertirse en agente libre tras esa temporada.
Las reacciones en Internet pasaron rápidamente del domingo al invierno. Los aficionados se preguntaban por la resistencia de Schmidt, cómo encajaría junto a Luis Gil y si los Yankees podrán contar con él para lanzar entradas decisivas en octubre.
Ningún responsable de los Yankees ha dicho que Schmidt no vuelva a ser titular en Nueva York. Pero la profundidad de la rotación, su plazo de recuperación y los planes de los Yankees para la postemporada lo han dejado relegado a un segundo plano, con tantas opciones de titulares que ya no puede seguir siendo tu opción predeterminada.
Los Yankees necesitan que Schmidt demuestre que la transición al bullpen funciona
Por eso es tan importante lo del bíceps, aunque las noticias médicas sigan siendo positivas. Schmidt no está intentando llegar a los 90 lanzamientos. Lo que quiere es demostrar que puede calentar rápido, salir al campo cuando lo necesiten y recuperarse para otra salida.
La transición ya ha dado lugar a dos momentos incómodos. Schmidt calentó el sábado por la noche, pero Boone se decantó por Michael Fulmer en la novena entrada de un partido empatado. Fulmer encajó el jonrón de dos carreras de Pavin Smith que decidió el partido. El domingo, Schmidt estuvo a punto de salir al campo, pero unos calambres se lo impidieron.
Los Yankees tienen un balance de 89-66, a seis partidos del Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, cuando quedan siete partidos por disputar, según la clasificación de la MLB. Ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada y ocupan el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana. Su última semana empieza el martes en el Yankee Stadium contra los Rays.
Si Schmidt pasa la prueba, esos partidos supondrán un reto más sencillo. Su objetivo inmediato ya no es volver a ganarse un puesto en la rotación. Se trata de demostrar a los Yankees que pueden confiar en él en el bullpen cuando empiece octubre.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- It has felt inevitable that the American League East race would be decided this week in the Bronx.
The Rays have led the Majors’ most competitive division for most of the season, and they haven’t ceded the top spot in the standings since reclaiming first place on June 27.
But the Yankees have always been there -- threatening and falling back, perhaps -- but never trailing by enough to diminish the potential importance of this week.
Well, here it is.
The Yankees will host the Rays in a four-game series at Yankee Stadium, beginning with a separate-admission doubleheader on Tuesday. Thanks to the Rays’ terrific homestand and the Yankees’ series loss in Phoenix, the question now is how much longer this race will remain alive.
The Rays arrived in New York holding a six-game lead in the division race with only seven games remaining. One victory by Tampa Bay will eliminate the Yankees from the AL East race and lock them into an AL Wild Card spot. So for the Yankees to have any chance, they must pull off a four-game, three-day sweep.
The stakes? As Gerrit Cole once said, “They’re high.” Let’s dive in.
What’s at stake?
Rays: Winning just one game will guarantee the Rays’ first AL East championship since 2021, giving them a bye through the Wild Card Series and home field advantage in both the AL Division Series and -- if they advance -- the AL Championship Series. They also need just one win to clinch the season series against the Yankees.
Yankees: Manager Aaron Boone acknowledges that it would be a “tall order” to keep the Rays from spraying bubbly in the Bronx, but that’s exactly what they intend to do. They entered the season looking to change the narrative after coming up short in their pursuit of the Blue Jays last year. They’re instead on the verge of settling for another consolation prize and needing to fight through a best-of-three.
How are the starting rotations lined up?
Rays: They will send their two best starters to the mound for Tuesday’s doubleheader. First comes veteran right-hander Nick Martinez, their clubhouse leader and most dependable source of innings. Tampa Bay has a 22-7 record behind Martinez this season. Then comes Drew Rasmussen, one of the AL’s top starters. The Rays haven’t lost one of Rasmussen’s starts since July 9, going a perfect 11-0 in his outings since then. Martinez will be pitching with an extra day of rest, while Rasmussen will be working on four days’ rest for only the seventh time this season. Left-hander Ian Seymour and right-hander Freddy Peralta would be in line to start Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.
Yankees: Carlos Rodón and Max Fried will start the doubleheader, in that order. Both have dealt with injuries this season but are rounding into form at the right time. In three September starts, Rodón is 2-0 with a 2.08 ERA, putting a bout with left elbow inflammation into his rear-view mirror. After twice landing on the injured list with a bone bruise in his pitching elbow, Fried is 1-0 with a 1.69 ERA in three September starts. Cole and AL Cy Young Award frontrunner Cam Schlittler follow in the third and fourth games of the series, respectively.
What has been going well for each team lately?
Rays: Um, everything? The Rays just went 8-1 during their final regular-season homestand, and they’ve won four straight series against the Braves, Astros, A’s and Red Sox. Since getting swept in a four-game series at Fenway Park coming out of the All-Star break, they’ve put together a 39-18 record -- the best in baseball since July 20. Their starting pitching has been particularly strong, with a 2.81 ERA this month that ranks second to only the Yankees. They have found different ways to score runs, as usual, including early rallies like Sunday and a pair of walk-off homers from AL MVP candidate Junior Caminero.
Yankees: These Yanks suddenly find themselves leaning on the strength of their pitching, believing the offense will eventually deliver. Ben Rice cracked his team-leading 39th home run, fulfilling a prediction Boone made in Spring Training. Rice said Boone was teasing him, coming up “one or two” short of his preferred total, so look for Rice to swing for his 40th this week. Austin Wells has hit three homers in his last six games, while Heliot Ramos has homered in his last two games. He could be an important piece if the Yankees are going to make October noise.
What are some areas of concern that could be an issue this week or in the postseason?
Rays: Plenty of Rays have picked up the slack, but leadoff man Yandy Díaz has had a tough month, with a .229/.286/.357 slash line in September. He sets the tone for their lineup, so it’s obviously important for him to be in top form come October. And this is really nitpicking, considering he’s 3-0 with a save and a 1.42 ERA this month, but MLB saves leader Bryan Baker has more walks (four) than strikeouts (two) in seven September appearances. He’ll need to be lights-out in the postseason, too.
Yankees: Other than Aaron Judge’s right calf strain, which the Yankees are treating like a top-secret matter of national importance, there are concerns bubbling about the state of the bullpen. Brent Headrick’s velocity has dipped and he may be showing fatigue after a Major League-leading 79 appearances. Tim Hill hasn’t been the automatic ground-ball machine of years past. Michael Fulmer gave up a game-winning homer in Arizona. But there’s no bigger issue than proving they can win without Judge, the engine around which their offense is built. They are 48-41 without him, compared to 41-25 with him.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Ken Rosenthal drastically misses the mark in Brian Cashman Yankees assessment
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: New York Yankees fans are frustrated. It's been 17 long years since they've enjoyed a parade down the Canyon of Heroes following a World Series victory.
